Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically is essential for visualizing and simulating cellular behaviors in computer graphics. However, creating accurate and efficient cell shape models is a challenging task, especially considering the complex cell morphology. Traditionally, this has been handled by using voxel-based systems or complex polygon meshes; however, these methods often require significant resources and still fail to capture fine cellular structures accurately. Our proposed approach leverages level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes efficiently. By utilizing level sets, we can easily combine multiple signed distance functions, facilitating the modeling of diverse cell types from different species. Our system generates compact, implicit cell shape representations that facilitate real-time visualization and support various computer graphics applications, such as cell shape synthesis and cell-based visualization. Furthermore, we develop an autoencoders-based method to utilize large, publicly accessible datasets for learning and synthesizing cell shapes. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in modeling implicit cell shapes through comprehensive visualization, performance testing, and applications in microorganisms and cancer cells. By utilizing level sets of signed distance functions, we can reduce storage requirements significantly (e.g., from 1.2 GB to 25 MB) while providing comparable visualization performance to voxel-based systems. Our source code will be publicly available for further research and development. The synthesized cell shapes can be accessed through an online interface, allowing researchers to generate new implicit cell shape representations based on existing cells. Our study highlights the potential of utilizing level sets of signed distance functions to model complex cell shapes efficiently. Implicit representation can be a valuable option for various cell shape modeling applications. Our approach may also be expanded to model other complex organic structures by combining multiple signed distance functions. The understanding and recreation of complex cell morphology can be beneficial not only for cell-based visualization but also for various therapeutic applications and bioinformatics analyses. Ultimately, our research aims to increase awareness about the importance of visualization in understanding cells and the need for accurate, implicit cell shape representations. The faster, real-time implicit cell shape modeling can facilitate a broader range of applications and knowledge about cells. Our approach may also inspire the creation of educational tools and resources that highlight the importance of cell shape modeling and visualization in understanding cells. Our method can be applied effectively to model complex cell morphology with the potential to expand therapeutic options, provide accurate bioinformatics analyses, and facilitate cell-based visualization. The large dataset used in our research can be utilized to understand cell morphology through implicit representation, facilitating accurate modeling and visualization of cells. Our approach may also be applied to model implicit representations of organ shapes as well as cellular microstructures

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, backlinks, and transclusions. While access technologies have effectively enabled individuals to engage with referenced content in digital forms, such content often goes unnoticed or overlooked when presented in print. As a result, individuals with vision disabilities are forced to manually locate the referenced materials, a time-consuming task that makes reading even more challenging. In order to address this issue, we have devised a innovative solution that leverages the application of Semantic Scholia, a visual representation model of knowledge built upon Wikidata, to automatically identify and provide access to referenced content in printed materials through a customized reading order. This concept may also have broader implications in facilitating the inclusion of reference information in diverse types of text and media. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of our solution, we conducted an experiment with a group of blind participants, demonstrating that our approach successfully enabled them to access referenced content in printed materials efficiently and efficiently facilitated the reading process. Additionally, the results of the study indicate a significant boost in reading speed among the blind participants. This paper outlines the underlying technical aspects and presents the findings of the study. Furthermore, we have established a partnership with Wikidata and Wikisource to ensure that our work aligns with their existing knowledge graphs. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to promote the inclusion of reference information in digital and printed materials while promoting accessibility for individuals with vision disabilities. Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. Its low mass and the presence of fluids against its body cause movement dynamics where speed increases as the speed of the waves approaches the speed of the waves along its body. Furthermore, we found that the centipede's movement dynamics can be explained using the framework for how fish move, taking into account the force of the water and the movement pattern of the waves along its body. Nevertheless, when we looked at the movement patterns of the centipede, we noticed they didn't match the predictions based on this framework. The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately model tsunami behavior that is affected by dispersal over long periods. Dispersive models are crucial in situations such as a massive ocean impact from an asteroid, and they are also essential in modeling complex events where basic shallow water equations fall short. High-resolution simulations that incorporate time-varying dispersive effects and spatially distributed inertia and friction are the key to an accurate model. However, achieving such high resolution in real-time simulations on standard hardware proves to be a significant challenge. In this project, we are focusing on efficiently speeding up hydrostatic nonlinear terms, developing a parallel algorithm that incorporates adaptive mesh refinement, and creating a legislative framework to guide the implementation of a fully accurate spatially varying dispersive model. Furthermore, we are collaborating with coastal researchers to develop a new approach for solving local friction using the Boussinesq model. Our simulation tool, dubbed SUSA-Tsunami, is an EF0-based parallel algorithm that incorporates adaptive mesh refinement and can model various tsunami scenarios with high spatial and temporal resolution. One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details the results of a novel quantum sensor experiment aimed at detecting dark matter particles utilizing three key candidates: fermions, scalars, and vectors. Envisaging a future spacecraft-equipped fermion-detecting quantum sensor, a study was conducted involving a 100-mK-cooled silicon photonic quantum circuit in the laboratory. Despite the laboratory detection limit exceeding the expected spacecraft detection limit, the experiment laid the groundwork for the next quantum sensor generation, which will have the capability to test the interplay between dark matter and ordinary matter. Furthermore, a simulation-based analysis was performed to evaluate the potential of a silicon-nanophw platform in a 3-year space flight to detect scalar dark matter with masses up to 10 GeV/c^2. The results showed that, under optimal conditions, the quantum sensor will have the capability to rule out the majority of dark matter theories involving scalar fermions. Ultimately, the integration of this quantum sensor technology with future space flights could significantly contribute to our understanding of dark matter. We derived statistical models of AGN polarization properties based on their optical brightness and angular sizes. We observed a lower bound for the polarization of sources smaller than 5 inches at 10 percent, with a steep decline in this metric as the diameter increases. We explored scale-dependent patterns of AGN polarization and considered the impact of this phenomenon on future cosmology experiments. We calculated the frequency of highly polarized AGN radio sources, finding them to be less common at lower frequencies and weaker optical brightness. The polarization of these sources could potentially hide cold cosmic dust polarization observed during cosmology experiments. We calculated an upper estimate for the dust polarization depression rate resulting from AGN interference, revealing minimal impact on sources larger than 5 inches; however, this effect might significantly affect dust polarization observations at smaller diameters, potentially reducing the signal by as much as 0.1 percent to 1 percent, depending on frequency. We analyzed how the orientation of magnetic fields, electric fields, and polarization change within AGN radio sources and their relationship with optical luminosity, identifying the importance of seed magnetic fields in their formation. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large parallel walls at a temperature $T$, where the plate's area is $A$ and the distance between the walls is $d$. We utilize the Casimir mechanism to investigate the radiation's statistical properties within this specific geometry and demonstrate that $N$ emitted photons exhibit unusual thermodynamic characteristics. Notably, at low temperatures, these characteristics are vastly dissimilar to those of an ideal photon gas for $N$ photons; however, as the temperature increases towards absolute zero, these characteristics converge with the expected behavior. Notably, utilizing the Casimir mechanism, we derive the statistical properties of $N$ photons without needing the traditional Planck distribution. Additionally, we derive the first-order critical phase transitions occurring within this system. Specifically, we show that the radiation behavior can undergo a phase transition from three-dimensional to two-dimensional at a temperature $T_* = \frac{\hbar d}{2\pi\sqrt{ABC}}$, where $C$ is the plate's curvature, and $B$ is the plate's width, and this transition is triggered by the plate's curvature. Notably, we also demonstrate a phase transition from $N$ to $N-1$ photons within this specific geometry, which can occur under specific conditions. This paper explores the phenomenon through analytical means, providing a complementary understanding via numerical simulations. Lastly, we define an area, denoted by $A_{N}$, within the phase diagram that characterizes the number of photons emitted by the plate. Notably, we show that the area factor, given by the ratio of $A_{N}$ for $N$ photons and $A_{N-1}$ for $N-1$ photons$, is always equal to $N$. Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework leads to an algorithm utilizing an additive Gaussian noise approach to maintain privacy, with an integrated noise generation process involving the optimization of an convex parabola under constraints. Following a formal proof of its bounds ensuring desired privacy levels, we test our algorithm on simulated data highlighting its potential as a new technique for handling dependent data privacy. Our approach, with minor modifications, can also achieve an additive noise disclosure mechanism for safeguarding sensitive data, particularly useful for spatial applications. Furthermore, we adapt this technique to meet stringent privacy demands, such as advanced protection for highly confidential data or metadata protection in advanced encryption methods. This adaptation involves incorporating additional constraints and efficient solvers to improve its efficiency and allow its application in more complex scenarios. The source code for this algorithm can be found at the code repository location. This research breaks new ground in bounding R\'enyi divergence privacy losses for dependent data sets and introduces an additive noise disclosure method, accompanied by an algorithm explaining its mechanics along with its potential uses and limitations. The study also highlights its potential applications in safeguarding data involved in the simulation of source code malware by manipulating the memory of a computer and protecting sensitive information on social media, particularly images and video. This research contributes to the field by defining the challenges and potential solutions to privacy issues related to location-based services in urban environments and outlining the steps to follow when privacy is deemed a priority. Furthermore, the concept of differential privacy enables the calculation of relative privacy levels between different data sets and between various service providers, measured in relative R\'enyi divergence. A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to build a sparse 3D grid map from a 3D point cloud. Distinguishing itself from conventional top-down image matching techniques, the proposed approach leverages a transformed 3D grid map suitable for deep learning and convolutional networks. An assessment against a substantial dataset derived from the SunCG dataset demonstrated the superiority of the NDT-Transformer method over existing benchmarks. Furthermore, the methodology exhibited exceptional performance in an actual testing environment at the Krefeld Tech campus, with a 93.10% recall rate, an F1-score of 92.34, and average precisions of 92.34%. Building upon the NDT-Transformer approach, the incorporation of multi-sensor fusion, enhanced 3D representation, and advanced deep learning models holds significant potential for further advancements. Recent years have seen an increase in language useages among younger populations, particularly in code-mixed languages like code-mixting English and Hindi in India. However, data preparation challenges, such as words consisting of letters from multiple scripts and mixed language use in the same sentence, make it difficult to hold language model training sessions. We tackle these obstacles by utilizing the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) to develop embeddings for individual words in English and Hindi in parallel. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach under real-world conditions, leveraging a large dataset of sentences from the Krishi Mobile Project to prove its robustness and scalability. We also successfully integrate USE with a neural machine translation model to produce high-quality translation memories. Notably, USE outperformed or closely matched the performance of FastText and Word2Vec on various metrics, all while processing at a scale that far superseded that of the aforementioned models. USE's superior performance, speed, and ability to operate seamlessly across script variations make it an ideal choice for training neural machine translation models and other language model applications that require data at a massive scale. We make USE available for download as an open-source tool. We also release the trained English and Hindi embeddings publicly to support research and other language-based projects. Furthermore, USE supports the training of embeddings for other languages written in the Devanagari script, such as Marathi and Nepali. We publish our research findings as a paper at the 53rd Annual Conference of the Association for Computational Machinery on Language.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or where environmental maps become obsolete due to sudden changes like traffic congestion, roadblocks, or construction. Triangulation-based methods offer an alternative solution, but their limitations are significant. In this research, we introduce 'n-ary Road Network Structure' as a data structure to generate spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms traditional triangulation-based methods, significantly reduces computational time and, most importantly, enables motion planning without relying on pre-compiled maps. Moreover, we showcase the flexibility of this technique by integrating it with two distinct motion planners: an edge road network planner and a node road network planner. Our proposed algorithm is thoroughly tested on a scene-based benchmark and real-world datasets, including the KITTI dataset. These experiments reveal its robust performance in environments with up to 85% occlusion, as well as its capacity to handle various types of road structures. The code and dataset associated with this research are available for download at the link: https://github.com/asharari/Arnos.git. Furthermore, this work can be viewed as a significant advancement towards transforming static maps to dynamic maps, a concept previously proposed in a paper titled 'Transforming Static Maps to Dynamic Maps', published in the Journal of Intelligent Robotics and Systems. In this study, we first identified the issue of map aging as a type of dynamic map change problem and established its relevance to the robotics community. Interestingly, this problem is different from typical dynamic map change issues, such as environment changes, as it specifically targets the evolution of navigation spatial boundaries in terms of feasibility. Consequently, we investigated an isolated case where the feasibility of navigation spatial boundaries changes and proposed a solution. Here, we present an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments, an area that complements our previous work on the dynamic map change problem. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed map. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful applications to both simulated and real-world scenarios. Results indicate a significant $4-5$ cm improvement in pose estimation accuracy compared to a standard point-cloud baseline. Furthermore, this technique has been successfully applied to an autonomous robot navigating an outdoor tunnel, utilizing only a single monocular camera. By integrating this method with induction loop measurements, a $95\%$ global consistency rate was achieved along with $85\%$ accuracy when comparing estimated camera poses to ground truth. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve C can be parameterized by a weighted set of piecewise linear functions on C's complement. Furthermore, if the curve is complete, this parameterization extends to the complete rational function semifield. Although this characterization was previously established for specific cases, its present form is more versatile and serves as a foundation for further generalizations, including treatments of tropical varieties and tropical cycles. The proof relies on a detailed analysis of the weighted linear functional framework and employs a novel application of a classical linear programming result due to Carath\'{e}odory. Additionally, this result has been incorporated into the established Berkovich tangent-tangent theorem as a means of illustrating its connection to the study of tropical varieties. With this result, the following Berkovich tangent-tangent theorem can be proven, expressing the finite rational function semifield of a tropical curve as a set of solutions to a system of linear equations: Let C be a complete tropical curve with n independent markings, and let K be its underlying tropical semifield. Then, the rational function semifield C(R) can be expressed as the set of solutions to a system of linear equations of the form f = ∑_{i=1, j=1} a_{i,j} x_i y_j, where a_{i,j} are rational numbers and x_i, y_j are independent markings of C, for i,j in the range 1 to n. Furthermore, this linear system has the property that for any fixed i, the corresponding f(i,y) are distinct for distinct y, or can be made distinct through a change of coordinates, and x^2 = 0 is not a solution when i=1. The parameterization of the rational function semifield of a tropical curve by weighted piecewise linear functions extends to the complete rational function semifield of its complement. The relationship between superconductivity and density of states in iron-based superconductors is studied, focusing on LiFeAs and optimizing the parameter for its superconducting transition at 18K. Utilizing different bandwidths in the model, we evaluate whether experimental DOS in LiFeAs is adequately reproduced. However, we encounter difficulties in replicating the observed ratio between the superconducting gap and the normal state gap, especially when considering spin-double-occupancy in doped compounds. Two approaches to account for this issue are then presented: (i) by taking into consideration spin-fluctuation effects that impact the superconducting gap, and (ii) by accounting for spin-triplet pairing contribution to the density of states. Subsequently, we investigate superconducting properties in optimal and low-doped regimes for two scenarios: weak spin-fluctuation effects and a prominent spin-triplet component. In the optimal superconducting regime, we identify a broad gap with average values of 6.0 meV and 3.4 meV for its peak height and position, respectively. Additionally, we find that the optimal superconducting phase exhibits a finite superfluid density at the Fermi level. In contrast, a low-doped compound presents a dual-gap feature with 4.1 meV and 2.3 meV for its gap heights and positions, respectively. Furthermore, we observe a significant superfluid density at the Fermi level in this specific superconducting regime. In the scenario with a prominent spin-triplet component, we identify a broad gap with average values of 6.4 meV and 3.9 meV for its peak height and position, respectively. Notably, our findings indicate that spin-triplet pairing provides an adequate explanation for replicating the observed relationship between the superconducting gap and normal state gap in iron-based superconductors, including in low-doped compounds. Finally, we find that the spin-triplet component is crucial for understanding the superconducting properties in iron-based superconductors. In particular, the scenario with a significant spin-triplet component is capable of explaining two-gap features in doped compounds, including in optimal and low-doped Fe-based superconductors. In this context, our findings are complementary to those presented in a recent study on spin-triplet pairing in Fe-based superconductors, including in a comparative study on the superconducting properties of the electron-doped compound BaFe1-xNaxAs2. We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal strategies for enhancing spontaneous assembly processes, based solely on the desired end properties and specified structural characteristics, and not relying on intricate detail design. This approach enables the rapid development of optimized particles for specific color production in linear chains, even in the presence of environmental disruptions. Furthermore, it allows the discovery of strategies for producing specific geometric patterns through mass assembly. These locally acting particle dynamics and temporal control strategies significantly facilitate the production of intricate structures. Additionally, we find that both particle properties and temporal control methods evolve in response to environmental influences. Finally, we explore the design of complex systems using a microfluidics-based protocol to create multiphase hybrid particles and demonstrate its potential in enhancing color production. However, it was discovered that detailed structural characteristics are often lost during the evolution process. To mitigate this, we propose incorporating a set of fundamental building blocks or a structural template to facilitate design, and showcase its effectiveness using a simplified spiral motif. This approach involves initially training particles to produce a model structure, then refining their design by combining the learned principles with a structural template, leading to the formation of the desired spiral pattern. Utilizing a simplified template-based design method allows for the production of particles that can create intricate structures, even when traditional design methods fail, due to the ability to focus on particle properties rather than specific geometry. The proposed template-based microfluidics protocol provides a promising solution to this challenge. The integration of neuroevolutionary learning, self-assembly, and microfluidics technologies opens up new avenues for the design of hybrid materials and their potential applications, and sheds light on their dynamics and behavior. By leveraging these technologies, we can uncover new information about hybrid materials and their interactions at the nanoscale. At present, the complexity of simulating these systems hampers in silico research. Nevertheless, future advancements in high-performance computing, hybrid algorithms, and abstracted modeling will facilitate a deeper understanding of nanoscale interactions and enable more sophisticated virtual assessments of materials and devices. This, in turn, will accelerate the discovery of properties and functionalities of hybrid materials and their exploitation in diverse applications and technologies. Ultimately, this research may contribute to the development of new technologies for data storage, energy harvesting, and other fields by revealing the unexplored potential of nanoscale interactions. Our research appears to suggest that certain chiral gauge theories, like QCD, might have a dynamical-Higgs-phase scenario, in which the theory's symmetry group is significantly expanded. This could lead to an infinitely large symmetry group. We have begun exploring how this phase might transition into the standard chiral phase found in theories with weak symmetry breaking. Since this transition likely involves significant changes to the theory's topology, our approach builds on a theory proposed by Atiyah and Manton in 1996. Although the theory is largely unexplored, previous studies by Manton and Rubinstein in 1999 and by Han and Amelino-Camerini in 2018 did investigate the transition from the dynamical-Higgs-phase scenario into the chiral phase. Our own analysis focuses on the topological transition and its potential methods for detection in real-world particle physics experiments. Two possible approaches for detecting this transition have been identified: one, in which monopoles become massless, is similar to a phenomenon observed in the color-electric phase of heavy-quark antigluon systems. Another, more global approach involves changes in the topological properties of the gauge theory's configuration space. Since these changes would result in significant increases or decreases in the theory's and related spaces' homotopy groups, they could be detected through an extensive analysis of experimental data. Experimental detection of this transition might be challenging, but it could be a key discovery that unlocks a deeper understanding of particle physics. Since this transition might be detected through an analysis of the entire energy spectrum of the particles, it could be identified at high-energy particle colliders such as the LHC. A related problem involves determining whether an imaginary part can exist in the axial coupling constant in certain heavy-quark antigluon systems. This problem is significant because an imaginary part in the axial coupling constant would have major implications for our understanding of strong symmetry breaking and the theory of chiral gauge theories. This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing open question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between the output solution u and initial condition u0, focusing on whether this remains stable in high dimensions. Our results demonstrate that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation is indeed stable in very high dimensions, with certain output conditions, for dimensions d of 3 or more and initial conditions u0 within a specific measure of L1. Conversely, we show that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation will become unstable in such high dimensions, with ordinary output conditions, for dimensions d of 3 or more and initial conditions u0 within a specific measure of L1. Relatedly, we prove a similar result for the family of equations studied by Wu and Zhang in 2017. Furthermore, we prove that the stationary Euler equation remains stable in all dimensions, with certain output conditions, for initial conditions u0 within a specific measure of L1. Our results combine analytical techniques from classical fluid dynamics studies with geometric techniques from the study of the outside environment by Wu and Zhang in 2017, and incorporate the use of a spectral framework developed by Tsurumi in 2019. This research introduces two security enhancements for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem to make it resistant to various attacks. By incorporating a symmetric encoding process using the Gabidulin matrix, and employing a modified public key verification method through a random challenge, it offers improved security against structural attacks. The first modification is inspired by McEliece, while the second adaptation is influenced by Lin and Snyder. The proposed system combines these modifications to achieve public-key encryption. We evaluate the performance of three different versions of the modified system, termed GLMS, SLG, and SLN, in terms of their public key sizes, computational overhead, and resistance to attacks. The results show that GLMS and SLG offer comparable performance under structural attacks, but differ in their resistance to information-set decoding attacks. Additionally, we investigate the potential for passive attacks on SLG and SLN, and find that such attacks are feasible yet costly, allowing both systems to remain secure against active attacks. We conclude that both modifications contribute significantly to enhancing the security of Loidreau's cryptosystem, making it suitable for practical applications due to its moderate key sizes and computational burden. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the modified algorithms in fingerprint verification, allowing for practical implementation using conventional hardware, and show that the fingerprinted version of SLG remains secure against state-of-the-art attacks. The proposed versions of Loidreau's cryptosystem, along with their associated algorithms and performance evaluations, have been made publicly available on GitHub. Specifically, the versions presented here exhibit a public key size of approximately 256 kilobits, with a computational overhead during encryption and decryption of about 0.32 and 0.45 milliseonds per bit, respectively. We anticipate that future improvements in hardware capabilities will further decrease the computational burden of these algorithms. Furthermore, we have verified that the modified versions of Loidreau's cryptosystem successfully resist passive attacks, with an estimated computational cost for an attacker exceeding $2^{55.2}$ bit operations. We have similarly validated the resistance of SLG to active attacks involving side-channel attacks, with an estimated cost exceeding $2^{53.2}$ bit operations. In accordance with our findings, we have applied the name Generalized Loidreau McEliece Snyder (GLMS) to the modified cryptosystem incorporating both security enhancements. scarcity conditions. In horizontal federated learning, multiple institutions collaborate on joint training, sharing processed, aggregated data. In contrast, vertical federated learning, also known as federated record linkage, facilitates data analysis by partnering institutions, where each contributes anonymous attribute values, but retains the corresponding identifiers. Our focus lies in enhancing the privacy of vertical federated learning, specifically record linkage, as we analyze the privacy risks and introduce a secure algorithm to achieve privacy in this context. This algorithm utilizes blockchain technology, heterogeneous federated learning, and a consensus mechanism involving hypernetworks, providing a secure and trustworthy data sharing system. First, we leverage noise injection and randomized encoding to protect individual data, then encrypt it for greater security. Next, we combine these approaches with a secure algorithm for computing attribute combinations, while distributing this computation among participating institutions. Their shared, encrypted results allow for reliable data analysis without compromising individual data confidentiality. This approach enables accurate data analysis in this context, relying on participants' adherence to the proposed protocol, and incorporates a mechanism for detecting potential data breaches. As such, it offers superior security, particularly against well-informed adversaries, through the use of quantum-resistant cryptography and distributed consensus mechanisms. Furthermore, all computations involved in vertical federated learning are proven to be private, given perfect network performance; and when considering the limitations of this context, such as network instability and delayed communications, our proposed system still offers superior privacy guarantees, particularly when compared to existing approaches that rely on randomized encoding and distributed computations. This evaluation highlights that current algorithms may fall short in ensuring data privacy, particularly in this context, and emphasizes the significance of integrating secure, distributed consensus mechanisms to achieve data privacy in vertical federated learning. Experimental results show the proposed system's effectiveness in ensuring data privacy through various network performance simulations. This approach demonstrates the proposed system's potential for achieving data privacy in vertical federated learning, and its general applicability to other data privacy-related challenges. To address this challenge, this study develops a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the interactions and resource allocations between agencies when faced with terrorist attacks on both physical and cyber-social targets. The proposed model, Smart City Defense Game, considers the interactions among three types of players: defensive agencies with limited resources, terrorist groups with unknown intentions and unpredictable attack frequencies, and intelligent social entities influenced by peer pressure. The model consists of two sub-game theories: one for agencies allocating resources and another for determining the target probability of attack. The analysis of this game reveals three possible outcomes, with the infeasible outcome of all layers being destroyed a la Titanising, and two viable outcomes where agencies successfully defend most Smart City layers and terrorist groups adjust their strategies according to agency investments. Building on this model, a multi-layered, multi-stratum game-theoretic model is proposed to address counter-terrorism investments, with each agency investing in three levels of defense: direct protection, cyber countermeasures, and social influence. The optimization of this model leads to increased investments and improved social influence among agencies when resources become redundant. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the practicality and feasibility of the proposed models and models parameters. Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model.  They considered these black holes within a large empty sphere of radius $r_B$, incorporating pressure in this model.  Investigating the thermodynamic properties of these black holes, they found a phase transition occurs between the black holes and the surrounding expanded space, occurring when temperature and pressure conditions are met.  Further analyzing the thermodynamic properties of these black holes, they discovered that Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes exhibit isothermal first-order phase transitions under specified pressure requirements.  Additionally, they found that the phase transition temperature and pressure of these black holes are determined by $r_B$, indicating a relationship between these thermodynamic properties and the expanded space's model.  When the radius of the expanded space is 2 times the radius of the black hole, pressure conditions allow for phase transitions, whereas charged black holes do not exhibit such phase transitions due to their electric pressures exceeding this threshold pressure under a critical radius condition.  Finally, comparing thermodynamic properties of these black holes, researchers found that the differences in thermodynamic properties, such as entropy and temperature, increase as the radius of the black hole increases for both Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes.  These findings imply a relationship between thermodynamic properties and the expanded space's model.  Applying this knowledge, researchers estimated a value for the expanded space's model's radius.  They determined the accuracy of their estimate remains uncertain and is dependent on further estimation efforts.  In conclusion, researchers explored novel methods for estimating expanded space model parameters through black hole thermodynamics. We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two covariant isobar models were employed to simulate this process, with the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians adopted from existing works. Model parameters, such as coupling constants and form factor cutoffs, were obtained by comparing calculated cross sections with experimental data on total and differential cross sections, initial-state radiation, and beam asymmetry. Including these resonances significantly improved the fit to experimental data, particularly on cross sections and beam asymmetry for a sulphur target. Additionally, we found that including certain high-spin resonances improved the resonance structure of calculated cross sections. We have also calculated other observables, such as the hyperonic decay contribution to the beam asymmetry and single-polarization cross section, demonstrating the potential for new experimental measurements to constrain the formalism effectively for high-spin resonances. However, we did not consider decay widths for resonances as form factors, instead fixing them based on present knowledge. Including proposed high-spin resonances enhanced the total cross section, specifically the $K^+ \gamma p \to K^+$ process, with significant high-spin contributions evident from energy constraints obtained from experimental data. Notably, we found high-spin resonance decay widths into $K^+\pi^+$ or $K^+\eta$ are generally lower than those of well-known resonances such as the $\Sigma(1385)$ and $\Sigma^*(1385)$ and $\Delta(1232)$. This suggests high-spin resonances may also decay to $K^+\pi^-$ or $K^+\pi^+$, with widths potentially higher than those for $K^+\pi^+$. Consequently, future experiments on kaon photoproduction, particularly off nucleons and nuclei, are recommended to probe high-spin resonance structure and decay properties. Furthermore, we found our models of in-medium high-spin resonances, calculated using the high-spin resonance density of states with increased width at the center of the spectrum in comparison to the free case, with some near the future spectrum threshold. However, we found that high-spin resonances in the region $p_\mu \sim 400$ MeV/c could exist under nuclear conditions. In contrast, we found no high-spin resonances that could exist both under free and in-medium conditions. This research is an initial exploration into the potential influence of high-spin resonances on particle production in dense nuclear matter and can serve as a foundation for future studies

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, including the 'leader-follower' and 'ring' models, to define distance limits based on estimated and actual vehicle positions, respectively. In the 'leader-follower' scenario, the lead vehicle acts as a reference point for following vehicles, while in the 'ring' arrangement, vehicles lack this reference, making distance control more complicated. To address this challenge, the study proposes a two-player differential game where the lead vehicle sets its distance based on follower estimates, and following vehicles optimize their positions by taking into account the varying estimates. This approach results in a stable equilibrium where the lead vehicle controls the distance between vehicles. For the 'ring' arrangement, this result is further refined by considering the limits on vehicle communication, leading to a comprehensive analysis of the conditions necessary for stable operation. This study provides explicit formulas for the maximum allowed communication latency and the corresponding minimum sampling rate required to maintain stable vehicle platoons. Notably, the study demonstrates that a minimum sampling rate inevitably has a lower bound that depends on the number of vehicles in the platoon. Furthermore, the study proposes an adaptive feedback control strategy based on the estimates generated by the differential game, and verifies its effectiveness through simulations, including a comparison with existing control methods. Simulation results demonstrate the potential for improved communication efficiency with reduced sampling rates compared to conventional approaches, and show that the proposed strategy can maintain a stable distance between vehicles under conditions of variable communication latency and noise. These features make the proposed approach suitable for diverse applications, including autonomous driving. Simulation examples illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, highlighting its potential for real-world application in vehicle platooning. Building upon this foundation, the study explores the application of the proposed differential game and control strategy to a broader range of interconnected vehicle systems, including autonomous driving. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. If the data is distributed, communication occurs to transfer data to the process owning the model. This paper proposes a method to minimize communication during SGD by synchronizing updates instead of exchanging data. This Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) technique requires no initial data transfer when the data is distributed. Experimental comparisons between CA-SGD and optimized SGD implementations confirm that it significantly outperforms the latter, especially when the data size surpasses the number of involved processes. This makes CA-SYD an attractive choice for large-scale parallel machine learning applications. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating a batch size into the communication-avoiding approach can balance the trade-off between computation speed and communication overhead. This motivates the design of an Asynchronous Parallel SGD framework, which applies the batched CA-SGD principle, successfully achieving performance improvements on a distributed cluster with distributed data. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the communication overhead in SGD, represented through the communication time model, confirms the advantages of CA-SGD. This research concludes that CA-SGD and its batched variant are applicable and beneficial in various real-world parallel computing environments, encompassing clusters, supercomputers, and big data processing systems. These methods also show potential in emerging multi- accelerator environments where data communication may cause energy consumption, heat, and thermal dissipation. Existing SGD optimizations, such as data compression and quantization, are compatible with CA-SGD, providing additional opportunities for further research. Finally, this research highlights the potential of the communication time model in forecasting the communication efficiency of different parallel algorithms and helps designers utilize parallel computing resources more effectively. From an implementation perspective, CA-SGD is compatible with a wide range of open iterative optimization libraries, such as MADLib, the Distributed Machine Learning Platform, the C++ Eigen Library, and the TensorFlow environment, at no additional development cost. Implementing the batched strategy requires a modified approach in the optimization library, which can be easily achieved through attaching a batched parallel SGD operator to the relevant parallel computing environment. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy on a distributed cluster with distributed data. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis, yet it has shortcomings. On one hand, the approach provides thorough risk analysis but falls short in supplying accurate expected returns. Generative Adversarial Networks, specifically the Conditional GAN model, have demonstrated potential in generating reliable expected returns based on historical time series data, thereby facilitating portfolio analysis that incorporates both risk and return. Nonetheless, the model is hindered by its limitations - it is incapable of handling missing stock values and is highly dependent on current conditions. In light of this, a novel Generative Conditional Autoencoders network model has been proposed that focuses on generating future expected returns based on incomplete and dynamic market situations. In testing the model's efficacy, a 12-year historical analysis was conducted on 21 major US stocks. When compared to the existing approaches, the proposed model delivered exceptional results, successfully generating less information loss-governing metrics KLL, RE, and JS, while outperforming the competition in risk analysis, as measured by annual portfolio return volatility. Furthermore, the model's generated expected returns were found to be more accurate, as reflected in the slight enhancement of the Markowitz framework's Sharpe ratio. In practical applications, the model's ability to handle time series with substantial gaps and drifter noise is particularly valuable for analysis of historical data from emerging markets or time periods characterized by significant events and market distortions. Additionally, the model can be adapted and easily integrated into existing backtesting systems for investment algorithms. A demonstrated case in point is analyzing 21 major US stocks over the 12-year period. In this study, the model's generated expected returns based on incomplete and dynamic market situations outperformed the competition, as reflected in the slightly higher Sharpe ratio of the Markowitz framework. Moreover, the model's efficacy was further validated through an examination of the generated expected returns on the largest 20 US stocks over the 12-year period, as against three traditional approaches. In practice, the model can be seamlessly integrated into existing systems, as exemplified by its successful integration into a live investment backtesting system, as illustrated in the accompanying video. In conclusion, the proposed model delivers superior performance, as measured by KLL, RE, JS, risk analysis, and Sharpe ratio - all key indicators of portfolio return analysis, and therefore has substantial real-world implications and applications. A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. In contrast to traditional dense neural networks, Bayesian neural networks yield a dependable estimation of the network's prediction accuracy. The study investigates the similarities between conventional and Bayesian neural networks, along with the effect of data augmentation. It is discovered that Bayesian neural networks are ideal for classifying tasks reliant on limited and uneven datasets, producing reliable results. The outcomes of this classification are instrumental in informing studies on blazar population dynamics, aiding in refining blazar luminosity function constraints, and guiding future observational endeavors. The classification results are accessible through a user-friendly online portal.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 380 social media users and interviewing 15 of them, to explore 
their views on sharing and consuming content when using different media formats. 
Through analysis, we uncovered the motivations, challenges, and preferences that 
drive users to engage in multimedia sharing on social networking platforms. Our 
keyfinding shows that users tend to favor sharing content when it is presented in 
a format that is easy to understand. Here, we present the outcomes of our study 
and highlight key implications for social media platform designers, with a goal of 
creating more inclusive online environments that reach a broader user base. 
Ultimately, this aims to foster a more inclusive type of engagement that 
encompasses a diverse range of users. The research paper can be found at:

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can be problematic, especially when information is lost due to the discrete nature of data collection. Our R code focuses on utilizing continuous time in MMRM analysis by incorporating a Bayesian approach with BMAwgt functions. We suggest a weighted Bayesian model where weights based on collection frequencies reassemble the collected data into a continuous curve. The weighted data is then analyzed as before, producing estimates analogous to those from the traditional method. Our solution enables the recovery of the mean trajectory under certain conditions and is available in our R package bAlzheimers through the bAlzheimers package. The package can be installed via drat, with the necessary code copied from the drat repository. Our analysis reveals comparable results between the proposed method and the standard procedure. Nevertheless, the weighted approach exhibits certain desirable properties and offers a clear and transparent way to incorporate data collection frequencies into analysis, particularly when time is measured continuously. Our code allows users to specify frequency weights in accordance with data collection rules, even condensing the analysis process. Furthermore, the unweighted and weighted analyses can be compared to gauge the impact of this conversion on inferences and conclusions. The proposed method can potentially enhance the analysis of continuous time data from clinical trials. Our code can be accessed online through the package repository. In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy by using distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk to create more robust navigation, given that each robot's movements are influenced by various factors such as speed and orientation. By utilizing a deep learning approach with the risk-averaged distributionally robust safety gauge, our method proves to be more effective than existing methods, particularly in optimizing collision-avoidance during the 3D trajectory planning of multi-robot systems. Through simulation testing of high-intensity flight maneuvers, our method exhibits better performance in navigating safely and efficiently, when compared to methods based on empirical distributions, actual trajectories, and 3D point cloud analysis. Multi-robot scenarios have been used to validate the robustness of our approach, with significant results demonstrated in autonomous drone flight missions. With the incorporation of distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk, our method successfully reduces collision risk by up to 30% when compared to the safest trajectory, thus providing a more robust and adaptive solution for multi-robot systems. By employing feature maps from variational autoencoders, our method has achieved state-of-the-art performance in multiple benchmarks, encompassing 3D trajectory planning and top-down navigation. At its core, our method resolves the uncertainty-related collision risk by leveraging deep learning to approximate risk gauge values, which has resulted in our method outperforming previous approaches by 30% in safe navigation, with minimal impact on overall efficiency. In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by grant-free access. However, interference from neighboring cell transmissions poses a significant challenge, rendering reliable data decoding impossible. We present a proposed technique that secures low-latency, low-complexity connections for mMTC users through grant-free access. Initially, individual user transmitters modify their transmission power to ensure a set signal-to-interference ratio, then employ discrete Fourier transform and frequency peak detection to facilitate reliable data decoding via an orthogonal variational reconstruction technique. Results confirm our method's superior performance compared to the standard sequence-hashing approach. Furthermore, we validate the practical effectiveness of our method by simulating its real-world performance under actual neighboring cell MIMO broadcast transmissions. The findings show our method's ability to provide reliable data decoding even when the channel estimation is partially accurate and neighboring cell MIMO broadcast transmissions are in operation. The proposed technique's low complexity and high reliability make it suitable for application across various mMTC scenarios. Such an access structure is termed 'universal' and can be fully visualized through a forest of paths that represent all qualified subsets, essentially defining the access structure in its most detailed form. This study delves into secret sharing schemes featuring an universal access structure and generally develops a detailed description using trees, paths, and nodes. It starts by examining specific cases - the access structure having two minimal qualified subsets - and derives a comprehensive classification based on the lengths of these subsets. Progressively, the research considers more general access structures with multiple and varied subset lengths, utilizing distinct methodologies to achieve this. Notably, the study introduces a novel method of constructing secret sharing schemes that involves selecting specific nodes from a universal access structure and defining a shared secret based on these choices. This approach is shown to work efficiently in nearly all examined cases, with exceptions identified and explained. Additionally, the research analyzes and compares secret sharing schemes with universal access structures and compares their performance in terms of efficiency. Finally, the study examines and resolves open questions regarding certain access structures with specific subset length patterns, and proposes further exploration into related areas. Some universal access structures were found to lack suitable schemes, leaving their properties and potential applications for future investigation. The research successfully answers the first query for the access structure structures D(n, k) with k >= (n/3) + 1, and presents a partially positive response to the second query. This study specifically identifies conditions under which scheme existence is certain and likely. In the process, the study raises several new questions regarding the determination of scheme existence for the access structure D(8, 3) and prompts further research into this area. Ultimately, the study highlights the need for continued exploration into universal access structures with minimal scheme existence probability, exemplified through the case of access structure D(8, 3). The long-standing problem of current dissipation in plasma turbulence is addressed. 
Plasma turbulence in the sub-ion scale range has been found to contain localized structures called
bubbles that migrate and move in opposite directions, carrying parallel currents with them.
Current dissipation cannot be fully explained by the measured currents generated by the moving bubbles,
suggesting that additional mechanisms, such as turbulent interaction processes, are required to
account for current dissipation. 
A study using the Wind spacecraft's magnetometer data on Earth's boundary
layer and the Ulysses spacecraft in the polar region revealed that current
dissipation in the turbulent sub-ion range can be partially accounted for by
the turbulent interaction of electron-scale turbulence, particularly electron
current bursts and island structures, and electron current incoherence.
Remaining current dissipation in some cases can be partially attributed to
electron current reconnection, while in other cases, potential other mechanisms
may be involved. 
A theoretical model has been developed to describe current dissipation in the turbulent
sub-ion range by turbulent interaction, and it provides a quantitative estimate of
its effect, compared to observations, and can be applied to a wide range of plasma
turbulence with various scales and its observed effects. 
This study offers a new understanding of current dissipation in plasma turbulence and
its role in the energy paradigm, and it has implications for future space missions

Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of such modifications when using pre-trained models for continual learning. We examine the properties of pre-trained networks and develop a basic strategy, which entails 'freezing' the pre-trained model, to both improve and facilitate continual learning with minimal memory requirements. Our results show that 'freezing' the pre-trained model significantly outperforms modifying it, while also significantly reducing memory usage and computational time. Notably, combining 'freezing' with a straightforward strategy, such as the most straightforward method (LFW), yields an performance comparable to complex, model-modifying techniques like REPLAY-38. Our research 'disproves' several proposed theories for continual learning. Specifically, we contradict the notion that build upon pre-trained models by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. Our results 'disprove' the theory that significant transference of knowledge to new tasks occurs. One potential explanation for our findings could be that the commonly used benchmark datasets for evaluation may not accurately represent real-world tasks, which require significant updates to the model parameters. Therefore, a new, more challenging benchmark dataset for the evaluation of the proposed techniques will be developed. As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, concerns about hate speech spread rapidly across these platforms, jeopardizing the stability of societies worldwide. In response to the severe consequences of hate speech, efforts to detect it have intensified, driven by both practical necessities and moral obligations. Among hate speech detection methods, machine learning-based approaches have shown considerable promise. Our study contributes to this endeavor by examining the capability of transfer learning, a technique that enables the adaptation of models from one domain to another, in identifying hate speech. Utilizing pre-trained BERT models, we investigated whether incorporating data from two distinct platforms, Facebook posts and Twitter, could enhance hate speech detection accuracy when applied to a third dataset originating from Jigsaw. Our analysis reveals that combining hate speech data from one platform is sufficient for detecting hate speech on Jigsaw, significantly surpassing the performance achieved through training models separately for each dataset. Additionally, we discovered that incorporating annotations is unnecessary for hate speech detection on Jigsaw. This finding holds implications for the practical application of hate speech detection, potentially addressing data availability issues on Jigsaw. Interestingly, we found that BERT exhibited a propensity for underfitting when working with the Jigsaw dataset alone but successfully addressed this issue by using annotations from one platform. Interestingly, we found that incorporating annotations from both platforms yielded unexpected results, demonstrating a greater accuracy without annotations from Facebook and a lower accuracy with annotations from Twitter. These counterintuitive outcomes are attributable to discrepancies in the labeling tasks between our annotation process and the Jigsaw dataset. Moreover, the incorporation of BERT's semantic information appeared to diminish the significance of n-gram features, leading to decreased performance when both were utilized simultaneously. Our study also identified several hate speech keywords that significantly contributed to the model's predictions, underscoring the importance of contextual understanding in hate speech detection. These findings are set to influence the development of hate speech detection systems, potentially aiding researchers and practitioners in this important field. Our work also incorporates a user-centered design that emphasizes transparency and explainability, introducing a novel visualization that facilitates the assessment of hate speech detection models. This approach is versatile and can be adapted for use in related applications. Furthermore, the incorporation of user feedback from subjects highlights areas for improvement in hate speech detection, notably hate speech classification and feature identification, underscoring the need for both technical and user understanding in this context. Lastly, our study highlights the serious consequences of hate speech on mental health, emphasizing the necessity for hate speech detection to address not only practical necessities but also moral obligations. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. Additionally, simulations of neuron pairs confirm our analytical predictions, highlighting the utility of these simplifications for modeling complex neural circuits. These developments provide a framework for efficiently assessing the emergent dynamics of large networks, informed by their individual component characteristics. Furthermore, they offer a useful complement to existing approaches, particularly in contexts where detailed biophysical modeling is excessively resource-intensive or difficult to justify due to the level of simplification involved. As such, these findings enable a deeper understanding of the trade-offs involved in developing computational models across different scales of complexity. Interestingly, the mean field equations derived for theta neurons exhibit a surprising resemblance to those derived from biophysical models of neurons, suggesting that the parameter setting of these equations could serve as an intermediate step in upscaling biophysical models or as a potential bridge between model development at different scales of complexity. Lastly, the analytical framework established in this work also enables the efficient examination of its own limitations and robustness, allowing for quantitative assessments of its reliability. By analyzing the range of applicability and potential systematic errors of these simplifications, we gain a more nuanced understanding of their practical usability and their potential impact on predictions of large-scale neural circuit dynamics. In particular, we investigate the effects of simplifying the squashing function, reducing the number of neurons in the network, and varying the spike frequency adaptation parameter. Ultimately, the analytical framework presented in this work is viewed as an evolving resource, intended to facilitate ongoing discussions about the limitations and applications of these simplifications, and to accommodate future developments that may further expand the scope and breadth of its content. By fostering dialogue about the inherent trade-offs involved in upscaling biophysical models of neurons, this framework aims to provide guidance on the most appropriate use of such simplifications, as well as their potential bridging role between different scales of complexity in neuronal modeling. repair template such as methods using transformation based repair or search based
repair techniques. We take a contrasting strategy in this research by harnessing
the potential of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to directly produce sample
repairing codes when given faulty input code and a target language. Our approach
has significant advantages in that it necessitates no prior repair knowledge and can
inhabit any feasible repairing code space. We define four fundamental elements of
repairing code for sampling purposes and present an architecture of GANs capable
of generating these elements. Our research also includes the implementation of an
inference procedure to select the most suitable repairing code from the sampled
options from the generator's sample space using a black-box, gradient-free search
method, with the aid of test cases. Experiments on three publicly available repair
datasets from GitHub indicate that this method is competitive with well-regarded
pre-existing APR approaches in terms of success rate. Notably, our research
demonstrates that GAN-based sampling can enhance the accuracy of sample space when
combined with the weak exploration method used in the experiments. Furthermore,
our research shows that by combining the weak exploration method with the heavy
sampling strategy yields a superior success rate compared to the alone heavy
exploration method in the dataset of Pyton3. Moreover, our research indicates
potential of deep learning in the exploration front of sampling in the search and
optimization space. Future research directions are presented in the research for further advancement. Our goal is to modify stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to be adaptive to function complexity.
For smooth, strongly-convex functions minimization, our modified SGD algorithm achieves a mean error bound of $\mathcal{O}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{t}{\log(t)}\right)\right)$ with probability $1-\nu n^{-\delta}$, where $\nu,\delta>0$, without assuming burn-in phase. This results in a mean error of $\mathcal{O}\left(e^{-t/\kappa}\right)$ and $\mathcal{W}^{\ast}$ convergence rates for $\kappa,\omega^{\ast}>0$. Furthermore, our modified SGD can be applied to non-convex functions minimization, offering near optimal mean error $\mathcal{O}\left(e^{-t/12}\right)$ with proper parameter selection. The modified SGD algorithm is adaptive to function complexity, requires no pre-defined burn-in period, and is capable of being implemented in online settings with even better performance. Through simulation examples and theoretical analysis, our modified SGD algorithm's efficiency and adaptability are demonstrated. The modification introduced is applicable to a broad range of stochastic algorithms, allowing them to adapt to function complexity, and our theoretical findings have been substantiated by valid lower bounds. Finally, our modified SGD algorithm's applicability extends to a wide array of stochastic algorithms aimed at minimizing convex and non-convex functions under different sampling techniques. Generalizing our results to other algorithms can be achieved by identifying their characteristics based on specific functional properties, allowing the application of our results to a wide class of algorithms. For instance, our results are applicable to algorithms such as stochastic variance reduction, Newton's method, and even random projection, among others. The generalization process is straightforward: first categorize the algorithm based on its functional properties and then apply the established $\mathcal{W}^{\ast}$ convergence rate, or use the established time-dependent bounds derived from the modified SGD algorithm, which offers even better performance, as seen with online settings. The theoretical analysis found that the burn-in period is not necessary when the modified algorithm is used; instead, the algorithm can be applied at any moment without influencing its mean error or convergence rate. The algorithm's adaptability and applicability were demonstrated through comprehensive analysis and simulation examples, and our results are even applicable even when the established theoretical guarantees do not apply, as seen with certain non-convex functions over compact domains. We introduce Inference Distillation, a novel model compression approach, combining knowledge distillation with inference acceleration. Traditional inference distillation focuses on retaining input distribution characteristics and output probabilities under given data, whereas novel distillation targets the precise replication of model inputs, outputs, and intermediate states. Our proposed method, incorporating teacher model internal states in addition to inputs and outputs, significantly enhances knowledge retention. However, naively incorporating intermediate states often results in information overload, causing model training and inference to diverge. To address this challenge, we establish a general framework for inference distillation and devise novel training methods to tackle information overload issues, allowing the model to learn internal states while maintaining its ability to make accurate predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can simultaneously achieve a 10% compression of a ResNet-50 LN model on CIFAR-10 while accelerating inference to 9.2% without compromising top-1 accuracy, representing a previously unattained compression-acceleration trade-off. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers attach the same private valuation to each item, known as unit-valued buyers. In this context, our main contribution is the design of an efficient, unbiased, and robust mechanism that doesn't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and works efficiently when the intermediaries can negotiate with buyers under a cost-sharing agreement. This allows the auction to perform optimally compared to a traditional second-price auction. 

We extend our findings to the case of $k$ distinct items where each buyer assigns private, independent valuations to each item, known as $X$-valued buyers. By leveraging high-type buyers to simulate uniform valuations, and combining this simulation with an extension of our intermediate design, we develop a robust mechanism that doesn't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and works efficiently when the intermediaries can negotiate with buyers under a cost-sharing or all-or-nothing agreement. This robust mechanism outperforms previous, existing mechanisms designed for such buyers. Furthermore, our research highlights specific scenarios where previous mechanisms inherit the robustness properties we've introduced. In particular, our mechanism shows that if the buyer-demand distribution satisfies a certain condition, known as stochastic independent valuations (SIV), then our robust mechanism performs optimally compared to a traditional second-price auction. In addition, our mechanism designed for $X$-valued buyers performs optimally compared to an existing, state-of-the-art mechanism when the buyer-demand distribution satisfies SIV. Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversations. To measure this synchronization accurately in two-person dialogues, we developed a dynamic approach that combines convolutional networks and transformer architecture to capture both immediate and long-term conversation contexts. By incorporating attention layers for analyzing both internal and external interactions, our model can learn meaningful patterns in social exchanges across various domains. Through classification experiments, we verified the effectiveness of our approach in identifying authentic and inauthentic conversations. Moreover, when testing our model with individuals having Autism Spectrum Disorder, our results indicate a strong statistical link between our entrainment measure and relevant clinical symptoms, regardless of age and gender differences. Our study lays a crucial foundation for using social entrainment as a clinical indicator. The implementation details and evaluation datasets can be found at https://github.com/ DiffCL/Entrainment. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires substantial cost
and time. A recent study has found that applying depth estimation from unlabeled
videos can be a cost-effective and time-efficient technique in pre-training
deep neural networks. However, using this method also poses internal knowledge
leakage risks, as the depth maps contain visual information of the training area.
To mitigate this challenge, we present an innovative approach called the
DepthMask, a lightweight, CNN architecture designed to remove identifiable
visual details from depth maps by blocking the source area. Our experiments
demonstrate that the DepthMask technique effectively protects trade secrets in
depth maps, while controlled evaluations confirm that it does not lower the
overall performance of the network. Moreover, we compare different methods for
masking identity areas from depth maps and show that the DepthMask method
achieves better results. Our findings reveal that using the DepthMask technique
significantly reduces the performance decline caused by pre-training on unlabeled
videos with unprotected depth maps, while it has little to no effect when the
depth maps are properly protected. Our code is publicly available on the GitHub platform.
