The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems in at most n - d iterations, motivated by Smale's mathematical problem 9, first introduced in the late 90s. A new approach in the third paper builds upon the facet pivot method's success by achieving even faster resolution of linear programming problems, completing them in at most d iterations. A natural extension of the concept to general optimization problems is presented in the fourth paper, where a new algorithm, named edge pivot, is proposed and analyzed. This algorithm was inspired by an analogous approach found in Burdett and Thomas's work. A comprehensive comparison between the facet pivot and edge pivot methods is performed, demonstrating the edge pivot method excels in several key areas, including performance, computational complexity, and applicability to various types of polytope vertices. Furthermore, it is proven the edge pivot has an almost linear time complexity of O(m + n). A practical demonstration of the edge pivot method's efficiency in real-world settings is shown through its application to the problem of hat guessing numbers, a classic problem in combinatorics, where the proposed algorithm achieves a near-optimal result. A numerical verification of the time efficiency of the edge pivot method has also been achieved. Finally, the fifth paper delves into the power of polyhedral decomposition in solving linear programming and general optimization problems. A new algorithm, named layer pivot, is proposed and shown to be capable of solving linear programming problems in at most n - 1 iterations. A natural extension of the layer pivot method to general non-convex optimization problems is also presented, where it is revealed the layer pivot method excels in several key performance metrics. A comparison between the facet pivot, edge pivot, and layer pivot methods is performed, demonstrating the layer pivot method excels in performance, computational complexity, and applicability to various types of polytope vertices. Additionally, it is shown the layer pivot has an almost linear time complexity of O(m + n). A numerical verification of the time efficiency of the layer pivot method has also been achieved. A comprehensive polytope decomposition theory is proposed,

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs become stalled on easier problems, the evaluation time bias negatively affects their search performance. Despite the efficiency benefits, adopting high-parallelism for APEAs also exacerbates the evaluation time bias issue. This study addresses the proposed solution to minimize the evaluation time bias in parallel computing systems. The group evaluation method efficiently distributes tasks among computing nodes, reducing the evaluation time bias without compromising the robustness of the algorithm. Experiments conducted on various multi-modal and non-modal functions demonstrate the group evaluation method's capability to mitigate the evaluation time bias, especially in high-parallelism systems and during the final stages of optimization. As a result, the group evaluation method accelerates the convergence to optimal solutions, reduces the standard deviation in evaluation times, and lowers hardware utilization variability. The method's effectiveness motivates the incorporation of parallel computing in multi-objective optimization, resulting in improved performance. The proposed methodology is versatile, applicable to a range of single-objective optimization problems in both Asynchronous PEAs and steady-state PEAs. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with periodic driving, this model necessarily becomes inconsistent as driving frequencies increase, especially in certain phases of the generated Floquet Hamiltonian. In this study, a condition is derived that indicates the generality of these inconsistencies and the absence of a straightforward Floquet generator in open quantum systems. Although it is possible to extend analytical high-frequency expansions to these systems, this does not necessarily lead to a consistent Floquet model. A distinct phase is identified in which the Floquet generator retains crucial spectral properties. In this phase, the dynamics of the open quantum system, governed by a Markovian master equation with high-frequency driving, can be approximated by a perturbative reduction to a time-independent Lindblad equation. In this context, the floquet Hamiltonian represents a crucial control parameter that facilitates a complete state reconstruction of the system via matrix inversion, when the Floquet Hamiltonian is known, even in environments indistinguishable from the environment in the standard Lindblad model. Consequently, introducing high-frequency driving into an environment modelled by a Markovian equation, with the condition that it induces a phase with a generic Floquet generator, appears to be a potential method for achieving such a reconstruction. In experimental applications, a suitable phase can be realised by introducing a detuning into the driving mechanism. Through detailed analysis of the temperature and Rh content dependencies of the magnetic ability and irreversibility, we classify the spin-freezing phase within the dynamic disordered regime of rare-earth magnets, characterized by a significant shift towards lower Rh content compared to the ferromagnetic-to-spin-glass phase transition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ability of magnetic ions to move and interact dynamically at low temperatures gives rise to a notable increase in the spin-freezing phase transition temperature and an enhanced ability to follow an external field, observed for Rh-doped compounds. By further exploring these phenomena under magnetic field influence, we uncover the ability of magnetic fields to overcome disorder and facilitate a disorder-driven reentrance of long-range ferromagnetism in the most Rh-rich compounds. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between disorder and long-range order in the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ series and sheds new light on the characteristics of the spin-glass phase in rare-earth magnetic systems. Furthermore, based on these findings and anisotropic magnetocaloric effect, we propose potential applications of these materials in magnetic refrigeration technology. These observations were made in giant molecular clouds located near the star-forming regions NGC 2264 and W51, spanning from -300 to +200 km/s. The data sampling frequency was 0.58 kHz, which corresponds to a velocity resolution of approximately 0.16 km/s. This phase is calculated using data from two decay modes: the jetiness approach in final state J/psi mu+mu- and the conventional approach using final state J/psi l+nu. The conventional method is currently more precise, but the jetiness approach may offer increased data utilization efficiency. This research utilizes simulated data to compare the precision of phi_s measurements achievable with 300, 300, and 1000 fb-1 of LHC data, considering the conventional method operating at LHC runs 1, 2, and 3, and the jetiness method operating at LHC run 2 and 3. The results show that the jetiness method may match or surpass the conventional method's precision under the same data collection conditions. Furthermore, the analysis finds that the jetiness method can yield comparable precision with significantly smaller data sets, potentially opening up opportunities to analyze data with reduced efficiency and during exceptional running conditions. While the study primarily focuses on phi_s measurements, its methodology can be applied to other CP-sensitive observables in a variety of systems. The investigation of these variables in future simulations may reveal further efficiency gains. The simulation also assesses the sensitivity of various observables sensitive to CP violation in the Bd system. It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant image information, but they may not always excel in using this information to make inferences about target datasets with different underlying characteristics. In an effort to overcome this shortcoming, researchers have employed domain adaptation techniques that aim to leverage a labeled target dataset to produce a more generalized network. This work proposes a novel domain adaptation approach that draws on the strengths of two diverse neural architecture search methods, employing one method to select features and another to select weights, and further develops a differentiable search framework that enables the optimization of domain adaptation based on target dataset performance. Experimental evaluations conducted using the MNIST, CIFAR, and SVHN image classification benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method's substantial improvements over traditional domain adaptation methods and widely-used neural architecture search approaches. Additionally, the results demonstrate the proposed method's competitive performance against state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. This work's innovative approach to domain adaptation based on neural architecture search promises to facilitate deep neural networks' ability to generalize across different target datasets. Researchers can access the search framework's source code to reproduce the results at https://github.com/leverl1/ADA-SAS. Recently, a new type of recurrent neural network called the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) was developed and shown to be effective at recognizing patterns on a variety of recognition tasks. Building on the principles of Legregne's law, which governs how memory is organized in the brain, the LMU uses a unique mathematical approach that is different from the conventional method of recognizing patterns used by Linear Statistical Models, including the well-known LSTM network. This study investigates how the parameters of the LMU, which is essentially a system where information is stored and retrieved through an access function, affect the ability of the model to recognize patterns. By analyzing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the LMU's transition matrix over time, we derive a set of analytical equations that describe how the LMU's performance changes under different conditions. In particular, we show that certain properties of the LMU's transition matrix, such as the eigenvalues, which determine the eigenvalues of the LMU, are crucial to its performance. By optimizing these parameters, we develop a set of 'optimal' conditions under which the LMU's performance is maximized. Through numerical simulations and comparisons with state-of-the-art models such as the LSTM and transformer, our results demonstrate the advantages of the LMU on benchmark datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR. Additionally, we show that the LMU's ability to recognize patterns using a small number of parameters is comparable to or even better than that of the LSTM and transformer. This study provides a deeper understanding of how the LMU's parameters affect its ability to recognize patterns and paves the way for the development of efficient pattern recognition systems based on this new RNN model. Furthermore, we present a hardware realization of the LMU, which uses a network of coupled differential equations to store and retrieve information through an access function, similar to the neural storage system found in the mammalian brain. By designing the LMu as a circuit with analog values, we demonstrate its potential applications in emerging fields of analog AI. To showcase its practicality, we successfully trained the LMU based on our analog implementation and achieved a high accuracy of 96.7% on the MNIST dataset. Ultimately, our results highlight the potential of the LMU as a building block for developing AI systems that are both efficient and scalable. Furthermore, its unique analog architecture may pave the way for the development of AI systems that integrate both digital and analog technologies. As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, the seemingly adjustable fundamental constants, and the unobserved sector that may hide within the mirror world.  A new area of research, feebly interacting particles, has significant implications for theories such as dark matter, the early universe's thermal history, and the origins of matter-antimatter symmetry.  To explore this concept, we propose the feebly interacting massive particle (FIMP) model, which can explain the universe's matter-antimatter imbalance through the process of lees-suppressed entropy.  The proposed FIMP model is compatible with various fundamental theories, such as string theory, the mirror world, and the idea of a multiverse.  Notably, the FIMP model is unique among dark matter models due to its minimal impact on the dark matter abundance, allowing it to be more in line with current experimental limitations.  As such, it offers a more flexible approach with broader implications for fundamental physics.  To uncover feebly interacting particles, we recommend a multi-faceted research strategy involving the development of specialized detectors, an in-depth analysis of the large Hadron Collider's data, and a thorough examination of the universe's cosmic features.  Along the way, we discuss the feasibility of creating the world's most sensitive low-energy antiparticle detectors, carry out an in-depth review of the FIMP model's theoretical foundations, and outline the boundaries within which the FIMP model can be integrated into fundamental theories.  Lastly, we initiate a discussion on the interplay between theoretical feebly interacting particles and experimental advancements, serving as a bridge between fundamental physics and particle science. Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration. We explore this complex phenomenon through an agent-based model focused on migration and language exchange. Our research reveals that migration significantly contributes to the creation of isolated language pockets, impacting linguistic diversity. We aimed to understand how migration influences language spread and extinction, and how it shapes the unique linguistic landscape of monolingual islands. Analysis of our model uncovers principles that can be applied to understanding real-world language patterns. We identify a specific migratory pattern that leads to the extreme fragmentation of languages, resulting in the predicted existence of monolingual islands based on the Zipf-Mannoulian law. Furthermore, we find that language exchange during migration enhances diversity, and that a balanced migration rate is crucial for maximizing linguistic differences. We extend the Zipf-Mannoulian law to describe the distribution of polylingual individuals. Lastly, we find evidence supporting the prediction that major languages tend to be associated with high population densities. We validate these findings by comparing them to the Roman Empire language distribution, a classic case study in linguistic research. Our results are made available in a comprehensive form for the scientific community. The code and data can be accessed via the link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jwaf.2022.103.002.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, but deep RL methods face two major limitations: their high demand for extensive game experience and instability, which often results in prolonged or erratic training processes. To overcome these challenges, research has focused on transfer learning within deep RL, yielding a new direction for efficient and stable reinforcement learning without extensive data collection. This conceptual paper introduces RLt2, a novel framework for flexible and adaptive transfer learning based on representation learning that enables efficient transfer between distinct environments. We also investigate several transfer learning methods within RL and propose a future research agenda for efficiently transferring knowledge from source domains to target domains, including evaluation, fine-tuning, and retraining methods. Additionally, we present a representation learning framework that can be applied to multi-objective RL tasks, providing an alternative to experience-based fine-tuning methods. By highlighting existing challenges and proposing a future research agenda, this study aims to accelerate the development of transfer learning applications within deep RL. Furthermore, we introduce several data augmentation strategies for RL in image-based environments, offering an alternative to experience collection through simulation or interaction with real-world environments. By integrating data augmentation, adaptation, and retraining, our representation learning framework enhances experience-based fine-tuning methods and opens new avenues for transfer learning and efficient RL without extensive data collection. We release the source code for RLt2, including its implementation and experimental evaluations, on GitHub. We explore global optimization techniques for a particular class of concave functions, where the behavior of local maxima is also analyzed. By employing a specific adjustment to the function, we can transform this class into a version of strictly convex functions, to which advanced optimization methods can be effectively applied. Additionally, our approach allows for the recovery of original function maxima from the modified results. The effectiveness of this technique is validated through numerical examples. Furthermore, based on this theoretical framework, a computational method for finding global maxima is developed, even when the function is defined by multiple variables. Interestingly, this algorithm can be specialized to solve convex network flow optimization problems, where the objective function is specifically crafted from concave kernel functions. Consequently, optimal solutions can be extracted from the modified result without incurring additional computational costs. To illustrate its efficiency, the proposed approach is applied to a network flow optimization problem rooted in hypergraph theory, where the resulting optimization technique achieves a $2$-approximation relative to a natural linear relaxation. Interestingly, this particular instantiation of the algorithm surpasses the previously established approximation standards for comparable problems. A computational example is also provided to demonstrate its computational efficiency under practical application. Lastly, our approach can be adapted for in-vehicle navigation systems, offering potential applications in this domain. With respect to theoretical analysis, a computational time complexity assessment reveals that our method operates within $ \mathcal{O}^*(2^{n + \ell}\cdot \mbox{FLOPS})$, where $\mbox{FLOPS}$ represents the number of arithmetic operations required to solve the LP relaxation. By comparing this complexity to other global optimization techniques, it is evident that our method outperforms the latter. Furthermore, this particular instantiation of the algorithm for kernel function maxima surpasses other state-of-the-art solvers, such as CPLEX, in terms of computational efficiency for smaller input sizes. Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely accepted specification technique in software
development, and its formalization through verification enables strong proof
of software correctness. This paper outlines a verification tool, Anima,
developed using Isabelle/HOL, which leverages the power of program translators
to validate software through high-level specifications transformed into efficient
machine code with preserved specifications. Additionally, we present a case
study verifying the ANSI C implementation of a sorting algorithm, insertionsort,
using high-level specifications and Isabelle/HOL's formal proof system. This
research demonstrates the feasibility of Hoare verification for extensive C
programs with moderate complexity, offering insights for similar verification
efforts on other programming languages. Although Anima's current focus on ANSI C
may limit its applicability to preprocessed code, mixed-language programs,
and real-world software development, the techniques discussed are adaptable to
other languages and domains with suitable preprocessors. Furthermore, future
integrations with existing verification tools and proof assistants could streamline
the process of Hoare verification and expand the scope of easily verifiable software. 
Finally, this paper contributes to ongoing discussions around formal verification
of self-modifying code, mutable data at translation time, and the practical
applicability of Hoare verification in real-world software development contexts.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining agreement among live nodes. RCanopus introduces a new failure detection method that uses a directed graph to measure node reliability and automatically detects and recovers from failures, ensuring that a failure will not cause an exclusive failure in the system. The protocol also implements a security mechanism that uses code signing and authenticated messages to prevent attacks from node failures, including protocols that use proxy nodes to disguise attacks, without compromising the high-traffic performance of the original Canopus. By adapting and integrating with existing Canopus-based systems, RCanopus provides robust failure detection and protection against malicious attacks, making it suitable for critical applications. The experimental results show that RCanopus can effectively improve the failure detection rate and outperform other similar protocols, all while maintaining code size within a reasonable limit and ensuring minimal performance impact when dealing with failures. The cost of using RCanopus is estimated to be around 8 kilobytes, making it a very efficient method. The virtual tree structure used in RCanopus contributes to its ability to effectively detect and protect against failures, resulting in a failure detection delay of O(h^2) and a latency of O(h), where h is the height of the virtual tree, and allows the protocol to handle failures that don't directly affect performance. The automatic recovery feature of RCanopus can rebuild the virtual tree in O(n + h^2) time. The performance-cost optimization of RCanopus makes it an ideal choice for various distributed systems. The accuracy and effectiveness of RCanopus have been tested using different failure types and scenarios, resulting in an average failure detection rate of 85%. The experiment results show that RCanopus can effectively protect against node attacks and failures, resulting in an average cost of 0.08% and 0.56% respectively, and an average failure detection delay of 0.32 milliseconds. The experiment results demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of RCanopus in protecting against attacks

In this issue, the primary concern centers around assessing the accuracy of these predictions rather than training the networks. In response, we developed a prototype system called PredictEvalu, which effectively monitors and evaluates the validity of deep learning-based robotic control systems. This innovative framework is built upon a tiny computer monitoring real-world sensor data and compare it with simulated data collected during training, utilizing a customized container to facilitate real-time processing. In experiments with a self-driving wheelchair and a neural network controlling a robotic arm, we showcased PredictEvalu's capabilities, leading to a significant reduction in failures and improved safety. The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition pushed the limits of short-term traffic prediction, leveraging high-resolution traffic volume and speed data, available in five-minute intervals. 
To adapt to new cities, as the 2021 challenge demanded, a more effective approach is suggested: predicting traffic in smaller sections of a city grid.
By breaking down test data into smaller squares, prediction accuracy and robustness increase.
While this strategy is straightforward, it offers a valuable lesson in processing traffic data.
To compare the efficacy of 1D and 2D methods, a novel self-attending model is developed, using dynamic systems to model input sequences and incorporating self-attention for capturing long-term relationships in data.
The model outperforms the previous best submission to traffic4cast, with a significant margin. 
A varying degree of temporal shifting in the dynamic filter is also explored and is found to enhance prediction quality. 
Visualizations of the model's weights reveal the long-term relationships in data that it identifies. 
Finally, the model is demonstrated to enhance prediction quality when compared to other competitors in the competition, including in cases where the new training data is limited to a single city.

Our focus lies on the inner proton radiation belt located at an altitude of approximately 1,000 km above the Earth's surface. The in situ TRAX experiment on the International Space Station has enabled researchers to study low-altitude proton radiation near the Earth. The radiation belt's inner region is likely formed through the ionization of ferromanganese particles entering the Earth's atmosphere at a 45-degree angle, a theory supported by observations of such an angle in low orbital points. The protons produced in this process are predominantly forward-directed, a phenomenon modelled using a spherically symmetric, three-body (Earth, ferromanganese particle, radiation proton) model. As a result, forward-directed proton radiation is expected to occur through multiple mechanisms: (1) the ionization of ferromanganese particles at a 0-degree angle of incidence, (2) three-body interactions between the Earth, ferromanganese particles, and radiation protons, and (3) interactions between the Earth's magnetic field and the azimuthal component of radiation protons. However, due to computational constraints, researchers have only computationally modeled the first mentioned mechanism in this study, with findings suggesting that such an angle-dependent mechanism can generate forward-directed proton radiation with energies of at least 50 keV. The results of the simulations indicate that the angle-dependent mechanism can generate radiation with energies of at least 50 keV. The simulated data further suggest that low-altitude proton radiation may be observable not only in the TRAX experiment but also in in situ measurements made at even lower altitudes. Such experiments could potentially detect proton radiation directed both forward and backward, with energy ranges potentially extending down to approximately 5 keV, a finding that may be verified using future TRAX measurements. Furthermore, researchers believe that low-altitude proton radiation could also be observable in the upper atmosphere through ground-based muon detector technology. In conclusion, this study has significantly contributed to the understanding of low-altitude proton radiation near the Earth by combining unique experimental data with computational models. Future studies are anticipated to incorporate additional computational mechanisms for enhanced understanding. The discovery of such proton radiation, whether detected in space or from above the Earth's surface, could potentially yield significant new knowledge of the phenomenon. A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. In 
this study, we evaluated the capabilities of three prevalent expressivity 
measures: multiplicity, depth, and width – combined with complexity in terms 
of polynomial degrees – within the context of artificial neural networks. We 
investigated these measurements for both binary and non-binary classification 
tasks using artificial datasets and real-world data from standard test suites. 
We found that the traditional understanding of expressivity, based on optimal 
weight distributions, is overly restrictive and does not always reflect actual 
training outcomes. Notably, we discovered that increasing network complexity may 
not always lead to better generalization, as over-specification can hinder 
performance. These findings are supported by extensive training experiments, 
which demonstrate that the upper bounds of expressivity can be exceeded when 
using non-optimal weight distributions, potentially due to the presence of 
dead and redundant neurons. Based on these findings, we recommend a revised 
formula for characterizing the expressivity of neural networks that takes into 
account redundant dimensions learned during training. This revised formula can 
be validated using neural network perturbation techniques and numerical 
singular value decomposition. Additionally, we discovered that neural network 
over-specification may be attributed to the development of redundant 
interfeature patterns, which can be identified using symmetry-based 
characterization techniques and numerical Fourier transform. This research 
establishes a connection between neural network characterization tools and 
neural architecture search methods. As a result, we propose an efficient 
algorithm for achieving good generalization by eliminating redundant 
high-frequency dimensions from neural network weights. This algorithm 
significantly improves the performance of random networks across various 
classification tasks, achieving up to a 2.5-gamma increase in accuracy for 1D 
tasks and a 1.5-gamma increase in accuracy for 2D tasks, while reducing their 
complexity by eliminating redundant dimensions. Furthermore, we found that 
combining our characterization method with neural architecture search produces 
results that surpass the current state-of-the-art in neural network 
characterization. The introduced methods are open-sourced at: https://github.com/guiguilg/NeuralNetworkExpressivityCharacterization.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a given arrangement. Inspired by the original rules on trees, we are investigating light-switching on cactus graphs, specifically comb-like structures that combine multiple trees connected by dual nodes. Our key finding shows that any given configuration on a cactus graph can be successfully toggled off, thus extending the winning methods from graphs with vertices no more than two and introducing a new technique for fully connected graphs with twenty or fewer vertices. Additionally, we have developed a method for turning off arrangements in-series connected graphs with twenty or more vertices. Furthermore, by applying the reduced-order approach, we have determined the minimum number of required clicks in cactus graphs with twenty or fewer vertices. These findings mark the first comprehensive solution to the light-switching game played on cactus graphs. Furthermore, they extend the winning methods from graphs with vertices no more than two and provide insights into the complexity of click sequences. Consequently, the total number of clicks needed to win on cactus graphs with twenty or fewer vertices has been calculated and is found to be bounded by a logarithm base 2 of the graph's vertex count. In particular, the simplest case of an linear graph with twenty vertices, which is a cactus graph itself, requires at most eleven clicks to win. As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based systems primarily operate node-by-node. We introduce the concept of neighborhood fairness, recognizing that GNNs primarily operate on localized neighborhoods. We distinguish between bias arising from limited training data and that introduced by GNNs operating in a neighborhood-by-neighborhood manner. We explore strategies to mitigate neighborhood bias induced by GNNs. First, we develop a weighted graph GNN that counteracts bias by increasing edge weights between similar nodes. Second, we incorporate a diversity-promoting constraint in the optimization framework of unsupervised GNNs, effectively optimizing multiple fairness metrics simultaneously. Third, we adapt a fair supervised GNN to address neighborhood fairness with a binary regularization. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods in addressing neighborhood fairness. Moreover, empirical analyses reveal that while weighted GNNs offer some improvement, incorporating diversity as a constraint leads to the most significant gains in fairness metrics applicable to various domains. Notably, we found the fairness performance of adapted diversity-promoting methods converging to that of their supervised counterparts, albeit with improved scores. Conversely, the performance of weighted GNNs exhibited bias due to their proprietary propagation of node properties. Finally, we highlight the practical implications of neighborhood fairness in real-world applications, aided by visual explanations that illustrate the rationale behind biased predictions made by GNNs, further advancing the fairness research in the field. This method splits decision-making processes into discrete parts: predicting demand and supply. This dichotomy leads to accurate predictions by arbitrageurs, which in turn triggers an inevitable collapse of bubbles. Unlike earlier theories, our model reveals that bubbles can thrive and prosper due to higher expected demands, even in the presence of negative social effects. Furthermore, our dual dynamic framework yields an alternative explanation for the arbitrage paradox, revealing that positive expectations do not always result in effective arbitrage. We've also found that conventional one-way influence models can impede market activity, whereas two-way influence models might revive dormant markets. Our studies, incorporating realistic market fluctuations, support the theoretical findings. Interestingly, our experiment shows that early bubble collapse is more likely under Monte Carlo simulations, contrary to dual dynamic theory's indication in the baseline analysis. This apparent contradiction highlights the significance of market fluctuations in determining bubble dynamics. We've further developed a finite mixture model to measure the relative prevalence of bubble occurrence and longevity among market participants. This model's analysis confirms that bubble enticements differ among individuals with varied arbitrage risks and social influence weights. Overall, our study contributes to temporary bubble theory by integrating these factors and providing a better understanding of bubble dynamics, particularly the positive social effect on bubble survival, the dual dynamic model's implications, and the variable arbitrage paradox, depending on the consideration of two-way influence. Lastly, our findings shed light on the distinct preferences of market participants. We've explored the theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of our study, offering potential avenues for further research into temporary bubbles, encompassing fundamental analysis, generalized expectations models, and stochastic demand/supply ratio. Ultimately, our goal is to merge the theoretical insights from our study with the practical outcomes of empirical experiments to gain a deeper understanding of temporary bubbles. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of enhancing dialogue modeling with semantic knowledge through a novel pre-training approach. This framework, which utilizes a graph attention network, enables the alignment of semantic representations with Abstract Meaning Representation units while considering the relationships between dialogue sentences. Experimental results indicate that our model enhances the understanding of dialogue context and achieves superior performance in downstream tasks, including a new state-of-the-art benchmark on the Ubuntu dataset. Furthermore, we achieve improved performance on the E2E Dialog dataset and contribute to the development of semantic dialogue models through open-source resources. The project's code is available for open-source review at https://github.com/PracticalAI/SEM-MwACT. Through this initiative, we seek to foster a community that addresses the challenges of semantic dialogue modeling. Additionally, we include a pre-trained model optimized for conversational tasks, dubbed SEM-MwACT, and make it accessible via the Hugging Face Transformers library, enabling a seamless integration with existing models and applications. The model's hyperparameters and training configuration are documented on the Models' Zerog Gitter platform, located at https://zerog.gh.io/SEM-MwACT. In the future, we aim to build upon this work by integrating it with the OpenAssistant dataset, developed by Facebook AI, and exploring its applications in downstream tasks. Ultimately, we believe that mastering the art of semantic dialogue modeling is within our collective reach. In the future, we will leverage community feedback to refine our model and address any lingering challenges in this subfield. By achieving a robust understanding of semantic dialogue modeling, we will unlock its applications in real-world contexts, ultimately achieving a deeper and more precise understanding of human interaction. In the next section, we outline the key contributions of our approach, specifically the use of semantic modeling in dialogue tasks, followed by a detailed methodology that encompasses data preparation, model implementation, and evaluation processes. Subsequently, we present our approach in context by highlighting its relevance to the broader dialogue modeling community, while also highlighting potential limitations and avenues for future exploration. In the final section, we showcase the performance of our model in comparison to existing state-of-the-art models on downstream datasets, followed by an analysis of our approach from multiple perspectives, culminating in a brief overview of the challenges and opportunities presented by semantic dialogue modeling.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be broken down into simple components, produces consistent and accurate results, and accurately represents the process of understanding an algorithm. By developing a clear and detailed scale for measuring interpretability, developers can use this framework to demonstrate the reliability and transparency of their algorithms, aligning with established standards. Additionally, this study highlights the significance of developing fair and accountable algorithms in rapidly evolving fields such as AI. Furthermore, this research connects the fields of programming languages and human learning to provide a foundation for a broader understanding of interpretability. In doing so, it addresses open questions in the field, including the minimal characteristics required for measuring interpretability. Ultimately, this study contributes to ongoing discussions about the principles of fairness and accountability in the AI community. A demonstration of this framework can be found online at https://github.com/jmjones12/interpret-measure. A more comprehensive version of this framework, along with additional technical details, can be accessed through https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07337. A subsequent paper expands on this research at https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07338. A related open question about the applicability of this research in the context of deep learning is discussed at https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07339. A more general framework for assessing fairness and accuracy is proposed at https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07340. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which employs a random tree-based approach to compute an anomaly score through ensemble learning. However, a conventional Isolation Forest may still be inefficient and unreliable in certain situations, particularly when dealing with large datasets. As an improved alternative, we introduce a more efficient unsupervised Iroh-Tree-based anomaly detector, incorporating ideas from decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting, which can effectively provide accurate classification results in various practical scenarios. Our proposed model builds upon conventional decision trees, using a first-pass pass approach to calculate anomaly scores, which can be combined to yield an ensemble classification result, demonstrated to outperform leading anomaly detectors across nine diverse dataset tests. The code for our model has been made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, we analyzed the computational complexity of our model, finding that its time complexity remains consistent with Isolation Forest, but with significant improvements in terms of efficiency -- especially in terms of reduced complexity from n^2 to n when dealing with leaf node visits, and a substantial 10- to 100-fold decrease in time complexity relative to leading anomaly detectors on actual data. Ultimately, our model was found to deliver faster classification results in terms of milliseconds, with even smaller discrepancies from normal behavior capable of triggering an anomaly classification. To quantify the performance of our model, we compared the results from Iroh-Tree to leading anomaly detectors using the AUC score, finding our model yielded high AUC scores across nine diverse dataset tests, with significant improvements in terms of accuracy -- especially a 0.03 increase in AUC score relative to prior works. The improved accuracy and reliability of our model was further confirmed through visual analysis of classification results, demonstrating that perceived outliers may not always be anomalous in nature, and highlighting the usefulness of our model in highlighting genuine areas of discrepancy. The improved validity and reliability of our model was further confirmed using the hit rate score, finding our model yielded high hit rates across nine diverse dataset tests, with significant improvements in terms of validity -- especially a 0.14 increase in hit score relative to prior works. Ultimately, our model yielded a significant 3.07 seconds faster classification time relative to leading anomaly detectors, with even smaller discrepancies from normal behavior capable of yielding accurate and reliable classification results. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has advantages, particularly the ability to change the data without altering the model parameters, it also has a significant drawback: the ability to do so may itself cause issues with underestimating return periods. In this research, we propose a more nuanced approach that not only allows for parameter adaptation without affecting extreme values but also guarantees that the estimated return periods remain consistently high. The proposed framework is based on an expanded version of Cramer-von Mises statistics and can be broken down into distinct components. First, we define a scaled version of the observed data following a high threshold as a shifted version of the data transformed through a known function. Secondly, we calculate an estimated value for one of the parameters by using a standard normalizing technique and maximizing likelihood. Lastly, we incorporate all parameters, including the one just estimated, into the model by employing a Bayesian approach using the observed data to form a joint distribution for all parameters. Additionally, we also address an issue with models that can be considered misspecified by developing a more accurate estimator for the parameters of the model. Through various tests, we confirm that under specific criteria our model will result in consistent estimates, thus addressing issues with the aforementioned problem of the parameter adaptation affecting extreme values but not the model itself. Furthermore, we also successfully test a version of the parameters adaptation that does not involve any distribution assumptions. These results collectively show that our approach provides accurate estimates while guaranteeing that the adaptation of the parameters will result in consistent estimates, thus addressing a long-standing issue in the modelling of extreme events. There has been a recent surge of new datasets proposed to leverage commonsense knowledge graphs (CSKGs). Traditional evaluation metrics, such as conceptual similarity, have been found insufficient for assessing CSKG completion tasks. This study investigates novel evaluation benchmarks derived from natural language understanding, specifically, language comprehension and generation. These new benchmarks, known as Natural Language Questions (NLQ), evaluate CSKG completion by framing knowledge completion as a language generation task. Experiments were conducted on eight existing CSKGs using their original models and new NLQ-based evaluation. Notably, results indicate that half of these models perform significantly better on NLQ than conceptual similarity, while also achieving better link predictions using the existing graph structures. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that NLQ provides a more comprehensive assessment of CSKG completion by little over twice the efficiency of traditional evaluation. This study suggests that NLQ can serve as a unified, efficient, and effective evaluation baseline for future CSKG dataset submissions and completion tasks. The proposed evaluation method is independent of dataset size, enabling CSKG submission and evaluation to occur at any scale. The new evaluation method is accessible at https://github.com/so2z/CSKG_NLQ. A subset of eight existing CSKG submission candidates has been prepared for demonstration purposes. The new evaluation method is intended to be used for both existing and future submissions. Any third-party access requests regarding the new evaluation method should be directed to pawpiti at gmail.com. In modeling systems of rival agents as games, the focus is typically on identifying a state where no agent can benefit from changing their strategy. However, for large-scale systems of numerous agents exhibiting regular patterns of interaction, it is impractical to directly determine each agent's optimal response to possible counter-moves from the other players, thus rendering access to Nash equilibria computationally infeasible. In such cases, it is more feasible to use approximate Nash equilibria as a practical solution. A novel algorithm is presented in this paper, designed to locate approximate Nash equilibria in finite, multi-player games where agents repeat choose actions based on their current beliefs. The algorithm's efficiency is analyzed and tested on a pair of multi-player games where strategy selection occurs in alternating rounds. The results show that in these "switching cost" games, the proposed algorithm converges to a specific type of approximate Nash equilibrium that accounts for payoff differences based on the agent's current beliefs and the available actions. Furthermore, two models of switching cost games are examined where one model assumes shared knowledge of the other agents' beliefs, and the results indicate that the algorithm's convergence to an approximate Nash equilibrium remains unaffected in this scenario. In testing the algorithm, it is observed that it converges to a specific type of approximate Nash equilibrium that accounts for the agent's current beliefs and the available actions. The proposed algorithm is shown to converge to a continuous version of approximate Nash equilibrium that accounts for the agent's current beliefs and the available actions. The algorithm's continuous version is referred to as the Continuous Approximate Nash Equilibrium.

transferring labels from a large, clean dataset to the images in question. To 
validate the effectiveness of this approach, it was tested on a dataset of noisy, 
crowdsourced images. The results demonstrated that this method outperformed other 
techniques in classifying images, with a notable improvement of approximately 5.5% 
and 4%, respectively. This method outperformed other approaches such as noise 
suppression combined with traditional classification and direct classification of 
noisy images. Furthermore, it was observed that the hybrid technique was more

efficiency and effectiveness of image-based applications in medicine, geography, and 
other fields where crowdsourced image datasets are commonly utilized. Furthermore, 
it is suggested that crowdworkers reflect on their image labeling decisions to 
improve the quality of datasets, thus reducing the need for noise suppression and 
improving the efficiency and effectiveness of classification models in the process.

establishing a standardized protocol for working with noisy, crowdsourced image

This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who introduced EvoCrash, a tool capable of replicating Java software failures via stack traces. It leverages a guided genetic algorithm to create reliable JUnit test cases. We examine EvoCrash's effectiveness alongside three existing tools: JCHARMING, JCrash, and MuCrash. We discovered that EvoCrash successfully replicated the majority of failures found in EvoCrash, JCHARMING, and MuCrash but outperformed JCHARMING and MuCrCrash while surpassing JCrash. Although EvoCrash failed to replicate around 11% of failures, it demonstrated accuracy in non-failing test cases. Notably, EvoCrash was able to enhance the performance of JCHARMING and MuCrash by two-fold on average. We further investigated EvoCrash's evolved JUnit test cases of 35 open-source projects listed in the BESERK dataset and observed that it produced highly effective and clear JUnit test cases closely aligned with actual program statements. These findings indicate that EvoCrash is a useful tool for software maintainers, planners, and researchers working in the area of crash reproduction. Moreover, it provides a practical method of integrating evolved JUnit test cases into existing tools designed to reproduce crashes. Photons are valuable tools used to explore the intense medium produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Recent research includes precise calculations of the influence of viscosity on photon emission in these collisions, taking place at RHIC and LHC. Thermal photons exhibit anisotropic movement patterns known as v_n coefficients, which are affected by viscosity and hydrodynamic movements in the collision process. We calculated the anisotropic correction due to viscosity and compared it to the suppression of hydrodynamic flow anisotropies in the 120 GeV Pb+Pb collisions and 2.76 TeV Pb+Pb collisions. The anisotropic correction due to viscosity is comparable to the anisotropic suppression in both cases, indicating that viscosity can be quantified using v_2 suppression. We also found that while medium effects and viscosity have comparable impacts on thermal photon v_2 coefficients, viscosity dominates over medium effects in determining v_3 coefficients. As a result,, viscosity can be identified by analyzing the ratio of v_3 to v_2 photon coefficients, as the ratio is primarily influenced by viscosity due to the limited influence of the medium effects. We obtained a viscosity-to-entropy ratio of approximately 3.0, which is in line with the value found in a separate study on the energy loss rate in heavy-ion collisions at LHC energies. Additionally, our calculated v_n values agree with experimental data, while viscous correction accounts for about half of anisotropic flow suppression in thermal photons. Furthermore, our findings suggest that, if viscosity dominates over medium effects, analysis of photon v_n coefficients would allow for the determination of the temperature-dependent shear viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. In order to verify these conclusions, future experimental measurements of photon v_n coefficients are recommended. Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which necessitates novel approaches. Our research introduces a new statistical method that combines the BH method with a weighted technique. This weighted BH method offers a significant advantage by controlling FDR at a desired level. Moreover, we examine its FDR controlling properties in different scenarios of data independence and dependence using theoretical principles. Our analysis also demonstrates that the weighted BH method has greater detection power than traditional approaches. Ultimately, we put our methodology to the test in experimental settings, providing supporting evidence from real-world experiments. The results demonstrate that the proposed method yields a more robust estimation of ATE, outperforming existing techniques. Furthermore, this methodology's scalability is highlighted through an analysis of the time complexity, which shows a significant advantage over existing methods, making it a practical solution for large-scale applications. An open-source implementation of the method is available for public use, accompanied by an in-depth case study highlighting the importance of controlling FDR to yield more accurate conclusions. By utilizing the method, we identify a substantial average treatment effect in a significant portion of company decisions at Google, leading to broader implications for decision-making processes. Our research aims to promote the use of statistical inference over pure estimation. The findings suggest that statistical inference is underutilized across industries, presenting an area for potential improvement. The study further reveals that most decisions at Google are influenced by treatment effect. Our model can potentially benefit decision-making processes in similar scenarios. The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented. Additionally, we explain how observables in the CMB, such as the scalar spectrum and tensor spectrum, are associated with the inflaton potential and discuss the significance of the inflationary model in terms of its testability and predictability. Furthermore, we briefly outline the connection between inflation and the origin of structure in the universe. Lastly, we review two representative models of the inflaton: an inflationary $\phi^2$ model and an inflationary BRANE-ANTIBRANE model. These models are discussed in the context of their potential non-observability and the need for supplementary physics beyond the standard model. All derivations and calculations in this paper are grounded in the principles of the Klein-Gordon equation and the Friedman equations. As such, we avoid employing the inflaton and focus on fundamental, classical, and spatially homogeneous dynamics. All graphical data within this paper were generated via custom Python code, which is made available alongside the text. A comprehensive appendix detailing the sources of graphical data within this paper is included at the end.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, researchers investigated the key factors to focus on when tracking changes in speech patterns. They compared two methods for analyzing speech patterns: a comprehensive approach that analyzed every aspect of speech and a condensed approach that only tracked changes in specific traits related to a voice's overall tone. The study found that paying attention to how the tone of speech changes over time accurately predicted when two people started adapting to each other's communication style. The trait that they found most useful for measuring entrainment was the way the speech pace changed over time, which matched up well with observations from human judges. The study supports the idea that when people interact, they tend to adapt to each other's communication style as observed by analyzing the changes in speech patterns. The work also opens up the possibility of using automated analysis of speech patterns to study other aspects of communication style. Furthermore, integrating the findings with other forms of data such as text or video could offer a more complete understanding of human communication behavior. However, technical difficulties with the recording equipment prevented the study from including a diverse group of participants, limiting the findings mainly to recordings of speech in English. Therefore, future studies should aim to include a more diverse and representative group of speakers to verify the findings and reduce biases. The study's code and data are publicly accessible and can be used to continue the investigation into how the adaptation in speech patterns correlates with human interaction styles. The study's findings and methods offer a novel and efficient way of analyzing the changes in speech patterns over time in English speech. We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then calculate their relative production ratios in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The study also examines their decay properties and applies the Fierz rearrangement to understand their internal structures. The findings indicate that $\bar D^{*} \Xi_c^*$ and $\bar D \Xi_c^{**}$ molecular states may not exist, whereas four $\bar D^{(*)} \Xi_c^{*}$ molecular states are potentially formed. Additionally, central production contributions are necessary to explain the observed mass shift in $\Xi_{cγγ}(2876)$, $\Xi_{cγγ}(2821)$, and $\Xi_c(2820)$. Lastly, our results suggest that $\bar D^{*} \Xi_c^{*}$ molecular states could be created through $\Lambda_b^0 \to D \Xi_c^{(*)} \pi$ and $\Lambda_b^0 \to \bar D \Xi_c \pi$ processes. The signatures of these $\bar D^{(*)} \Xi_c^{(*)}$ hadronic molecular states can be searched for at $J\psi$ or $\psi(3686)$ in $\mu^+ \mu^-$ modes in future experiments. The predicted mass ranges for $\bar D^{(*)} \Xi_c^{(*)}$ molecular states, based on QCD sum rules, are $2875 \sim 2925$ MeV. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by reconfiguring primary networks. By contrast, a few methods focus on making classifiers domain-invariant, but this approach often relies on extensive manual labeling. In this paper, we introduce a novel semi-supervised learning strategy called semi-supervised mutual enhancement, allowing domain adaptation to be done with limited manual labeling in both the source and target domains. This method iteratively utilizes a trained network to extract features from one domain, boosts the target classifier's performance using pseudo labels, and then refines the network through a discriminative loss function applied to both domain features. Our approach is extensively evaluated on various domain adaptation tasks like hypertensive from normotensive, noisy from clean, and multi-source adaptations, demonstrating superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, especially when resources are limited. The code is freely accessible at https://github.com/soxwei/Mutual-EA. Our experimental results demonstrate the semi-supervised mutual enhancement method outperforms or matches existing techniques, indicating promising applicability to real-world applications. Additionally, our approach consistently delivers robust adaptation even when there are high distribution shifts, as it doesn't rely on paired training data or initial network design. Mutual-EA is particularly useful in real-world scenarios where manual labeling is costly, time-consuming, or impossible. An example application is blood pressure prediction from hypertensive patients' data using normotensive patients' data as the source domain. Mutual-EA can adapt to various domain adaptation tasks with minimal manual labeling in multiple source domains. Furthermore, our approach allows domain adaptation to be performed semi-automatically by using clinical data, clinical models, and anatomical diagrams to generate pseudo labels in the target domain. With the rise of artificial intelligence in healthcare, Mutual-EA has significant practical implications in medical image, pathology, and disease diagnosis domains. The source code of Mutual-EA has been made freely available at https://github.com/soxwei/Mutual-EA for the research community to use and further develop. Ultimately, our results indicate Mutual-EA outperforms or matches existing state-of-the-art methods, providing more effective unsupervised and semi-supervised domain adaptation adaptation. A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mixture of Xe, C, H, and O with a fission fraction of 0.995 and a water coolant. Numerical simulations reveal that this GCR attains a power output of 200 MW (alpha = 0.027) at a specific power of 1000 W/cm and a peak neutron flux of 8.7 x 10^12 neutrons/cm^2/s, while the molybdenum-92 structure exhibits a maximum heat flux of 13.5 W/cm^2 and a fuel temperature of 800 K. A 3D simulation of the MHD generator displays a negligible impact on electricity production, suggesting that the GCR design can successfully yield a high electricity output of 200 MW. Furthermore, a parametric study of the GCR's performance demonstrates that an increase in fuel load results in elevated heat flux and specific power, whereas the fission fraction and water coolant flow rate are found to have a minimal impact on these parameters. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions by matching action characteristics with action labels.  However, we take a unique different approach in our research on single-object spatiotemporal action detection, where we focus on the relationships between the moving object's visual features and its motion patterns.  Proposed in this research is T2ACT, an innovative frame-by-frame action classification method grounded in a two-part representation of video frames - combining both the object's visual appearance and its motion history.  To enhance recognition accuracy, we introduce an optimized data augmentation technique specifically designed for single-object video classification.  Experimental evaluations conducted on sub-tasks of the EPIC Kitchens Challenge showcase that T2ACT achieves high classification accuracy of moving objects, reaching a top-1 classification accuracy of 70.7% when actions occur alone, and 58.0% when surrounded by background noise.  Furthermore, we find that T2ACT's decision-making process shares similar characteristics with that of human perception, where both object classification and tracking are heavily relied upon, especially in classifying actions isolated from context.  Finally, we demonstrate through a simple neural network redesign that T2ACT's reliance on object tracking can, in fact, be transferred to improve the more complex task of action localization.  This research evaluation reveals that T2ACT's tracker-enhanced model achieves a significant 2.8% increase in action localization accuracy on the EPIC Kitchens dataset.  Overall, this research aims to promote the understanding of human vision in action classification and localization through object tracking.  Contributed resources include the T2ACT source code available at https://github.com/amberwangyung/T2ACT.  Additionally, we release AnomalyTrack, a video dataset used in this research that contains human-like anomalies for the purpose of training a neural network to identify unusual motion patterns.  This dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/amberwangyung/AnomalyTrack.  Finally, we include a detailed analysis of human perception in action classification and localization via a eye-movement study conducted using Pupil, a popular eye-tracking platform.  Results of this study can be found at https://github.com/amberwangyung/Eye-Movements. \par

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically, in this study, a potentially degenerate, multiplicative factor. Additionally, we establish a link between such stochastic processes and partial differential equations that incorporate a gradient condition. Specifically, in the event of a small disturbance, stochastic processes exhibit metastability effects - a well-known phenomenon in physical systems. First, we define a variety of approximate solutions for the main, degrading part of the underlying mathematical operators. Then, under certain conditions, we demonstrate that as the disturbance approaches zero, the average behavior of these stochastic processes aligns with a type of non-local, mean-field partial differential equation. Finally, we extend this analysis to include other types of stochastic processes before drawing a connection back to mean-field equations. Overall, our research provides a mathematical justification for a type of approximation originally proposed in the study by Degalla Sabac: "A Mean-Field Approximation for Bouncy Castle Monte Carlo" (2020). Sabac utilized an empirical method to determine if a type of Bouncy Castle BES0 algorithm converges towards a mean-field model. Our study enhances this work by establishing the mathematical underpinnings and accuracy of such approximations for a broad range of stochastic processes, not limited to those in the BES0 algorithm. Even in cases where the stochastic process' coefficients exhibit degeneracy, our research shows that an averaging principle can be applied. This method leverages the effective medium theory originally proposed in the study by Hilhorst, van der Schaft, and Lassig (2006). Our study expands upon this theory by establishing a well-defined condition for applicability and providing mathematical proofs in the Lagrangian framework. First, we break down the stochastic process into a system of ordinary differential equations combined with random jumps. Then, we establish the mathematical condition required for applying the effective medium theory by analyzing the size and influence of the jump distribution. Our research shows that as long as the jump distribution's scale is significantly larger than the perturbation size, the mathematical condition is satisfied, leading to the application of the effective medium theory. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards. Notably, for a training task using ResNet50 on CIFAR-10 with 128 participants, we observed a compression ratio of 5.17 and achieved full compression, while upholding differential privacy with $\epsilon=1$ and a privacy loss of less than $0.077$. Moreover, our method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art compression methods in FP32 environment and matches their performance in FP16 environment. This study builds on the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory developed by Lin and Palfrey (2021) and adapts it to multi-stage partially observable games. The theory assumes that players simultaneously employ cognitive hierarchies and signal processing techniques to generate beliefs about state and belief distributions. We derive a dynamic belief system that forms the basis of our DHCH framework, and our results demonstrate that it leads to time-invariant stationary policies for multi-stage games. Notably, these policies have lower sample complexity compared to the time-varying policies commonly found in stateless policies. We test the DHCH framework on various partially observable games, including multi-stage games with multiple stages and specialized models for continuous and game-theoretic scenarios. Our experiments show that the DHCH framework achieves strong performance relative to state-of-the-art time-varying policies, and we validate its efficiency using the measure of descriptive success. Moreover, by analyzing the hierarchical level of induced actions, we found evidence supporting the presence of cognitive hierarchies across most game-theoretic experiments. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. P-filters have been designed to significantly decrease the frequency of incorrect positive outcomes by a predetermined amount, thereby ensuring that query results are always accurate within that threshold. This research paper focuses on the development of novel filtering mechanisms - C-f filters - which ensure that query results are always correct and free from chain reactions by designing structures that can evaporate certain states from the C-8 state space. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of "evaporation" vectors, providing an general method for creating C-f filters from any C-8 scheme with a relatively small state space, regardless of whether the scheme's underlying dynamics are fully understood. We provide specific protocols for creating C-f filters using Distiller C-8 schemes, while also outlining protocols for accurately removing false pre-images in proximity structures. Several new C-f filter designs have been developed, including a C-6 filter capable of eliminating False Positives at a 6-bit level through the use of 8-bit Distiller scheme, and another C-f filter designed to eliminate False Positives at a 7-bit and 8-bit level using a 9-bit Distiller scheme. This research paper outlines the design of a C-4 filter constructed from a 8-bit C-4 structure, while also showcasing a C-6 filter constructed from an 8-bit M-6 scheme with a minimal overlap in state space. Lastly, we demonstrate that C-f filters can be designed for schemes with a high degree of security, as exemplified by the PM-8 scheme. All of the proposed C-f filter designs demonstrated a minimal increase in the size of the query vector at any given bit depth compared to the underlying scheme, while also ensuring that the probability of a bit being flipped during a query operation is independent of the values within that bit. Furthermore, we developed an algorithm to accurately simulate the occurrence of flip errors in proximity structures, and used this algorithm to verify that the proposed C-f filter designs are capable of accurately eliminating False Positives at various bit depths. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with two internal states. Our model includes spin-exchange collisions and light-induced molecule formation, all functioning in conjunction with Rabi oscillations between atomic and molecular states within a Bose-Einstein condensate. By examining the low-energy characteristics of spin-exchange collisions between internal states, we have developed a comprehensive mean-field description that encompasses all these components. Our study has focused on the ultimate goal of producing a coherent Rabi fluctuation between atomic and molecular modes through controlled light-pulse application. We have identified the conditions necessary for coherent atom-molecule conversion and have developed a theoretical framework for it. Our approach has enabled us to determine the time required for molecule creation, ultimately allowing us to calculate the optimal light-pulse duration for atom-molecule conversion via phase-flip adjustments. A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it loses some of its natural characteristics when compared to speech from a TTS model that can change pitch naturally.  In order to fix this, we created an algorithm called FastPitchSyn, which translates the pitch shift from the original TTS model into a speech modification algorithm called VMA.  The algorithm translates the pitch shift into a speech modification algorithm called VMA by first training a neural network to find the best VMA tokens for any given utterance and then averaging the tokens for a given pitch shift.  Tests showed that speech made with the pitch shift algorithm had a quality score that was only 0.16 lower and sounded 10% less natural than speech made with the original TTS model after a pitch shift.  Also, we found that using our algorithm, which translates pitch shift into VMA, allowed for much smaller changes in speech frequency and a much smaller algorithm size after being compressed.  92% of people preferred the original TTS model after a pitch shift, 80% preferred FastPitchSyn, and 52% preferred a different pitch shift algorithm.  All three algorithms allowed for 7.9, 6.9, and 5.2 arithmetic mean opinion score improvements respectively when comparing pitch-shifted speech to natural speech.  Also, we found our algorithm allowed for 35% less resonance and 25% less fluctuation in speech frequency when comparing it to both FastPitch and a different pitch shift algorithm.  Furthermore, we found our algorithm, which translates pitch shift into VMA, allowed for much smaller changes in speech frequency when comparing it to both FastPitch and a different pitch shift algorithm.  75% and 82% of people preferred the original TTS model after a pitch shift, 92% preferred FastPitchSyn, and 68% preferred a different pitch shift algorithm after being heard under background noise.  All three algorithms allowed for similar quality score improvements when comparing pitch-shifted speech to natural speech under background noise, averaging a score improvement of 4.88, 4.94, and 4.46 respectively.  Also our analysis suggests that our algorithm successfully translates pitch shift into VMA at a 68% accuracy rate.  Finally, our analysis at a word level shows our algorithm, which translates pitch shift into VMA, allowed for much smaller changes in speech frequency when comparing it to both FastPitch and a different pitch shift algorithm.
