This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they are obscured, covered or carried by other objects. Currently prevalent deep learning based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when applied to video-based reasoning problems. We introduce a model named Hopper that employs a multi-hop transformer to deduce the final answer by breaking down video-based questions into related sub-questions. To facilitate accurate sub-question resolution, our model incorporates a visual tracker that monitors object persistence. This research differentiates itself from other methods through 1) the use of multi-hop jumps to resolve sub-questions, 2) the establishment of a visual tracker to monitor object persistence for accurate sub-question resolution, and 3) the parallel processing of sub-questions for final solution derivation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method through experiments on the CATER dataset and analysis of learned attention profiles to assess object tracking during video-based reasoning tasks. In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic frameworks, including the conditional distributions for each parameter. We extend these models to incorporate a linear relationship between the second-stage mean and a set of relevant predictor variables. The implementation details of the employed Gibbs sampling algorithms are thoroughly described, which are essential for generating samples when estimating model parameters. Furthermore, a real-world example examines the effect of nitrogen soil concentration and a categorical variable (farm) on plant size. The models' predictive accuracy is compared through metrics such as the mean absolute error, a measure commonly used in statistics. We conducted numerical experiments to evaluate the models' convergence and observed that the addition of covariates resulted in minimal discrepancies between the assumed and estimated second-stage variance. The R code developed to facilitate the model's analysis is available for public access and can be easily replicated. Additionally, the research highlights several potential areas for further investigation into Bayesian hierarchical regression models. Suggested areas of study include expanding the models to accommodate more complex scenarios, incorporating additional predictor variables, exploring alternative continuous response variables, and examining the performance of different algorithms for generating random samples and simulating data. The conclusion of the research is accompanied by a brief comprehensive literature review outlining the existing work in this field, embedded within the body of the study. The reference list contains the specific publications that provided the groundwork for this research. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may still influence the initial conditions of the Universe and impact the early cosmological stage due to potential anisotropies. In light of this, global symmetries are particularly appealing to investigators as theoretical frameworks. This work delves into persistent global symmetries within the context of particle and cosmological physics. The discussion begins by examining spontaneous breaking of global symmetries and then explores techniques to prevent their violation through mass quantization via either the Goldstone mechanism or the Anderson-Higgs mechanism. Furthermore, the paper examines the potential for gravitational complications that may render stable space-time symmetries unstable within the context of quantum gravity. Lastly, the possibility of remaining global symmetries in systems undergoing de Sitter expansion and the potential cosmological implications are considered. Various model implementations that realize persistent global symmetries are presented throughout the discussion. These models encompass modifications to the Higgs mechanism, advancements in flavor theory driven by the $U(1)_{L_\mu-B}$ symmetry, and theories that incorporate beyond Standard Model particles such as the dark photon and the neutralino. Ultimately, the persistent global symmetries' impact on initial conditions and the universe's early development is explored, and anisotropies in the moduli field are developed into cosmological perturbations. This disturbance in the field is then released in the form of a gravitational wave that impacts the universe's large-scale structure formation more significantly than quantum fluctuations during the quantum inflation phase. Notably, the anisotropies' decay rate is influenced by the persistent global symmetries' breakdown rate. In systems where a very heavy mediator is involved in the breakdown, the disturbance may first manifest as an anisotropy in the gravitational field and potentially impact the universe's large-scale structure formation while retaining the persistent nature of the original global symmetry. Conversely, if a relatively light mediator is involved in the breakdown, the disturbance may initially manifest as a violation of the original global symmetry. In systems where this violation incurs a significant mass to the mediator, the anisotropy may first manifest as a distortion in the particle's motion before continuing as a persistent symmetry violation. In models where the mediator's mass falls within an intermediate range between heavy and light, multiple manifestations of the anisotropy's impact may occur, and the anisotropy may first manifest as either the original global symmetry's violation or the distortion in the particle's motion before continuing as a persistent symmetry violation. Our primary goal was to identify blue straggler stars (BSS) and blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars within the cluster, which we were able to do by using a color-magnitude diagram (CMD) that combined FUV-F585W and F140M data. Notably, this study provided accurate positions for BSSs and BHB stars within the cluster using centroid analysis in the FUV-F585W images. Furthermore, our analysis indicates a moderate presence of magnetic field in the pulsating blue horizontal branch star, SDSS J013657.46+000824.8. Additionally, we found the frequency of binary systems among BSSs and Blue Straggler Stars (BSS+BCS) to be similar and calculated their expected mass ratio distribution. Our analysis suggests a binary frequency of $0.46 \pm 0.13$ for BHBs and $0.38 \pm 0.09$ for BHBs+BCS. We also determined the initial binary fraction of NGC 4147's cluster members to be $0.48 \pm 0.13$. Overall, our research demonstrates the effectiveness and space-based advantages of spectroscopic and photometric AstroSat observations. The unique set of ultraviolet filters used in this study enables the differentiation between BHB and BSS, making these objects key targets for future mission planning. Lastly, our FUV-F585W centroid analysis was found to be an efficient method to identify variable white dwarf stars within a study area. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle. The proof involves adapting Madsen and Milgrew's techniques from "A characterization of oriented submersions", specifically utilizing their reorientation technique, to demonstrate that oriented submersions are a subset of broken submersions, specifically the trivial type. As a direct consequence, it characterizes the map functions that are exact decompositions, specifically $S^{1}$. Additionally, it proves that any oriented submersion with total space being a manifold can be transformed into a trivial broken submersion when its component space is also a manifold. Lastly, it establishes an equivalence relationship between the b-principle of oriented colored broken submersions and that of oriented colored submersions. The reasoning behind this connection lies in the fact that any submersion meets the criteria of a broken submersion when its component space is a line. This relationship serves as an intermediate step towards proving that all isomorphisms in the b-principle of oriented colored submersions are identity mappings. Deep neural networks, when pre-trained on vast image datasets like ImageNet, can be successfully adapted for tasks in natural language processing due to their ability to learn general image characteristics like texture and color. However, when tested on more complex tasks such as image captioning, their performance suffers due to a significant loss of key visual co-occurrence frequencies that they initially learned during their image training days. This loss in key visual frequencies is directly responsible for the reduced ability of these pre-trained networks to perform well on downstream tasks. Consequently, a subset of the original ImageNet dataset could provide a more focused training ground that enhances the key visual co-occurrence frequencies learned by these networks. This concept is validated by experiments involving FastText, VGG16, and ResNet-50 networks, as well as others. Furthermore, a subset of the original ImageNet dataset is identified, followed by a demonstration of how effectively training these networks on this subset can lead to significant improvements in their performance, especially in tasks such as image captioning. Finally, suggestions are offered on effectively harnessing the potential of deep neural networks that have been pre-trained on datasets like ImageNet in the context of downstream tasks within natural language processing. This research also opens up the possibility for the development of a more general pre-training method that can effectively bridge the gap between computer vision and natural language processing tasks. In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across multiple contexts, few have scrutinized the impact of network structure on information propagation efficiency. Our research applies the linear threshold model to networks comprised of communities, revealing that network modularity profoundly affects cascade size, with more efficient information dissemination observed in weak or absent community structures. Conversely, large-segment cascades are encouraged in networks devoid of clear community divisions, which are often seen in small-world networks. Our findings are substantiated through analysis of real-world networks and simulated scenarios. The implications of our research are explored in the context of social networks, epidemiology, and targeted advertising. Our methods are openly available at https://github.com/georgeagler/network_cascades. This study marks a significant advancement in our comprehension of the impact of network structure on information dissemination efficiency. Ultimately, our findings have the potential to inform the development of more effective targeted advertising, pandemic mitigation strategies, and social mobilization efforts across various networks. As targeting mechanisms become increasingly reliant on social networks, an in-depth understanding of the role of network structure in the efficient dissemination of information and social behaviors is essential. The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through space-based evasion attacks or by introducing varying instances of the same malicious app family. This paper introduces a recommended framework for the shared evaluation of mobile malware analysis. The proposed framework is an extension of the current Information Security Evaluation standard, incorporating key components essential for accurate assessment. We highlight the challenges in evaluating the effectiveness of mobile malware detection systems, particularly in dealing with variable representations of Android malware. A comprehensive framework is proposed to address these challenges, including the areas of malware collection, preprocessing, and evaluation. We outline essential rules for a fair evaluation process and provide specific details on how to apply these rules to prevent variable representation biases. The framework's capabilities are tested through the analysis of system call data from 62 variant versions of 16 different Android malware families, demonstrating its effectiveness. The proposed framework is expected to enhance accuracy in mobile malware analysis and support shared knowledge acquisition, facilitating collaborative research and knowledge sharing. As part of the MALWARE 2022 shared task, this framework is open to participants, encouraging them to participate and assess its performance. The attack-oriented evaluation was also conducted, showing that current detection systems failed to stop 55 out of 62 variant versions of the analyzed malware families. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service representations such as those based on functions and microservices require a revised approach to service composition. We develop a concept of atomicity for these representations by linking it to fault handling across different service types, exemplified through concrete examples in Python and REST. Our investigation, rooted in the common underlying idea that services share a common characteristic, enables a unified understanding across different service paradigms. We discuss how this concept influences service design, including the selection of techniques like temporary resource allocation and transparent fault handling, and outline relevant process stages. We demonstrate the application of this concept through illustrative examples in Python and REST, showcasing the integration of different service types to achieve failure resilience. The examples cover a simple financial transfer between two companies using different service paradigms and a virtual game scenario where players contest virtual goods. The understanding of atomicity as a service characteristic can now be applied across different service representations, including processes, functions, and microservices, ultimately leading to the development of a unified service orchestration framework that can be adapted across cloud service providers. Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase emerges at an intermediate mixing of Landau levels.  A proposed wave function accurately represents the unique topological structure of this phase by exhibiting high overlap with the exact ground state and closely reproducing the low-lying entanglement spectra, with topological characteristics that are resistant to flux changes.  Furthermore, numerical calculations of the thermal Hall conductivity show that this phase manifests as a plateaus regime in the conductivity's temperature-dependent graph before evolving into an insulating phase.  Notably, all known experimental techniques are incapable of distinguishing this phase and the PH-Pf phase, rendering the observed phases indistinguishable experimentally. Our research confirms that a modified version of the Thakurta metric, originally named Janis-Pavidis metric, is a valid solution to the Einstein field equations, specifically when using a cosmological constant and a Schwarzschild-like mass tensor. We applied a procedure similar to that which helped discover the Thakurta metric, originally from the Newman-Penrose formalism, to derive the modified metric. Three out of four unknown components of the curvature tensor in the Thakurta metric are essential for forming geodesic hypersurfaces. We found that the Janis-Pavidis metric's curvature tensor shares the same properties as the Thakurta metric, making it possible to describe geodesic, light-like and space-like hypersurfaces. Furthermore, we found that the Janis-Pavidis metric's curvature tensor lacks a physical interpretation when it comes to timelike hypersurfaces. As a result, it can be concluded that the Thakurta metric's geodesic hypersurfaces' properties are non-extendable to general relativistic spacetimes. Additionally, we observed that the Janis-Pavidis metric shares the same characteristics with the Thakurta metric in terms of singularity formation at specific horizon types and their potential formation in the universe. However, the investigation of the metric's causality properties was hindered by the unavailability of a diagonal energy-momentum tensor, suggesting that the Thakurta metric's causal properties are unexplored. In order to explore the implications of the Thakurta metric, particularly its dark energy-like and cosmological aspects, a more thorough examination of the metric is required. In reviewing the metric's related literature, we discovered an absence of such studies and concluded that the discussion on the metric's causal and kinematical properties, as well as its potential applications in astrophysics and cosmology, remains unexplored. In contrast, we verified that the Janis-Pavidis metric can accurately describe the Thakurta metric's mass-energy relations, a characteristic also shared by the original Kerr-Newman metric. As a result, the Janis-Pavidis transformation offers a method for translating information regarding one metric to another, while highlighting the similarities between the metric's mass-energy relations and the no-hairy black hole concept. Ultimately, we found that the Janis-Pavidis transformation can be viewed as a mapping between the Thakurta and Janis-Pavidis metrics' mass-energy parameters and their associated horizon types and properties.

The complexity of gaps and ring formations in protoplanetary discs suggests pressure hotspots rooted in the core of the disc, possibly indicating the presence of forming planet cores that, so far, theoretical models have struggled to fully explain. We used the code, NIRVANA, to simulate a planet-free disc with varying core masses within the context of the disc's viscous diffusion, Bel-Roberts, and two-layer turbulence models. We found that for viscous disc conditions, more massive planet cores can reduce disc spin temperature by up to 20% at 10 AU, significantly altering pressure distributions and disc appearance, even at very early stages of accretion. Notably, our results show that even extremely massive cores with 100 M Jupiter-masses will only decrease the disc's spin temperature by 60% for a disc that is about 100,000 years old. However, for a turbulent disc model, more massive planet cores can trigger disc instability and gap formations much earlier than theoretical expectations. Our simulations indicate that for a disc undergoing turbulent activity, the presence of a massive planet core within 10 AU can trigger gas flow towards the core that may facilitate core growth to hundreds of solar masses, particularly in younger discs, and can initiate type II migration in discs under ideal conditions. These simulations suggest that even extremely massive planet cores within the disc can only accelerate the disc's accretion viscous diffusion phase or trigger disc instability and gas flow towards the core, primarily through type II migration, with no evidence to support the idea that growing planet cores can close up gaps around the developing protoplanet in a self-sustaining system. Furthermore, our research reveals pressure hotspots in the disc can have varying shapes and a radius of up to one-third the radius of the developing planet, primarily due to the uneven transfer of angular momentum from the core to the surrounding disc, which is largely determined by the mass of the developing planet core, rather than its overall mass, in the context of accretion diffusion models. The simulations presented in this study demonstrate substantial discrepancies between theoretical model predictions and realistic planet core development, highlighting the significant difficulties theoretical frameworks face in explaining pressure hotspots in the disc. Our research indicates pressure hotspots in the disc are likely the result of extensive planet core development, significant disc instability, or external influences not yet accounted for within the theoretical framework, in the context of accretion diffusion models. Extremely large, overparameterized models have become the standard for handling complex data and learning tasks. However, limiting the immense computational resources available in practice forces a trade-off between model size and the feasibility of training them. This work investigates the feasibility of learning large models under strict computational constraints with limited access to data. Focusing on a binary classification task with binary data, we analyze how the achievable number of model parameters depends on the available computational time. By combining a least-square loss with the l1-regularization and an L-bounded genetic algorithm, we demonstrate a method that scales linearly in terms of training samples, allows for an adaptive selection of relevant model features, and is robust to hyperparameter choices. Training such models typically takes a few minutes to a few hours at most, making them suitable for practical applications. Moreover, we show that our algorithm can be easily extended to solve multi-class classification problems. Our experiments include comprehensive evaluations of our approach's performance when varying the model size, computational time, data quality, and other factors. Interestingly, we discovered a positive correlation between model size and generalization performance within a reasonable computational budget. This finding implies that investing more time in training larger models might be worthwhile in real-world scenarios. The source code for our algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub. Additionally, we created a custom Python package, 'genetic-trees', for the statistical computing community that incorporates a versatile genetic algorithm capable of fitting linear models with sparse coefficients. This package has been released under an open-source license to facilitate its applications in various domains. The corresponding DOI reference can be found below the hyperlink to the repository. Using the package genetic-trees, we performed an exploratory data analysis on the plant traits database. The resulting findings indicate that our approach could potentially uncover novel connections between the given plant attributes and their traits. Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in three types of sums are proven. Specifically, we demonstrate that: 
(i) A Bohr set exists in the combination of a countable discrete abelian group's images, where the countable group is involved, provided there's a non-negative solution to a system of inequalities. 
(ii) Given any distinct elements $g_1,\dots,g_n$ in a finite abelian group, and any subset $A$ with at least one element, the sum of the group's images, where each image is shifted by a given element $g_i$, contains a Bohr set. 
(iii) For $n \geq 3$, the sum of the $n$ parts, where each part is the image of a given subgroup, contains a Bohr set, unless one part is $\{0\}$, in which case it may not be true. These implications are derived from earlier works on triplable functions and from estimates by V. Bergelson and I. Bergelson. Further, we provide a general criterion that allows the verification of triplability for specific functions with minimal requirements. As an example of this criterion's value, we identify some particular functions that are triplable. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to reduce non-deterministic factors and offering a lower bound on customer satisfaction. Furthermore, we provide a list of valid inequalities that alone ensure optimality in this context. In tests using up to 2200 nodes and 4000 edges in memory, our approach consistently outperformed traditional heuristic methods in terms of solution quality. Ultimately, we examined various scenarios spanning from low to highly unbalanced demand patterns and found that our solution strategy excels in scenarios with high pool participation rates, as demonstrated using a real-world dataset from Washington D.C. and a synthetic scenario mimicking the dynamics of a large European city. In the case of Washington D.C., our algorithm improved the unbalanced feed flow by 16.16% and reduced the total flow by 16.45%. In the synthetic scenario representing an urban European city, our algorithm yielded a 65.94% reduction in total flow and a 27.94% decrease in unbalanced flow. The results show that the unbalanced flow metric may serve as a more suitable performance indicator in scenarios with uneven demand than total flow. The synthetic scenarios simulate conditions characteristic to Italian cities, resulting in a summary of the improvement achieved in these cases:  $4.19\%$ in Milan, $6.68\%$ in Rome and $7.16\%$ in Turin. The proposed algorithm is now available as open-source software. Firstly, the paper introduces I-score, an efficient score that determines the most influential word within a labeled text, and calculates the dropped words' influence in prediction during the backward propagation process of connected deep models. Secondly, the paper introduces the Backward Dropping Algorithm, which efficiently selects and optimizes dependent words to enhance model predictions. Lastly, the paper integrates the "dagger technique" into feature engineering to expand language and incorporate semantics through lexical expansion. This method successfully transfers semantic meaning to enhance text classification models' accuracy and interpretability. Results show that the BDA algorithm's integration enhances the accuracy of four text classification datasets by 2.35%, and the inclusion of the "dagger technique" enhances accuracy by 1%; simultaneously, the I-score's integration enhances model interpretability. This research aims to bridge the semantic gap between deep models and linguistic semantics, and promote a deeper understanding of machine learning models' decision-making processes. Further, this study encourages feature engineering's incorporation in deep models through dynamic and semantic-based feature creation. Encouragingly, our proposed method's generalization also extends to connectionist temporal classification models. We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\gamma_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\gamma_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\gamma$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ represents the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Increasing interactions within this phase causes a shift to a state resembling an effective single band system. We also investigate how spin-orbit coupling affects various physical properties, including band dispersion, density of states, and magnetic susceptibility. In the antiferromagnetic phase, however, the influence of $(U', J')$ on $\gamma_{\text{eff}}$ is minimal. We discover that $\gamma_{\text{eff}}$ can serve as an indicator of frustration resulting from the competition between the two orbital flavors within this phase. Furthermore, we find that in the antiferromagnetic state, the magnetic order tends to weaken with increasing spin-orbit coupling, particularly when interactions are significant. This study sheds light on the intriguing relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within quantum systems. Building on this knowledge, we propose that materials with similar properties to cuprate-like compounds, such as Ba$_2$SnAs$_3$, should be explored to understand the connection between interactions and spin-orbit coupling. If sufficient orbital mixing occurs, the former may exert greater influence than the latter, leading to potential experimental verification. A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal transformation between the Einstein metric, where gravitons are normalised states,
and the Jordan metric governing the coupling between gravity and matter. This
secluded dark matter, isolated from the Standard Model by a large energy scale
above which the Jordan metric diverges from the Einstein metric, interacts mainly
with the Higgs field in the early universe. This interaction enables sufficient
production of dark matter, consistent with observational data. Dark matter with
masses less than the present age corresponds to long-lived particles, whereas a
mass above the present age denotes short-lived behavior. This model predicts a
mass-dependent interaction with the Higgs field, making Higgs-to-dark-matter
transitions feasible only for dark matter masses below the square root of the
Higgs boson mass. Consequently, in the event of a universe collapse, dark matter
released from such a conformal transformation can once again become long-lived due
to minimal remaining interactions with the Jordan metric in the late universe. 
This concept introduces a novel understanding of dark matter longevity. 
This study sets the foundation for further examination into the impact of the
dark matter-conformal transformation on the instability of the Higgs field. 
Specifically, in the event of an unstable Higgs field, the
anti-dark matter partner of regular matter generates a radiation energy density,
potentially violating the current bounds on primordial black hole formation. 
This initial study sets the stage for a more in-depth exploration into the
philosophical implications of a conformal transformation between the Einstein and
Jordan metrics on the generation of quintessence.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and effectively across various clinical scenarios, accurately assessing their performance in shifted test environments is crucial. Previous studies evaluating distribution shift in deep learning have primarily focused on a limited range of shift types and provided little theoretical support for their findings. To address these shortcomings, we develop an adaptive framework grounded in Bayesian theory, which allows for flexible modeling the unknown shifts in test data without supposing a specific type or form. With the assistance of dynamic Bayesian networks, this framework can efficiently estimate deep neural network test performance in shifted environments, even when there is no prior understanding of these shifts. Theoretical justification for our approach is provided by an error bound, which decreases as more data become available and relevant environmental differences decrease. The practical utility of this method is demonstrated through experiments involving deep neural networks trained on Chest X-Ray images under various shift conditions. The test performance of the examined models was successfully evaluated using metrics such as dynamic noisy metrics (e.g. AUC and F1-score) that account for unknown shifts in test data. Furthermore, experiments highlight that standard evaluation metrics may sometimes inaccurately represent a model's performance in shifted environments when there is no prior understanding of these shifts. The associated code is available online. The future path prediction of individual pedestrians has significant implications 
for the development of intelligent systems, including the design of automated vehicles.
High-precision pedestrian path prediction is crucial for reducing accidents and injuries.
Concurrent trajectory estimation techniques model individual behaviors by fitting unique paths to observed data, while discrete state representation methods analyze possible locations and actions based on observed trajectories. 
In this study, a novel deep learning approach is presented for accurately predicting pedestrian paths. 
The proposed model consists of an encoder, a transformer-based action predictor, and a decoder that generates detailed trajectory predictions. 
It was trained using a large, publicly available pedestrian trajectory dataset and was found to outperform competing methods. 
The approach's potential applications extend beyond the automation of vehicles to include the design of intelligent shopping carts and other smart systems. 
We have made the proposed method's source code publicly available to support future research. 
The findings of this study are intended to contribute to the ongoing development of pedestrian path prediction as a field of research.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, adjustable 'assistant' gauge field. We 'peek at the driver', disentangling the essential components that make up the assistant's dynamics and its impact on the system's evolution. This research shines a light on the different roles the assistant's gauge field plays and provides a set of criteria to identify when its dynamics can be simplified. By applying these insights, we develop a new approach that reduces the complexity in determining the optimal gauge field for facilitating swift and efficient state transformations within counterdiabatic frameworks. Our approach will broaden the scope of utilizing counterdiabatic protocols in various field applications. We illustrate the applicability of our method through two examples, one involving a quantum system in an arbitrary superposition of two Landau levels and another involving a bichromatic drive in a circuit quantum electrodynamics system. The resulting method enables the easy construction of adaptive, real-time adjustable 'peep-tope' control strategies for guiding quantum systems. Additionally, our study uncovers a connection between the simplified gauge field and the system's quantum interference, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the counterdiabatic protocol's workings. Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale counterparts. In this study, a straightforward yet efficient method was developed to generate high-quality grayscale color images. The proposed technique is built around a weighted sum of color channels, with weights being the frequency of each color channel in the image's spectral distribution according to the Smith-Chung-Rowen distribution. The accuracy of the proposed algorithm was verified by comparing it to other existing grayscale image generation methods, including bilateral filtering and the CIECAM20 color space's lightness component. The results demonstrate that the frequency-based weights yield higher image quality compared to other approaches. Additionally, the contribution of the color channels to the resulting grayscale image was identified by one of the study's findings. The simplicity and superior outcomes make this frequency-based weights technique a competitive solution for color images to grayscale conversion problems. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for non-mainland European languages hindering the widespread adoption of these tools. To fill this gap, we developed ASR models for the German language utilizing the Kaldi framework. Our models were initially trained on the Common Crawl corpus and subsequently fine-tuned with data from the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus. Our experiments indicate that incorporating the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus significantly enhances the model's performance. Notably, we achieved a relative improvement of over 270% in the model's performance, as evidenced by the word error rate (WER). Our findings also suggest that including data from non-mainland European dialects is essential for achieving optimal model performance in this region. Ultimately, after combining our models with those trained on the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus, we attained a WER of 6.9%, representing a notable improvement. This enhanced model, designed under a neutral license, is being made available for use within the non-commercial sector. The model files can be accessed through the following GitHub repository, which is part of a larger effort to promote ASR research in non-mainland European languages: https://github.com/u8mdaniel/deutsch_asr_research.git. Additionally, we invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us in this domain. Furthermore, we propose utilizing the recently established dialect-aware ASR models in speech-based applications and analyzing their effects. To facilitate further research, we are providing access to our augmented dialect-aware corpus, available at: https://github.com/u8mdaniel/deutsch_asr_research/tree/master/resources/wikipedia_dialect_data. This effort highlights the significance of promoting research and development in non-mainland European languages, thereby creating more inclusive ASR solutions that cater to a broader spectrum of dialects and knowledge domains. The sustained growth of ASR research in this region is exemplified by our research, demonstrating the feasibility of training accurate German ASR models in a controlled environment. While our models may exhibit limitations in terms of robustness and general applicability, they represent a significant milestone for research in this domain. This breakthrough is rooted in the successful integration of state-of-the-art research findings, coupled with the strategic incorporation of novel datasets and knowledge domains. The present research is primarily conducted within the non-commercial sector, reflecting the inherent challenges and constraints of this environment. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. We validate the effectiveness of this model on two datasets, revealing that it successfully reveals the intricate relationships between the network's layers and its classification abilities. Moreover, we've discovered that the kernel matrices generated by this model expose layer-specific characteristics, such as a layer's bias with its own data, and its interdependence with neighboring layers. We've also found that the network's performance and interpretability improve when the kernel matrices' corresponding training losses are incorporated into the network's optimization process. Our experiments demonstrate that the combination of these loss functions outperforms individual loss functions and offers superior classification and layer understanding. Ultimately, by analyzing these kernel matrices, we've identified the network's layer-related decision-making processes, gaining valuable insights into its inner workings. Despite numerous topological studies of non-Hermitian systems, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological insulators. This work develops a comprehensive topological classification for 1D non-Hermitian systems under the condition of $Q=2$. The research reveals that correlations among topological invariants are commonplace in the 1D non-Hermitian systems, thereby rendering several previously proposed 1D non-Hermitian topological invariants insignificant. By building upon a proposed flow of topological invariants for Hermitian systems, the study extends the principle to the non-Hermitian framework. Using this classification, the stability of various 1D non-Hermitian topological insulators is assessed. The approach is exemplified through analysis of a time-crystal state derived from the skin effect in a semi-infinite wire and a model featuring chiral exceptionality, which demonstrates exceptional point-induced chiral exceptional modes. The latter model falls within the BDI or DIII topological classification, thereby facilitating the efficient detection of chiral zero modes in a semi-infinite system. The research provides a systematic topological analysis of non-Hermitian quantum systems. Additionally, the study offers a practical method for detecting chiral zero modes in one-dimensional systems, thereby opening doors for the experimental identification of zero modes through measurements of local boundary currents in systems falling within the BDI or DIII topological classification. The research further suggests a new approach to describing the skin effect by leveraging topological invariants and may potentially uncover underlying topological mechanisms driving this phenomenon. The effect of Hermitian bulk-boundary coupling on the classification of topological insulators is investigated and is found to be essential for specific 1D non-Hermitian topological classifications. Various models exhibiting non-Hermitian bulk-boundary coupling effects are discussed, including models featuring chiral exceptionality with Hermitian bulk-boundary couplings. The study finds that introducing Hermitian bulk-boundary couplings changes the BDI classification but retains the BDI topological invariants for systems with $Q=2$. The research provides a comprehensive topological classification for 1D non-Hermitian systems under the condition of $Q=2$. The study challenges previous proposals regarding topological invariants for individual 1D non-Hermitian topological insulators while confirming their validity for systems falling within different topological classifications. Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation in the desired characteristics. We have compiled a comprehensive dataset in Russian comprising human speech with prelabeled warmth and competence attributes. We have successfully applied Gaussian Processes to predict warmth and competence from frequency domain spectra of speech, and from selected critical window features including F0, which significantly influences warmth perception. We have also presented a regression analysis indicating that warmth's underlying attributes can be primarily described by the ability to produce F0 within a specified range, F0 standard deviation, and the presence of certain high-frequency harmonics. Moreover, we have established that these attributes can be artificially created and incorporated into synthetic speech via parametric speech generation, thereby enabling the incorporation of human warmth into speech generated by Text-to-Speech systems. We have conducted two listening tests to confirm that the generated attributes effectively enhance warmth and do not negatively affect competence. We have achieved significant success in achieving warmth in synthetic speech through various feature engineering techniques, notably combining bass boost with F0 statistics. The technique has also been shown to effectively make synthetic speech more competent by incorporating spectral features that closely match those of human speech. We have repeated the listening tests using new test materials to confirm our findings and demonstrated that our proposed method successfully enhances warmth without compromising competence, and that the generated attributes can be seamlessly integrated with the existing Text-to-Speech system without requiring retraining. We have also explored the human desire for warmth in synthetic speech and the social implications this has. We have determined that warmth can be an invaluable attribute for any Text-to-Speech system aiming to enhance its overall social acceptability, and that its integration is feasible through parameteric speech generation based on frequency domain spectra or engineered acoustic features. We have also shown that warmth can be a valuable differentiator for various Text-to-Speech systems, and that their varying ability to produce warmth can be a key factor in their future competition. In conclusion, our research focuses on understanding and practicing warmth in synthetic speech and we hope our findings will contribute to the advancement of emotional voice synthesis. A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop interactions, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the range of approximately 0.01-50 GeV. Stabilization of dark matter occurs due to a combination of non-zero modular weight and adiabatic vacuum expectation value transfer effect from charged lepton fields. Furthermore, the model suggests a non-zero CKM phase theta responsible for dark matter mass and decay characteristics. Consequently, we examine various dark matter density constraints, including ReSB, and also investigate associated experimental signatures, such as missing energy, and develop a complete bosonic dark matter framework. We have analyzed collider constraints from LHCb, and we have found that our model accommodates a non-zero CP phase theta that aligns with observed dark matter density. Future prospects for finding associated signatures are presented. 

Key phrases: bosonic dark matter, radiative seesaw, A4 modular symmetry, U(1)_(B-L) gauge symmetry, light dark matter, CP phase, ALP, baryon asymmetry, non-thermal reheating, bosonic dark matter density, LHCb constraints, missing energy, collider constraints. 

Note: The model's bosonic dark matter density is achieved thermally unpowered in this study. We have analyzed the impact of such a scenario on the model's parameter constraints. We have found that in this case, the dark matter density is met within a narrower mass range, and we have also examined its effects on the scalar's decay characteristics and the baryon asymmetry. Consequently, the model's non-thermal production of bosonic dark matter has been examined in terms of its implications and future prospects.

This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces containing all possible low-dimensional subspaces of a particular dimension. In doing so, it develops an inverse Golay codes theory that applies to various types of subspaces. A specific case is presented where the low-dimensional subspaces are defined by unit vectors with a particular property. A constructive approach is provided for an omnidirectional precoding scheme using these higher-dimensional Golay complementary matrices. Additionally, this research establishes relationships between the properties of subspaces contained within Golay complementary matrices and those related to twisted Reed-Muller codes. A particular case is presented where the low-dimensional subspaces are defined by specific polynomial functions. A proposed omnidirectional precoding approach using these higher-dimensional Golay complementary matrices exhibits compatibility with diverse channel environments, as demonstrated by its performance in the FMCW radar system, which relies on linear frequency modulation. Results indicate that our precoding design outperforms or complements current solutions. This research also provides a foundation for exploring connections between other types of complementary matrices and omnidirectional precoding techniques. Further studies focus on developing high-efficiency, omnidirectional precoding algorithms using sparse signal recovery techniques. As an example of this, a proposed precoding method using sparse signal recovery and the exponential discrete Fourier transform is presented. This design approach utilizes the ExDFT's minimal basis property to develop an efficient, specialized form of the permuting Fourier transform. This research showcases our precoding method's versatility by applying it to a binary circular array. A novel deep convolutional autoencoder is designed to dynamically balance the need for information and the constraint of limited computational resources. By integrating various hyperspectral image characteristics through a custom feature fusion strategy, the proposed method effectively detects changes across diverse spectral and spatial scales. A two-stage approach is employed for change identification, where the first stage utilizes a label-free framework to generate an unsupervised change map and the second stage incorporates prior information to rectify uncertainties and refine the change information. Thorough evaluations on several real-world datasets demonstrate the substantial advantages of the proposed method over state-of-the-art approaches for various performance metrics. Moreover, an extensive investigation into the influence of various hyperparameters is conducted to provide researchers with practical guidelines for real-world applications. All the source code and pre-trained models are freely available on GitHub for easy reproduction of the study's results. Ultimately, the proposed method delivers an average change map that outperforms current techniques in accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. It is poised to become a reliable tool for various remote sensing applications, including forest health monitoring, environmental studies, and land use analysis. To showcase its potential in real-world applications, the proposed method is utilized for forest change detection, where it successfully captures the gradual changes in tree species over time. It is envisioned that the proposed method can be adapted to other applications with minimal modifications. A detailed analysis of the method's failure cases is conducted to identify potential avenues for future improvements. With its high accuracy, computational efficiency, and adaptability to various applications, the proposed method is anticipated to serve as a foundation for developing advanced change detection techniques in hyperspectral images. It is planned to release an updated version of the code that incorporates additional improvements for application-specific tasks. Interested researchers are invited to contribute to the development of the code by identifying novel trends and perspectives in the field. Furthermore, a comprehensive dataset with the corresponding ground truth is intended to facilitate unbiased evaluations and stimulate future research in change detection for hyperspectral images. A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-entropy dataset comprised of 77 molecular fluids. Our research demonstrates a strong, linear correlation between residual entropy and log viscosity for nonpolar, associating fluids at temperatures above their athermal correlation regimes. Similarly, we establish a correlation between residual entropy and log viscosity for polar, non-associating fluids within a broader temperature range. These findings significantly advance the existing entropy-visibility paradigm, which was initially proposed for nonpolar fluids. Our results substantially expand the scope of applicable liquids, including both nonpolar and polar categories. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified, general model capable of accurately predicting viscosity for a wide range of molecular fluids up to three times as efficiently as existing neural network predictions, while incorporating additional benefits. Our modified model encompasses the use of pre-calculated, third-order virial coefficients to broaden its temperature applicability. Overall, this study provides a valuable framework for forecasting viscosity in various fluids using their specific residual entropy values, which can be determined through computationally efficient virial expansions, while outperforming complex neural network predictions. Our research may lead to enhanced predictions of physical properties and accelerated discovery in various fields. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our research focuses on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model size to minimize memory access and transmission. (iii) an enhanced prediction accuracy through integration of context information from previous keywords. Experiment results demonstrate the CNN achieves a 4.5% error rate with a model size of 2.5KB and 0.56KB model footprint, suitable for execution on devices such as the Raspberry Pi. Keywords: context-based keyword spotting, deep neural network, machine learning.

In the case of general lattice gauge fields, even in two dimensions, there isn't a topological structure that can adequately capture the properties of the Dirac operator's chiral determinant. However, for specific scenarios like confining potentials and discrete symmetries, certain topological concepts apply, enabling the derivation of rigorous relations between the Dirac partition function and topological lattice theories. By incorporating these relations into the path integral formulation, we demonstrate that the partition function can be expressed through the sum of terms that involve gauge fields' magnetic configurations and specific lattice subgraphs. Subsequently, we show that the partition function can be reinterpreted as the partition function of an effective topological lattice theory defined on a graph containing edges, vertices, and points of degree three. These general lattice theories' partition functions are amenable to analysis through the Hamiltonian formulation, a approach we employed to determine the phase structure of the effective theory. Our results for zero-temperature and general lattice gauge fields' Dirac partition functions hold at least up to two dimensions. In the case of zero confining potential, the partition function exhibits a duality relation, a phenomenon that can be directly interpreted as a gauge-reduction that occurs within the original Dirac partition function. If the discrete symmetries' properties are taken into consideration, the partition function can be re-expressed as an integral over unitary gauge transformations or, equivalently, as an alternating series involving the products of the Dirac operator's chiral determinant and special lattice vectors' oriented paths. In the case of discrete $\mathbb{Z}_N$ symmetries, this last representation enables the derivation of the asymptotic expansion of the partition function, a result that can be applied to various scenarios like confining potentials, general lattice gauge fields, and two-dimensional SU(2) Yang-Mills theory's partition functions. By leveraging these general results from the theory of asymptotic expansions, we are able to determine the large-N behavior of the partition functions for a range of theories, including general lattice gauge fields, SU(N) Yang-Mills theory, and QCD, up to any number of dimensions. In the specific case of two-dimensional QCD's partition function with N = 3 colors and L = 16 sites, we have determined its asymptotic expansion, a finding that may be applied in the analysis of lattice-boltzmann simulations. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Additionally, we demonstrate its practical application to different categorical data contexts. Furthermore, we provide an open-source R package called GLASC to facilitate implementation.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diverse functions like web browsing and multimedia capabilities as well as support for mixed criticality systems.  Achieving a high level of resource efficiency and performance for these mixed criticality systems, however, poses a challenge when using traditional hypervisors due to the inherent resource overhead they incur. 

As an alternative to addressing these requirements and challenges, this research paper introduces T-Visor, a mini hypervisor designed for embedded systems.  It is written in C and optimized to run on Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms.  T-Visor, in particular, offers advantages for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems by providing a framework for scheduling priorities and ensuring the secure, hard real-time capabilities through the Client-Server (C/S) scheduling model and Resource Sharing (R/S) model.  The effectiveness and performance benefits of T-Visor, however, has not been fully realized when using the traditional hypervisor in embedded systems, likely due to the limited research focus and analysis. 

The experiments conducted to evaluate T-Visor, however, revealed notable gains and improvements, specifically, the overhead percentage lower bound is estimated at 0.78% and the overhead percentage upper bound is estimated at 2.47%.  These gains and improvements suggest that the scheduling models provided by T-Visor can effectively minimize additional overhead when supporting mixed criticality systems and the offered support is generally efficient and reliable.  The experiments further revealed that the scheduling models offered by T-Visor can be utilized not only in hypervisor mode but also in other mini hypervisor modes with minor losses in performance.  The research, therefore, confirms that T-Visor can efficiently support mixed criticality embedded real-time systems with resource efficiency and minimal resource overhead. 

The research also offers guidance and advice for optimizing performance and resource efficiency when using T-Visor in embedded systems, suggesting that the scheduling models provided by T-Visor can significantly enhance the overall overhead efficiency when scheduling priorities and ensure the secure, hard real-time capabilities through the Client-Server (C/S) model and Resource Sharing (R/S) model. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are typically positioned in this alignment. Most stitching algorithms assume a common perspective axis, which results in inaccurate calculations if the cameras are tilted. Furthermore, few algorithms address this scenario, and the complexity of vertical alignment often hinders their implementation. To overcome these obstacles, this research introduces the VANS algorithm, which utilizes structure from motion to derive scene geometry when alignment details are unclear. VANS estimates the epipolar lines by calculating the camera rotation alone, without needing full reconstruction data, to facilitate increased efficiency. Building upon the CPAS algorithm, VANS enhances the accuracy of feature matching, geometric optimization, and rendering. Experimental outcomes confirm that VANS achieves superior feature matching and geometric accuracy compared to related techniques. Moreover, VANS produces high-quality results on a range of real-world images, even when single-image information is insufficient. Finally, VANS demonstrates increased resilience when confronted with moving objects. To facilitate easy adoption, this algorithm is designed to work seamlessly with existing stitching software, providing similar output quality. VANS has been successfully integrated with an Android app, Panorama, which demonstrates its effectiveness using a single camera input. Furthermore, this app allows users to adjust viewing angles, providing a more immersive user experience. User evaluations of the app reveal positive feedback regarding the app's usability, outshining competing alternatives. To promote widespread adoption, this research provides open-source implementation of the VANS algorithm to stimulate further development in the field. By integrating VANS with existing stitching software, this method enables precise alignment without reconstrucing the entire scene, contributing to increased flexibility to render images in various orientations. VANS has the potential to produce high-quality panoramic images from any input, outperforming existing algorithms in alignment accuracy. Moreover, this algorithm's implementation results in minimal memory usage, allowing seamless deployment on devices with limited resources, such as smartphones and tablets. To promote further research, this paper releases the dataset used in this study, providing a common benchmark for evaluating panoramic stitching alignment. Finally, this research demonstrates the effective integration of VANS with existing stitching software, providing easy examples of its use that can be easily replicated. Several use cases are provided, including the successful stitching of images captured from a car window, around a pole, in a tunnel, and from a flip screen device. When two coupled populations of oscillators are considered, there are cases where the populations exhibit synchronized and asynchronous behavior simultaneously. We have derived a general theorem that describes the convergence of solutions to this type of coupled system, also providing conditions under which the solution reaches a steady state. Our approach employs matrix analysis and a new diagonalization method for coupled system linearization. Additionally, we have established a criterion for the convergence of solutions in the specific case of coupled oscillators with Robust-Parametric-Synchronization. This criterion is based on the eigenvalues of a constructed Kronecker matrix. We demonstrate our theoretical findings with applicable examples. Moreover, one of these examples is related to the thermomechanics model proposed by Gureja, which describes the thermal exchange between a solid material and its surrounding environment. In this model, the solid material tends to desynchronize with the environment, which in turn remains in a synchronized state. We show that the solution to this model converges to a steady state. Furthermore, we have extended our theoretical framework to the case of multiple coupled populations of oscillators, obtaining a corresponding generalization of the new diagonalization method and matrix analysis. As an illustration of this extension, we have analyzed a coupled system consisting of three populations of oscillators. We have derived a condition for the convergence of solutions that depends on the eigenvalues of a constructed $D$-block Kronecker matrix. Lastly, we have established a criterion for the convergence of solutions in the specific case of coupled oscillators with Robust-Parametric-Synchronization in the presence of noise. A significant advantage of Model-Based Reinforcement Learning algorithms is their ability to obtain high-level performance over Model-Free algorithms. However, these algorithms often struggle to adapt to unseen environmental settings. Our research tackles this issue by modifying the probabilistic primal reinforcement learning framework to make it robust to minor variations in the environment. The method works by limiting the uncertainty in the prior of a Gaussian Process to likely environmental trajectories, facilitated through a novel Dirichlet process prior. In our experiments, this approach yielded high-level performance along with a notable capacity to adapt to unseen environments, surpassing current robust reinforcement learning methods in multiple benchmarks, including cartpole, mountaincar, and walker2d. The method also extends multiple variants of PGPR, a non-asymptotic model-free algorithm, to robust reinforcement learning. The framework further enables transferring knowledge from one environment to another, similar to PILCO. In our study, this transfer was feasible with low-level state variables in cartpole and walker2d, as well as with mountaincar's rich observations. The research and code are accessible online. The code can be found at https://github.com/ErwanMeilhac/RobustPILCO. The research can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10177. 

Key Contributions
----------------

* We present a novel Gaussian Process prior based on a Dirichlet process to limit uncertainty in RBILCO, a modified Robust Model-Based Reinforcement Learning algorithm.
* We extend multiple variants of PGPR, a non-asymptotic model-free algorithm, to robust reinforcement learning

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a closed symmetry algebra without a central extension or anomaly, whereas other research suggests that quantizing these charges results in a deformation when combined. This paper reexamines this problem considering updated understanding of superrotation charges and finds that quantization of eBMS charges within a new phase space, which includes a spin memory mode, leads to an algebra without a deformation. The degenerate vacua are characterized by the soft news and a Schwarzian mode corresponding to deformations of the celestial metric by superrotations, potentially reconciling two manifestations of asymptotic symmetries through null infinity asymptotic quantization and celestial holography. The former approach is related to a new first-class constraint, while the latter provides a dual description through the deformation of the primary charge operator representing superrotations. This reconciles two seemingly conflicting algebraic structures, a permutation algebra and a commutator algebra, associated with eBMS quantization and celestial holography. Furthermore, this reconciliation allows for a duality between the two approaches and a translation to a more comprehensive language, specifically conformal field theory. As a result, this reconciliation frees the degenerate vacuum of the deformed algebra from constraints from null infinity asymptotic symmetries, while the Schwarzian mode reflects a specific type of memory associated with superrotations that persists at infinity. Additionally, this research indicates a connection between superrotations and global charges of asymptotically flat spacetimes and further suggests a link between superrotations and the global charges of general topologically static spacetimes. Finally, all charges generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null and past infinity combine to form a comprehensive symmetry algebra without a deformation, thereby providing a complete quantization of the eBMS algebra. This research combines two theories: null infinity asymptotic quantization and celestial holography, and provides a dual description through the decomposition of the stress tensor on the celestial surface, thereby achieving a comprehensive symmetry algebra without a deformation. As an extension, this research indicates a connection between superrotations and the global charges of asymptotically AdS$_3$ spacetimes. Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. When faced with one example at a time, the major issue is avoiding the confusion between classes, especially when encountering a new object without any prior knowledge. This problem is referred to as 'one-shot learning.' A technique called multi-modal learning, particularly the use of visual and linguistic models, shows promise in tackling this challenge. We introduce a new approach centered on language to recognize objects in this scenario. This method leverages the hierarchy within the language model to recognize objects and applies it to the recognition of objects alone, thus creating a singular, self-sufficient model. We test the effectiveness of this approach, referred to as Hierarchical Distributed Dense (HDD), against existing state-of-the-art models in multi-modal, one-shot learning scenarios. Our experiments show that HDD achieves comparable accuracy to the current best methods, while also demonstrating that its hierarchical approach is more adaptable and less reliant on specific datasets. This makes HDD a suitable candidate for recognizing objects in complex, real-world environments. Additionally, we present a new dataset, called 'WSBop,'which features a wide range of objects and their corresponding semantic relationships. This dataset is designed to facilitate research in hierarchical learning and offers a single-view dataset with diverse objects. We also present an alternative version of the HDD model that is capable of utilizing multiple views in tandem, thus making it a suitable candidate for multi-modal learning applications. We compare the effectiveness of the HDD model against existing state-of-the-art models in multi-modal learning scenarios. Our experiments show that the HDD model is as effective as the current best methods in multi-modal learning applications, while also demonstrating the advantages of utilizing the hierarchical structure of the language model in learning processes. The HDD source code, including the new dataset 'WSBop', is available for public access at https://github.com/alejovg/hierarchical-distributed-density. Approximately 4 billion people worldwide are threatened by intestinal parasite infection, leading to various health issues and lost productivity. Traditional diagnosis methods are often unreliable, involving physical examination or visual assessment of stool samples. Machine learning-based image analysis has shown potential in this context, as recent research has already utilized convolutional neural networks to classify parasitic species in stool images. This study went a step further, employing a transfer learning approach with a pre-trained convolutional neural network to classify seven distinct intestinal parasites. To achieve this, the researchers compiled a dataset consisting of 2,671 images from seven parasitic classes and 1,023 images from two control classes, sourced from the OpenI dataset. They then adapted the ResNet50 convolutional neural network by removing its final fully connected layers and added new classes to facilitate the classification. Utilizing the Adam optimizer and evaluating the adapted network on the OpenI dataset, the researchers achieved high classification accuracy, recall, and precision rates of 0.97, 0.97, and 0.97 respectively. Additionally, the study demonstrated the adapted network's robustness in classifying the parasites even when the dataset had been reduced to a fifth. This research highlights the effectiveness of the ResNet50 architecture in this specific application and provides a basis for future research in this context. Further studies will focus on reducing classification time, eliminating classification errors due to background variations, and broadening the classification system to include more parasite species. The study's source code and classified images can be accessed through the link https://github.com/PranavGupta16/IntestinalParasitesClassification. Similarly, the modified code can be viewed at https://github.com/PranavGupta16/IntestinalParasitesClassification/tree/master/code. In teaching and learning, ineffective communication often leads to confusion, and referential ambiguity is a major obstacle. A classic illustration of referential ambiguity is the scenario where two people see a group of three people, including one who has a hat colored red by design and another who has a hat colored green by design. The red-hat person is randomly assigned a hat color as well. The teacher observes that some people have red hats and says, "Show someone who has a red hat," in an effort to communicate information to the learner. Due to the teacher's use of an ambiguous reference, the learner cannot deduce any specific initial color distribution of the hats. In order to overcome referential ambiguity, a new approach to model the teacher's language has been developed, building on a logical framework known as the "Handshaking Game." This approach involves analyzing interpersonal communication as interactions within a graph. In graph-based communication, a new reference model, called the "Follow-Path Reference Model," has been introduced. In this model, the teacher selects a path starting from the learner and uses it to specify the target individual. By employing the "Interpersonal Handshaking Game," it has been demonstrated that the new reference model is effective in facilitating the exchange of information. Furthermore, the concept of "depth" in referential ambiguity has been introduced and quantified in terms of the path length. Utilizing the "Interpersonal Handshaking Game," it has been demonstrated that the depth of referential ambiguity is bounded by the product of the degrees of the teacher and learner. In the scenario described above, adding an additional green hat to the red-hat person would enable the teacher to say, "Show someone who is farther away," in order to communicate a red hat to the learner, thereby reducing the referential ambiguity to a bounded degree. By modeling interpersonal communication as interactions within a graph, the new approach provides a logical framework for analyzing the complexity of referential ambiguity. In addition to the classic illustration, several other scenarios have been identified that demonstrate referential ambiguity. For example, when teaching and learning take place in a circular setting, the learner may be confused by the teacher's reference to a neighbor. Furthermore, the new approach has been applied to the "Water Distribution Problem," where two people seek to communicate information about the water distribution in a network of pipes. The Ramsey sequence is a widely employed technique for determining resonance frequencies in quantum systems, encompassing applications in both superconducting qubits and atomic clocks. To optimize the efficiency of measurements, the timing of pulses should be precisely coordinated with the system's dynamic properties. In the present study, the Ramsey sequence measurements for spin qubits were performed using a time-domain approach, resulting in the acquisition of a complex spectral function by applying a maximum likelihood estimator. Notably, the method was found to enhance the overall measurement efficiency by up to 60% compared to traditional methods, as exemplified by simulating a specific type of double-quantum-dot qubit. Moreover, the technique is adaptable to a range of spin systems and serves as an invaluable tool for refining measurements within quantum sensing applications. Furthermore, the spectral function obtained through this method can facilitate the extraction of key physical properties, such as the decoherence rate. As an example of its utility, the decay rate associated with the dephasing induced by inductive coupling was found to be on the order of MHz, despite this type of coupling being relatively weak. Ultimately, the approach described may be easily incorporated into existing Ramsey sequence experiments, and its implementation is described in detail through a publicly available, user-friendly code framework. This research aims to contribute to the advancement of spin qubit-based quantum sensing by drawing upon established techniques from atomic clock science. Publicly accessible versions of the code used in this study can be found at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/QuantumArk/RamseySequencePython. Furthermore, the code is compatible with the CUDA architecture, utilizing GPUs to accelerate the simulation, and running on standard hardware found in most laboratories. As an additional resource, the code includes exemplary simulations of a semiconductor spin qubit exposed to an XY-coupled environment and a Floquet-engineered quantum simulator, where the latter is confined within an optical microcavity. Lastly, the approach described serves as an open invitation for further developing and refining methods to analyze Ramsey sequence measurements, and its potential applications extend beyond spin qubit systems into atomic clock science. In the future, the code framework may be expanded to encompass a broader range of quantum system types. Furthermore, the study highlights the remarkable potential for leveraging quantum sensing technology to improve understanding and refine measurements of weak forces and interactions in quantum science and technology. The developed metrics incorporate known methods as special cases and offer insights into their behavior, as well as a new method: Gromov centrality, which measures the discrepancy between a network and a perfectly connected graph. This discrepancy is shown to be directly correlated with the triangle inequality excess, indicating that Gromov centrality can serve as a more refined triangle inequality test.
