A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. By integrating this 'copy mechanism' into established Seq2Seq models like CNNs and Transformers, we can significantly boost their performance. We put this enhanced architecture to the test using state-of-the-art datasets containing questions that involve novel knowledge elements. Compared to their standard counterparts, our results indicate substantial improvements across all datasets. Additionally, by incorporating the copy mechanism into the Transformer architecture, we can reduce the training time by nearly half while maintaining excellent performance. Furthermore, by fine-tuning this mechanism, we can also enhance the model's ability to avoid copying unnecessary elements and thereby prevent information overload in generated queries. Overall, our novel approach showcases the efficacy of combining neural networks with attention mechanisms to produce high-quality SPARQL queries. By addressing the key issue of limited knowledge coverage, our results outshine previous achievements in this domain. This work introduces a novel method for systematically assessing academic contributors by leveraging the performance of conferences, journals, and schools. A key part of this approach involves a sophisticated ranking system for conferences known as venue scores, which are derived from vast amounts of data from articles, citing other articles within the same institution. Building on this framework, a model is developed to continuously evaluate researchers' scores based on their interactions with the venues through submission and publication of articles. This model offers a fair and transparent metric for evaluating individuals and organizations based on their performance. Moreover, it provides a measure that corresponds to commonly used indices such as h-index and citation impact. Our approach is practical, demonstrated by its application to a real-world use case where it helped eliminate a redundant component of the author evaluation system. This efficiency gain enabled our system to score over 120,000 researchers in under 3 seconds, resulting in a significant reduction of processing time. Ultimately, the score-based model offers substantial advantages in terms of ease of interpretation, fairness, and efficiency, making it a valuable tool for academic management and evaluation processes. This work also includes a free, open-source implementation of the model and a discussion of its practical applications and inherent limitations. Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine neural networks and control feedback loops. Ultimately, these tools facilitate the analysis of safe control systems and support deep reinforcement learning with robustness guarantees. This resource is intended for control engineers familiar with traditional verification methods, as well as machine learning professionals looking to apply verification to their models. It provides an accessible introduction to the field, bridging the gap between verification techniques for neural networks and their control systems applications. Additional information on the methods discussed in this paper can be found online through open-source codes on GitHub. Specifically, the web address https:// NeuralControl.github.io provides a central hub for accessible code and a comprehensive overview of the methods presented in this tutorial.

Tensor completion techniques aim to recover incomplete data in various applications like computer vision and graph learning. In this context, a new and sophisticated approach called the Layer-wise Low-rank Tensor completion (LLT) method is developed, combining the principles of sparse and low-rank tensors. LLT is characterized by two key components - sparse and low-rank tensors that capture different patterns in the data. By layering these patterns in sequential stages, the method leverages each layer to enhance the performance of the other, ultimately enabling more efficient data recovery. Notably, the studies focused on LLT focus primarily on recovering a single tensor from partially observed data. In contrast, the proposed work extends this concept to address the challenge of aligning multiple tensors. Two notable issues that arise in this context are dealing with tensor alignment and minimizing noise. To address these challenges, a new tensor alignment approach is developed that aligns tensors with partial observations, and the noise is controlled through an optimization process that incorporates an adaptive constraint. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LLT across different scenarios and the substantial benefits it provides over competing methods. Moreover, the methods developed in this context generalize well to real-world applications, including video de-noising and video based object detection. Our code is publicly available for review at https://github.com/amanaps/LLT. We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs. IGNS are computed by repeatedly applying a function that uses maximal independent sets, and they are related to other iterative graph algorithms such as the Truss Enricher. We demonstrate that maximal independent sets play a crucial role in understanding how information flows through these algorithms, and we establish conditions under which these algorithms produce consistent outcomes in the long term. Our study also examines the effects of different parameters on the output of Truss Enricher, and it introduces a new parameter that influences the algorithms' behavior. To facilitate empirical analysis, we develop a method to approximate the equilibrium point of these algorithms. Finally, we verify the practical applicability of these findings by conducting experiments that compare the performance of different iterative strategies. These experiments reveal that shorter runs of IGNS can produce better results for certain tasks, and they highlight the importance of carefully tuning algorithm parameters in real-world applications. The theoretical concepts explored in this study rely on a broad understanding of graph theory terms, such as weighted graphs, maximal independent sets, and spanning trees, which are reviewed in the conclusion along with their implications on the Truss Enricher algorithm. Additionally, we introduce the concept of Weighted Nearest Neighbor Hops, a method to compute the shortest paths between graph nodes, and show its connection to previous research on graph search algorithms. Our final analysis also touches on the applicability of the FGL'20 bound in ensuring the stability of multi-stage graph algorithms. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the graph theoretical basis for Iterative Graph Normalization (IGNS) algorithms, and it highlights their widespread applications across various research fields. The findings and conclusions are supplemented by 8 open questions and 2 proposed utilization scenarios that require further exploration. The study's relevance to Truss Enricher is demonstrated through an illustration of its application to crime forecasting in a real-world dataset, and an alternative use case is presented to showcase its efficacy in graph-based data mining tasks. The research output and findings are made available through the project's GitHub repository for public access and feedback. Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. Based on the observed H30α data, we determine a total SFR of 0.17 Msun per year, which closely matches the SFR derived from far-ir data. Our deep H30α observations allow us to identify 41 supernova remnants, 20 of which were previously unreported, and provide SFR and supernova remnant (SNR) suppression weight estimates. Our analysis indicates significant SFR suppression in SNRs with small molecular gas densities, equivalent to about ten percent of the total SFR in NGC 5253. However, this SFR suppression does not appear to be heavily influenced by the properties of the surrounding medium in terms of sound speed or primary-to-secondary ionization ratios. Furthermore, we are able to measure the H30α-based SFR for NGC 5253 in just a few hours, demonstrating the technique's potential for observing and tracking SFRs in small galaxies over the coming decades. As the molecular gas in NGC 5253 extends far beyond the observed area, we expect this method to significantly underrepresent the total SFR in very low-metallicity, star-forming galaxies. Conversely, we expect this method to significantly overrepresent the total SFR in high-metallicity, star-forming galaxies. Our analysis suggests that the H30α region is optimal for measuring SFRs because it strikes a balance between being strongly emitted by H30α and relatively clear of radio continuum emissions. Therefore, we expect future observations using this technique to yield accurate SFRs in galaxies with star formation rates between 0.01 and 1 Msun per year. Observations of the H30α region in this manner should be particularly effective in accurately measuring SFRs in galaxies with low star formation rates and large molecular gas reserves. This study aims to bridge this gap by classifying social media posts into non-feeling depressed, mildly depressed, and severely depressed states of mind. The analysis is based on a newly created dataset consisting of 5,460 social media posts categorized into three levels of depression. The data was generated from crowdsourcing with both expert and non-expert participants, ensuring accuracy by adhering to expert labeling.  The study conducted thorough evaluations of cutting-edge models such as RoBERTa, BERT, DistilBERT, XLNet, and Transformer on the dataset, while also testing the robustness of these models in handling data imbalance by employing undersampling, oversampling, and balanced data strategies. Ultimately, the study reported the best result achieved by fine-tuning RoBERTa on social media posts with expert labeling, achieving balanced F1 scores of 0.73, 0.68, and 0.76 for non-feeling, mild, and severe depression, respectively. This type of hedging is crucial for ensuring that the value of a financial asset does not fluctuate, thereby maintaining its initial value. Historically, advanced methods like dynamic programming and stochastic programming have been ineffective in handling complex scenarios. Therefore, simpler reinforcement learning approaches were explored, marking the first attempt to apply this type of learning in portfolio hedging. Initially, the problem was cast as an off-policy learning problem to optimize the hedging strategy, and actor-critic algorithms were utilized for continuous action spaces. To further develop the methods, additional constraints such as linear budget and stock position limits were incorporated, and multi-agent portfolio hedging with collaborative learning was also introduced. To verify the effectiveness of the new methods, portfolio hedging with various complex securities and derivatives was tested, including multiple stocks with multiple derivatives. The results showed the new methods' ability to handle high-dimensional states and continuous action spaces effectively, offering better solutions than traditional approaches and comparable performance for derivative pricing. Additionally, the new methods' ability to learn off-policy was demonstrated, providing a significant advantage over previous methods. These advancements enabled the development of simple reinforcement learning-based solutions for portfolio hedging, offering a substantial improvement over current state-of-the-art techniques. In today's commercial recommender systems, techniques like sequential prediction and real-time personalization play crucial roles. Most current approaches rely on neural networks to forecast users' immediate next actions. We present a novel model that challenges this prevailing trend by employing a different method. Our model uses a discrete Markov process to model users' activities and leverages neural networks to enhance the Markov transition probabilities. This approach has several benefits. Firstly, the model can easily incorporate existing knowledge about activities and their relationships. Secondly, the representation learning of the Markov transition probabilities can be seen as a form of unsupervised learning. We conduct experiments on three large-scale commercial platforms to demonstrate the model's effectiveness, achieving a 27.0% improvement in miss rate and a 16.6% improvement in recall at a 25% recall threshold compared to sequential recommendation with neural networks. We also investigate various methods to further improve the model, including constrained maximum likelihood optimization to preserve the sparse structure of activity probabilities. Our model is successfully applied to recommend items in real-time. The model's activity predictions are used to guide item recommendations by applying a ranking filter to the top-suggested items. We compare this approach to traditional recommendation techniques and observe a 1.0% improvement in average offline ranking loss. Finally, we deploy the model in a production environment and evaluate its impact on a large-scale commercial platform. The results demonstrate that the model's activity predictions can forecast unusual user behavior, enabling engineers to proactively develop targeted anti-abuse strategies. Conversely, the model's enhanced understanding of activity relationships facilitates the discovery of novel areas requiring anti-abuse focus. We believe that the model's unsupervised learning of activity relationships has the potential to address the prevailing challenge of scarcity in data-driven anti-abuse strategies. We hope that the model's successful application across three distinct commercial platforms serves as a model for tackling real-world challenges in the industry. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these features by segments, a second BERT model aggregates the multiple segments into a unified feature for final classification. By combining both classification stages, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 0.9164 in macro F1 score. This approach demonstrates strong potential for real-world application by significantly reducing the computational complexity from previous models. Notably, we found that utilizing CT scan images in consecutive segments was the most effective configuration. Additionally, we performed an in-depth error analysis by examining the confusion matrix and corresponding t-SNE plots to further understand classification results and accidence cases. Multiple experiments were designed to examine the impact of varying scan length on the network's performance. Importantly, we discovered that utilizing CT images in consecutive segments demonstrated considerable improvements in accuracy and stability. Finally, we compared our approach with a network specifically designed for random volume classification and found that utilizing CT images in consecutive segments significantly enhanced its performance when combined with attention mechanisms. As COVID-19 continues to evolve and spread globally, it causes widespread illness and substantial economic hardship. Neither pandemic nor outbreak status has hindered our efforts to develop a reliable diagnostic framework. By combining CT scan images from multiple segments and utilizing double BERT for feature extraction and classification, we achieved exceptional results and demonstrated significant complexity reduction from previous models. This approach boasts exceptional generalizability, as evidenced by outstanding performance in validation and testing. Ultimately, we believe this diagnostic framework holds significant potential for application in real-world COVID-19 diagnosis and the development of effective countermeasures against the resulting economic difficulties and global health risks.}

Historically, mathematical models examining the interactions between rapid evolutionary change and ecological processes have focused on single populations or basic two-species interactions. In order to enhance our understanding of more intricate relationships, researchers must delve into the mathematics underlying these interactions. This article delves into the dual nature of eco-evolutionary models, which simultaneously undergo both smooth and non-smooth transformations. To illustrate these dynamics, mathematical and numerical analyses are used in a global context, rather than in a particular environment. The model's evolution is governed by a differential equation with a random variable that is influenced by the interaction between the population and its surroundings. This interaction is represented through the single-species model's carrying capacity, which is adjusted by the evolutionary rate of the trait. By adopting an arbitrary unit for time, population size, and the evolutionary rate, the model displays a complex set of behaviors, which are similar to those found in a logistic equation with a random component. Using elementary mathematical techniques, we demonstrate that the model's various coexistence phases are marked by smooth and non-smooth transitions. Finally, we present the model in a form that is simple to analyze, which highlights the model's capacity for complex behavior, which was previously observed in more complex models. By studying these dynamics, we may uncover new information about how ecosystems adapt to changes in the environment. A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing the performance of speech models across various languages and tasks under a unified framework. By expanding the speech representation paradigm to include self-supervised learning, our study demonstrates the potential of models like ResNet-1d and U-Net to achieve significant improvements in multiple speech applications by up to 16% relative error margin relative to non-self-supervised models when using identical feature inputs, thereby underscoring the value of this approach. Notably, our self-supervised model also surpasses the state-of-the-art in speech recognition, outperforming the Wav2Letter model by about 11% relative error margin on the Timit dataset. Furthermore, our study reveals that self-supervised models exhibit a higher degree of linguistic indestructibility, thereby enhancing robustness when faced with challenging conditions such as noise interference. Overall, our study shows that self-supervised speech representations possess a remarkable degree of versatility and flexibility in terms of their practical applications. The associated code and model weights can be freely accessed on the SUPERB challenge's official website at https://superbchallenge.github.io.

a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges.

AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually diminishes arbitrage challenges, though this benefits investors at a decreased rate. 
Conversely, the inclusion of numerous tokens worsens the arbitrage dilemma. 
We furnish empirical support for our primary model outcomes by using detailed transaction records of AMMs. 
AMMs have emerged as the dominant type of decentralized exchange over the course of Ethereum's development, 
yet their theoretical foundations have been examined inadequately to date. 
Our research aims to fill this void.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by varying underlying assumptions. We introduce an innovative approach that uses Bayesian estimation for model-weighted summary statistics to perform this analysis. This method evaluates multiple models simultaneously, providing a clear picture of the range of possible parameter estimates. Our focus is on model parameters influencing the mean and variance of key distribution parameters. We create a simple yet efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm with effective convergence monitoring, allowing for rapid generation of multiple posterior distributions. Our approach is applied to real-world data sets through an intuitive data analysis software package named "sanalysis", designed for R and Python programming languages. We showcase our method's utility with actual data examples. Furthermore, additional guidance and tools are provided through an interactive Shiny web application, which facilitates user-defined model specifications and simulation scenarios. We also present a step-by-step tutorial that demonstrates successful completion of Sensitivity Analysis, accompanied by a corresponding case study. Finally, although our approach is versatile and can be applied to various problem types, it is specifically tailored for dealing with missing outcome data in parametric models, block monotonicity, and right-censoring issues. All relevant code and data are freely available on public repositories for reference.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform. Additionally, a companion document details the accompanying radiofrequency coil development, which is described in Fermilab LARP-19-30.0. Lastly, a forthcoming document at Fermilab LARP-20 will focus on the platform's control systems. 

Key outcomes:
1. A new cryogenic platform has been created to support large-scale quantum computing applications in the millikelvin temperature range.
2. The platform has a 2-meter diameter by 1.5-meter tall cylindrical shape with a 0.5-meter wide central hole for radiofrequency coil access.
3. This innovative platform is built using six large superconducting radiofrequency pieces and is cooled by a mixture of helium-4 and helium-3 through a unique heat exchanger for efficient low-temperature achievement.
4. A dedicated evacuation chamber allows for vacuum creation above the platform while an external helium-3 transfer system ensures reliable cold gas management, thus minimizing heat input into the system during operation.
5. A unique 3D superconducting qubit structure holder provides support and allows for easy access to qubits from all sides for experimentation purposes.
6. A new radiofrequency coil design developed specifically for this platform will provide a high-quality signal while minimizing heat input into the system. This development is described in a companion document at Fermilab LARP-19-30.0. 

Targeting the achievement of extremely low millikelvin temperatures requires sophisticated temperature control systems, thus a forthcoming document at Fermilab LARP-20 will detail the design and functionality of these systems.

Previous research indicates substantial misuse of cryptographic APIs in Python, 
but the full scope of issues is unknown due to limited studies focusing only 
on specific mistakes, such as incorrect hashing functions. In our research, we 
evaluated seven common crypto libraries used in Python by scanning the source 
code of 1,113 Python projects on GitHub, a platform hosting a vast range of 
open-source software. By applying standardized testing methods, we discovered 
high-frequency incidents of crypto errors, including incorrect usage of crypto 
libraries and invalid input passed to these libraries. According to our findings, 
91.7% of the analyzed projects exhibited some form of crypto API misuse, and 
85.9% of the misuses were discovered in projects that otherwise adhered to standard 
best practices. Furthermore, our study uncovered that the primary reasons for 
these mistakes were difficulty in understanding the limitations of data types and 
functionality provided by crypto libraries. In addition, we found that the 
frequency of crypto-related mistakes varied depending on the misused library and 
the category of project. By integrating our findings with guidelines on proper 
cryptographic practices, we were able to suggest improvements in code quality 
and fundamental programming skills. In total, we identified 2,444 unique instances of 
crypto-related mistakes; these flaws are available for independent verification on 
the https://github.com/saseemir/PyMisuse repository. By integrating our findings 
with established security evaluation frameworks, we were able to assess the 
security quality of the analyzed projects. Our results showed that 68.9% of the 
projects exhibited "excellent" security quality, whereas 11.4% displayed 
"poor" security, in contrast to previous studies reporting "poor" security 
characteristics for around 50% of the studied projects. In addition, we found 
significant positive correlations between code hygiene metrics and established 
best practices, including proper handling of data protection. In particular, 
adopting standard data protection mechanisms significantly lowered the occurrence 
of crypto-related mistakes. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the same 
code review tools can be utilized for both improving code quality and reducing 
crypto-related mistakes. By presenting the methods employed for our study, we 
encourage the community to validate our results and extend the research to

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and includes BMOA as a special case with p=2. Our analysis focuses on the maximal subsemigroups of composition operators on BMOA_p and VMOA_p. We find that the maximal subsemigroups of compact operators on BMOA_p and VMOA_p are finite. Furthermore, we prove that the maximal subsemigroups of bounded linear operators on BMOA_p and VMOA p are also finite. These findings extend earlier results for BMOA and VMOA. Our method involves creating a new invariant subspace within BMOA_p or VMOA p, using a general subsemigroup of composition operators, and then demonstrating the finiteness of the semigroup on that subspace. This process can be repeated to achieve the desired results. As a consequence of our semigroup analysis, we derive the compactness and hyponormality criteria for the double operator mean with the weighted Lebesgue space L^2(ℋ) as the domain. Similarly, we establish the weighted hyponormality criteria for the double operator mean with the weighted Bergman space AP(ℬ) as the domain, where 0 < p < ∞. In particular, we recover some well-known results for the unweighted cases (p=2) and recover some recent results for the weighted cases (p ≠ 2). Our findings also include a new result for the weighted hyponormality of Toeplitz operators on AP(ℬ) with 0 < p < 2. Moreover, we demonstrate that the weighted Bergman operator with 0 < p < 2 is a degree-one perturbation of a hyponormal operator if its symbol ℘ is continuous on ℋ. In conclusion, we present some examples of finite subsemigroups of composition operators on BMOA_p and VMOA p. These examples illustrate that subsemigroups can be generated by finite sets of operators that may not be compact, linear, or even composition operators themselves. They highlight unique properties and provide a deeper understanding of the BMOA_p and VMOA p spaces. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a challenging task for historical languages due to the limited availability of relevant reference data. Although the Leiden Corpus of Netherlandic Texts (LCNT) offers a relatively large amount of text annotated with POS, the existing annotations are insufficient to enable POS tagging using fully-supervised machine learning methods. The combination of lexical search and hidden Markov models (HMMs) is commonly used in domain adaptation and cross-domain POS tagging, typically leveraging dictionaries and word n-gram models from source domains. However, these models are incapable of handling data structures in which POS tags are linked to word forms. To address these challenges, we develop word-form-based POS tagging models for 16 languages, including Dutch, the major dialects of Dutch, and other closely related languages. The results show significant improvements in precision and recall compared to existing methods, with precision rates ranging from 52.14% to 75.86% and recall rates ranging from 51.65% to 74.84%. The developed models achieve a balanced combination of accuracy and efficiency, with the ability to handle new texts in a timely manner. The effectiveness of the models is evaluated using the F1-score, which indicates their potential for applying state-of-the-art POS tagging models to the developed datasets. The steps involved in the development process are described in detail, including the creation of word-form-based dictionaries and n-gram models. The models and associated data are made publicly available for further research. The study is a first-step investigation into the application of modern natural language processing (NLP) techniques to the LCNT. The study presents an analysis of the strengths and limitations of the existing POS tagging method, and the potential for improving the accuracy of POS tagging using advanced techniques. The research highlights the difficulty in POS tagging under various data scarcity conditions and identifies areas for further exploration. We establish novel, necessary and sufficient conditions for a demand function candidate to be considered valid. This involves reformulating known conditions on demand functions by expressing them in terms of the corresponding utility functions. Leveraging these conditions, we design an algorithm to construct a utility function from a given demand function. We also prove that, in most cases, this algorithm is the only method that yields a valid utility function. Additionally, this research examines properties of utility functions derived from concave demand functions and provides new evidence of non-concave demand functions that yield multiple valid utility functions. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which a demand function can be perfectly reconstructed from its utility function. Finally, this research also formalizes the concept of a unique 'original' demand function corresponding to a given utility function and establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for such original demand functions to exist. Furthermore, we provide a method to uniquely reconstruct an original demand function from a utility function when certain conditions are met. Notably, this is possible for any monotonic utility function when supplemented with an additional inequality. We have also generalized this result for specific types of non-monotonic utility functions. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities resulting from spoken dialogue interactions. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI assistant designed for seamless, voice-based and visual data exchange between humans and machines. CitySpec effectively caters to the needs of small and medium-sized cities in the United States, particularly in regions where Spanish is widely spoken. Its development involved a novel, multi-stage framework, where we first created a comprehensive data base combining street scenes and corresponding signage, followed by the development of a cutting-edge AI-powered model to extract and interpret visual data. We leveraged this database to train a sophisticated AI model that could accurately identify, read, and understand Spanish street signs. We then incorporated this model into CitySpec, enabling the platform to efficiently specify, validate, and monitor various city services, including those related to COVID-19. We conducted a series of user studies, involving both English and Spanish speaking city officials, to test and refine our design, ultimately demonstrating the efficacy of our approach through a successful deployment in two cities, Paterson and Tampa. CitySpec boasts several innovative features, including a sophisticated visual data extraction and interpretation engine that can adapt to diverse languages, a flexible AI-based framework enabling real-time data processing, and an intuitive, user-centric design enhancing the user experience through easy data presentation and dialogue management. By combining these capabilities, CitySpec achieves an exceptional specification efficiency rate, enabling users to create high-quality, machine-readable specifications in just a few minutes, with minimal input. We observed a remarkable 95% accuracy in visual data extraction and 98% interpretation accuracy in both English and Spanish languages. Moreover, our platform's design and deployment resulted in a notable 90% user satisfaction rate among city officials. We thoroughly evaluated 24 comparison systems, including both automated and semi-automated AI assistants, and concluded that CitySpec stands out from the competition in terms of its flexibility, user experience, and overall efficiency. Notably, CitySpec's performance surpasses existing systems by an impressive 2.7 times in terms of specification efficiency. Furthermore, its design and deployment demonstrate a notable cost-effectiveness, saving city officials an average of $300,000 in annual costs. In conclusion, CitySpec represents a pioneering visual data enablement AI assistant, offering a unique and innovative solution to the challenges faced by city officials in their day-to-day activities. Investigating metal-insulator transitions triggered by surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films is essential for understanding and optimizing spin-orbit interactions and developing novel spintronic applications. Our results indicate that films grown in vacuum primarily acquire the rock-salt semiconductor (RS) termination, although some samples exhibited the metal-free surface (MFS) termination. However, the insulating phase was consistently associated with the MFS termination, whereas the RS termination was linked to the metal phase. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client loan repayment histories and demographic profiles.
This study compares the performance of several machine learning models – including Random Forest, Decision tree, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost – using data from a private Ethiopian bank, to determine which model excels on KMeans SMOTE over-sampled data.
Upon conducting the evaluation and exploration of feature selection methods, the results demonstrate that XGBoost achieves the highest F1 score, highlighting that factors such as age, employment duration, and applicant income hold greater importance than collateral-related information when evaluating credit risk for individual clients. 
Ultimately, the application of XGBoost enhances the bank's capacity to predict non-performing clients, informing more discerning lending policies and decisions. 
Based on the findings, a proposed system combining XGBoost, KMeans SMOTE over-sampling, and an enhanced decision-making system could significantly benefit banks serving low-income and middle-class clients in countries like Ethiopia, by accurately predicting individual credit risk.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Experimental evaluations confirm that OCNs significantly outperform standard DCNNs in image classification tasks, including orientation-dependent scenarios. Additionally, our OCNs share a similar architecture to DCNNs, making them easily integrable into existing deep learning frameworks used in various computer vision applications. This allows users to simply swap the convolution layers with our OCN modules to enhance the robustness of existing models. Our OCNs, which outperform all existing methods according to the current state-of-the-art evaluations, will be made available as part of the Pytorch deep-learning framework for public use. The Pytorch code for the OCNs can be found at: https://github.com/Jing Zheng/OCNs-Pytorch. Our theoretical proof, code, and experiments can also be accessed at: https://github.com/Jing Zheng/OCNs-Pytorch/tree/master/OCNs-Pytorch. Our research demonstrates that a single module based on LGFs is sufficient to enhance the robustness of standard DCNNs in image classification tasks. This suggests a potential future direction where a single module could also be beneficial in other DCNN applications that involve orientation-dependent tasks, such as image segmentation, detection, and reinforcement learning. To our knowledge, LGFs have not been used as a single module or incorporated into deep learning frameworks in previous works. Our research demonstrates a novel application of LGFs, which initially were used in medical image analysis, to orientation-dependent tasks in computer vision. The integration of LGFs into standard DCNNs is a non-invasive approach to enhancing existing deep learning frameworks to perform multiple tasks, including orientation-dependent tasks. Our research suggests a non-invasive method to improve the robustness of standard DCNNs in image classification tasks, which leverages a single module based on a single Gabor filter. The simplicity and efficiency of our OCNs make them a practical solution for tasks that involve orientation-dependent changes. The theoretical proof, code, and experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our OCNs

A vertex coloring of $G$ with colors $1 \le i \le t$ is called an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring when the colors on the vertices of $R$ form a sequence based on the colors assigned to them in a specific order, and for every edge $(u, v)$ in $G$, the color assigned to $u$ is less than the color assigned to $v$.  Given a graph $G$ and integers $r,t\ge 2$, the $R$-sequential $t$-coloring number, denoted by $\chi_{R,t}^*(G)$, is the minimum number of colors in an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring of $G$.  Given a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $R_G$, the paper provides results on $\chi_{R,t}^*(G)$ and makes claims about the optimality of certain $R$-sequential $t$-colorings of specific graph families like Cartesian products, compositions of graphs, and strong products.  The paper also provides bounds for $\chi_{R,t}^*(G)$ and offers generalizations of known bounds for $\chi_{R,t}^*(G)$ when $t=2$.  Furthermore, the paper introduces the concept of $k$-limited coloring of ordered graphs and presents a generalized version of the order limit property of the $R$-sequential $t$-coloring number.  Finally, the paper provides a list of open problems related to the $R$-sequential $t$-coloring number. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distributional parameters, they are still considered reliable when the data follow a multivariate normal distribution due to the strong properties of the permutation distribution. However, under non-normal data conditions, these estimates can be considered unreliable as they depend heavily on approximated distributional parameters. In an attempt to overcome this issue, alternative methods for data-based correlation coefficient estimates have been developed using the distance between permutations of the data, specifically the maximum, mean, and median distances. Although these approaches offer the benefit of not relying on approximated distributional parameters, they still possess inherent weaknesses. As demonstrated by simulation studies, these methods can be overly conservative when the data does not exhibit normal distribution, resulting in potential false negative findings. In an effort to address this problem, a new method based on Bayesian credible intervals has been proposed, offering the advantage of not relying on approximated distributional parameters and exhibiting relatively smaller overlap with null hypotheses under non-normal data conditions compared to alternative methods. The new method employs confidence intervals by utilising the permutation distribution to establish a non-parametric reference distribution for the correlation coefficient, thus allowing for comparisons between observed values and credible intervals resulting from different permutations. While still reliant on approximations for quantile calculations, this approach offers significant improvements over alternative methods. Furthermore, the proposed method can be considered data-driven as it does not assume knowledge of the underlying distribution. In addition to correlation coefficient analysis, the technique has potential applications in other fields that commonly utilise non-parametric methods. The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, we propose a novel post-hoc method called CogRe, which produces an interactive lightbox to facilitate user understanding by providing clear and customizable item information. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across diverse scenarios to evaluate our approach. The results indicate that CogRe surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in providing transparent and trustworthy explanations while also providing a more appealing user experience compared to black-box recommendations. The method also demonstrates its practicality in various human-centered recommendation tasks through practical applications. The source code of the CogRe method is available at https://github.com/ghypogog/CogRe. Additionally, a live demo can be accessed at https://explainablerec.github.io/demo/. The study highlights areas for potential improvement in the field of post-hoc explanations and suggests future research directions. The findings also shed light on the current shortcomings of post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent dependability, serving as a baseline for future studies in this domain. In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicating existing data points through a ranking-based selection process, ensuring inclusions of all minority class observations. Various techniques are explored to accomplish this, including per-class selection and a novel hybrid approach combining these mechanisms. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach, especially the hybrid method, overcurrent state-of-the-art algorithms responsible for handling class imbalance problems, especially in the nearest neighbor classification context. This methodology's potential utility in classification tasks becomes apparent, and suggestions are provided for future research directions. Additionally, a comprehensive R package, named nnimb, is developed to facilitate implementation of these methods in real-world scenarios. Detailed step-by-step descriptions outlining how to implement these methods using graphical schemes are included in the appendices. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications. This research provides valuable insight into the mechanism regulating droplet growth in nano-coating and biological fluid dynamics. The new theoretical model can be used to explore a wide range of slip coefficients, from those reported in typical laboratory experiments to extremely low levels common in rare events. As a result, this model offers valuable control over droplet formation by controlling the film thickness and presence of surfactants. Additionally, this research demonstrates that large drops can form on fibers with high levels of nano-coating quality, contradicting a previous hypothesis suggesting that large drops are only possible with low nano-coating quality. In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental physics behind droplet formation, enabling designers to control droplet size by regulating film thickness and spinnability. The new theoretical model can also be applied to medical devices and other fields where liquid droplets play a crucial role. Furthermore, this research reveals that rare events, such as extremely low slip coefficients and thin films, significantly contribute to the typical droplet size observed in laboratory experiments. A low-cost robotic system utilizing an ultrasound probe is proposed to ease measurement procedures, particularly for those without prior expertise. This system is designed to identify vertebral bodies on ultrasound images with high accuracy and produce measurements similar to those obtained by established manual methods. A dataset of 42 patients suffering from scoliosis of varying curvature levels was used for the system's evaluation. Measurements obtained through the proposed robotic approach exhibited an average discrepancy of 1.26 degrees from established reference measurements, demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability. The proposed robotic solution successfully demonstrated its capability to improve curvature measurement accuracy by leveraging low-cost ultrasound imaging technology. This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (amalgams) for directed spaces are defined through subspaces of the smash product of a space and its one-point compactification.  We demonstrate that these amalgams encompass the standard powerdomains when considering continuous functions.  Moreover, by disregarding continuity, the op-powerspace provides a comprehensive description of subspaces, and the cl-powerspace offers a compactification of spaces with the same structure.  We also prove the equality of the op-powerspace and the cl-powerspace for specific cases where the space has a bounded index or is directed topological group.  Notably, the op-powerspace of a one-point space is the two-point Sippel-Lai monoidal envelope, and the cl-powerspace of an indexed disjoint union of one-point spaces is the unit interval with its Lebesgue interval topology.  This study presents novel space constructions - the op-powerspace and the cl-powerspace - for one-point compactified directed spaces and one-point spaces, respectively. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown significant benefits due to their high accuracy and efficient training capabilities. Despite their strong performance, they require large amounts of labeled data which often contains noise during the labeling process, leading to a significant decrease in robustness. Traditional methods focus solely on improving model design in an attempt to enhance resilience. In contrast, we aim to develop a data augmentation technique that identifies and corrects noisy labels by utilizing the model's uncertainty predictions and previous clean data. This method involves generating new samples using the posterior distribution and combining them with the model's output distribution through an energy-based technique. Our proposed technique outperforms existing methods by providing a substantial enhancement in top classification accuracy when utilizing the clean dataset and the largest dataset with minimal noise, and an impressive 6.5% increase in the extremely challenging completely noisy dataset. Our technique also demonstrates an average enhancement of 3.2% in robustness compared to the best traditional method, according to comprehensive computational tests across 12 medical datasets. Furthermore, we observed that our technique successfully reduces the number of noisy labels and retrieves about 85% of the clean data. This finding indicates our proposed technique's great potential for use in medical image classification by retrieving most of the clean data from a dataset with noisy labels. Experimental results are available online at https://github.com/NataliaC3/QMixu. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs by leveraging a modular clock addition technique. This method involves the use of special evaluation contexts, as found in the $\lambda^{\mathit{p}}$ language, which allows for context sensitive evaluation limits to be imposed without modifying function definitions. This method was effectively applied to simplify a clocked version of the Boy function in HOL. Additionally, this technique is compatible with $\mathrm{CPO}$-based semantics and contributes to the emergence of the $\lambda^{\mathit{p}}$ language as a standard solution for total logic specifications that require termination proofs. Furthermore, this method was also used to add clocks to div 0 and recursive functions, and results in a small clock size in all cases. Moreover, this method reveals certain div 0 and recursive function properties that fail to appear in HOL with total functions. To further validate this approach, a div 0 termination proof was developed using this method, as well as a special recursive function, mirroring a previously published paper. While a purely functional solution cannot circumvent all clock additions, we contend that our method outperforms other clock addition alternatives, thereby offering an improved solution compared to total functions logic and reducing the intrusion of clock mechanisms. This method was implemented in HOL and used in the formal verification of functional and transfinite iterative constructs. It can be downloaded at http://www.cs.ru.is/~femke/lambda-p.html. A similar implementation in the Coq library of the Hoare-Logic language at http://www.cs.ru.is/~femke/hoangle.html confirms that this method allows for sound and safe inference of program annotations. Finally, this method's potential applications extend beyond clocked termination proofs, as demonstrated by a sound and safe constructive transfinite iterative construct derivation. The study of computability of transfinite iterative constructs provides an appropriate testing ground for these novel clocked logic developments. The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multiclass topics, particularly focusing on three methods - Random Oversampling, Gaussian Noise Injection, and Easy Ensemble. It compares these methods to the SMOTE algorithm, which alleviates class dominance by generating new samples from underrepresented classes. The study's findings indicate that in a low class scenario, the easy ensemble method significantly outperforms the other oversampling methods. On the other hand, when classes are relatively balanced, the easy ensemble method's performance declines in comparison to Random Oversampling and Gaussian Noise Injection. The analysis also shows that the easy ensemble method nearly matches the efficiency of SMOTE in a 2-class scenario, but is slightly inferior in a multiclass context. Therefore, the easy ensemble method is recommended for classification tasks involving low-class scenarios and relatively balanced data sets, as it offers high accuracy and simplicity. Conversely, when dealing with multiclass dominant class issues, the easy ensemble method's performance tends to be inconsistent, making SMOTE a more reliable choice. The easy ensemble method's underlying nature suggests potential improvements could be achieved by integrating it with other algorithms that address class imbalance, such as Adasyn, resulting in a hybrid easy ensemble algorithm that generates synthetic samples from the skewed distribution. The integration of easy ensemble and synthetic learning is proposed, combining the capabilities of easy ensemble and binary synthetic learning to address challenging multiclass classification problems. The first easy ensemble algorithm generates new samples from the minority class, while a trained binary model uses the new easy-generated samples as training data to improve the classification of the minority class. The hybrid easy ensemble algorithm significantly enhances multiclass classification performance by reducing class imbalance issues. The study evaluates the performance of the proposed hybrid algorithm - easy ensemble and binary synthetic learning - using 11 multiclass, low minority data sets from various sources, showing improved performance compared to easy ensemble and SMOTE algorithms. The analysis also indicates that the proposed hybrid algorithm doesn't completely rectify class imbalance issues and may not always enhance multiclass classification when taken independently. The synthetic samples generated by easy ensemble can have reduced generalizability compared to the original minority class. The fusion of information may lead to decreased accuracy when limited by reduced sample size. Consequently, the classification of the new easy-generated samples - minority - majority can sometimes induce more errors than easy ensemble and SMOTE algorithms. The proposed hybrid easy ensemble and binary synthetic learning algorithm may lead to information dilution due to a decrease in the original minority sample size. This study analyzes the relationship between COVID-19 news coverage in the United States and its relationship with the regional and national death rates from the pandemic. Utilizing data on daily COVID-19 news from various sources and death rates from the American Community Survey, the researchers applied a network-based approach to examine time-varying correlations between news coverage and death rates at local, state, and national levels. They found significant correlations between news coverage in specific regions and death rates in those areas, as well as the ability to predict future correlations based on recent trends. When comparing news coverage to other variables such as mobility and temperature, the researchers found that news coverage was the best indicator of future death rates. They also discovered that news coverage in one region was associated with death rates not only in that region but also in surrounding areas, indicating a broader spatial impact. Furthermore, the results indicate that news coverage in certain regions was more responsive to changes in death rates in nearby areas and to national death rates, than to changes in local death rates. This study provides a unique understanding of the relationship between local news and COVID-19 mortality, offering insights that are both timely and long-lasting. Equipped with this knowledge, public officials can make more informed decisions, such as creating targeted policies to guide individual behavior, by utilizing up-to-date news coverage data as an indicator of people's perceptions of risk. Additionally, the findings suggest that news coverage can serve as an essential tool in enhancing the impact of policies aimed at behavioral change, such as increased mask-wearing. Ultimately, the results emphasize the significant role that news plays in shaping public awareness and the vital function that journalists perform in communicating vital information during crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic. They also highlight the limitations news coverage has in capturing all the key aspects of the pandemic, like mobility trends, which other data sources reveal are crucial variables in understanding behavioral change. In the long run, the study sets the stage for exploring news coverage as a general indicator of public awareness across various health crises, much like a sensor tracking shifting public perceptions of risk. By expanding the scope of its research, the study can provide vital insights into the critical role that news plays in shaping public discourse during global catastrophes such as pandemics, influenza outbreaks, and natural disasters. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus. By leveraging the capabilities of a superset of experienced policies, our method generates hypothetical experience gained by exploring these policies. The learned cloning functions also allow us to generate diverse, exploratory data, enhancing the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning. The proposed algorithm enhances data efficiency compared to current approaches and is evaluated on fundamental operations such as navigation and switching, ultimately demonstrating improved efficiency. Experiments also indicate that our method successfully discovers useful features when using simple parameterization or when incorporating neural networks. Furthermore, it enhances the efficiency of imitation learning when the training dataset is limited, allowing it to match or surpass the performance of learning strategies that actively collect new experience. The research was published in the NeurIPS 2021 conference. A codebase supporting the research is publicly available at: https://github.com/nmortas/pcplus. Atomic magnetometers that oscillate on their own offer enhanced sensitivity, a wider detection range, and improved durability.
We've developed a protocol to create a unified coherent detection technique for these oscillating magnetometers and classical lock-in amplifiers.
This new method, presented here, achieves unification by leveraging the far-off-resonance light from atomic magnetometers and modulating it coherently.
The results show that detected signals are proportional to the magnetization signal's frequency and amplitude.
Consequently, this approach enables accurate signal inference despite the limited linearity of atomic magnetometer detection and noise from light interference.
To validate our new detection theory, we tested it using an atomic magnetometer with a directly modulated light source as well as another atomic magnetometer with a separate modulator.
Experiments using the first configuration showed a minimum detection limit of 0.08 fT Hz^-1/2 at 1 kHz.
The second configuration yielded a detection threshold of 0.12 fT Hz^-1/2 at 1 kHz, very close to the theoretical minimum detection limit.
Both test cases demonstrated detection coefficients of 0.88 and 0.81, respectively.
We ran comprehensive simulations to assess potential interference from unwanted signals and identified suitable conditions for practical application. Additionally, this research offers a new approach to detecting frequency changes in atomic magnetometers. The detection coefficients achieved in this study are comparable to those obtained with classical lock-in amplifiers. We simulated various scenarios to calculate detection efficiency, a measure of the proportion of detected signal magnitude to total signal magnitude. For a signal with 10 pT amplitude and 10 Hz frequency, the detection efficiency in the two test cases was approximately 94% and 76%. We simulated an atomic magnetometer with a large modulation depth to address concerns about detection efficiency. As shown, the detection efficiency can be as high as 80% for certain high modulation depths and signals with 10 pT amplitude and 10 kHz frequency. However, this may come at the cost of additional noise. We compared coherent detection to other popular detection methods and found that it offers improved signal-to-noise ratio. A future area of interest lies in the use of coherent detection for various types of atomic magnetometers. Future research aims to extend the principles of coherent detection to other atomic magnetometer types. Future work will focus on integrating the coherent detection principle developed for self-oscillating atomic magnetometers to detect modulation frequency changes in other atomic magnetometer types, including Ravon-type, bulk, and vapor-cell atomic magnetometers

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Further analysis shows the algorithm's convergence in a distributed setting, backing up numerical demonstrations with real-world applications like joint clustering and Newton's method for its effectiveness. Results also highlight the proposed algorithm can successfully resolve issues other algorithms struggle with, like the widely-used LIBSVM dataset. The research further estimates the performance speed-up of the proposed algorithm over standard methods, providing valuable insights for practical implementation. The findings suggest an optimal balance exists between minimizing communication rounds and speed, which can be achieved depending on specific task requirements. Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigated the viability of leverage transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, making them part of the Indo-Aryan language family. Initially, we assembled and compiled datasets for each language, then designed and implemented a classification model, combining xBERT with additional language-specific features. Notably, our model demonstrated a high accuracy of 0.813, surpassing the benchmark. Furthermore, we analyzed the performance of our transfer learning-based approach and noted that performance improved when incorporating more training data. Notably, our model performed notably better on Hindi (0.813) compared to Bengali (0.533), highlighting a significant gap in data resources for this task. We also explored the effectiveness of human evaluation, which validated our model's results, demonstrating that most incorrect predictions were concentrated in the 25% outlier section. Based on these findings, we recommend increasing data resources for hate-speech detection in low-resource languages such as Hindi and Bengali. We also suggest exploring the use of multi-classification models that incorporate context, such as word and sentence embeddings, to enhance accuracy. Finally, our shared resources, including data compilation, model implementation, and additional language features, are available at https://github.com/amanmahawar/Hate-Speech-Classification-in-Hindi-and-Bengali. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-reflective questionnaire format to capture experts' diverse views. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading novel, unseen text instances during training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse array of obscure and rare words, making up just 1% of the entire dataset.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology. The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to efficiently integrate multi-dimensional dynamical systems in low-dimensional state spaces with high accuracy, outperforming traditional time integration methods. It has notable advantages, including incremental benefits and adaptability. To further improve its performance, an enhanced ASK method, dubbed high-order ASK (ASK-H), was developed, which employs sparse grid techniques to approximate the solution of multi-dimensional differential equations. By doing so, ASK-H significantly decreases computational costs while maintaining high accuracy compared to its original ASK counterpart. In this study, ASK-H's theoretical foundations, parameters, and implementation details are thoroughly examined. We also demonstrate its application in solving two complex real-world equations, the 2D Navier-Stokes and 2D Schrödinger equations, where the ASK-H method showed substantial potential for modeling and state prediction in these systems. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of ASK-H is made available for cross-validation and testing by the research community. The full details can be accessed at https://github.com/hi-ron/ASK-H_C. Additionally, this study highlights that sparse grid techniques, initially explored in the late 20th century and still expanding, require further development to meet the present demands of modern complex modeling and simulation. In the future, a deep investigation into the theoretical properties of sparse grid methods is anticipated to yield promising results. This review provides a comprehensive explanation of quantum mechanics transitions through potential barriers, emphasizing the calculation of resonance parameters. Original methods to compute these parameters are also described, and a discussion on their significance is explored. Furthermore, the review delves into the CMWC model, which describes the quark composition of hadrons, and applies the outlined techniques to determine resonance parameters in this context. By setting the CMWC model boundaries, the calculated parameters can be compared to experimental data, ultimately enabling the verification of the model's validity. Notably, the numerical results obtained can be used to compute depth and breadth of potential wells required to match experimental data. In a related finding, the scalar octet forces' relative strengths to the strong interaction constant were calculated and determined to be in the order of $10^{-3}$ (with regard to $f_\pi^2/G_\pi$), while the scalar non-resonant interactions' width was found to be on the order of $10^{-10}$ eV, essentially non-existent. Furthermore, the calculation of the CMWC radii for various particles like mesons, baryons, and others revealed distinct size differences among them. Interestingly, the calculated scalar non-resonant widths can also be used to estimate the CMWC model's lifetime, which is comparable to the estimated lifetime of the universe itself. Notably, the entire known mass spectrum of hadrons can be generated from the CMWC model's parameter space with a dimensionality of 400, highlighting the model's simplicity. Finally, the review explores potential future applications of the CMWC model in addressing long-standing enigmas in particle physics. In the realm of fundamental physics, the CMWC model addresses several key issues at once: the quark composition problem, scalar octet forces and non-resonant interactions, the quantization of gravity problem (at least in terms of scalar gravity), and the black-hole information paradox. In the area of experimental particle physics, the review notes that future CMWC-related experiments could facilitate a systematic search for long-lost cosmic particles. In the area of fundamental cosmology, the review inquires whether the CMWC model could help resolve long-standing cosmic enigmas in the universe's early stages. Notably, the review suggests the CMWC model could help explain two key cosmological paradoxes: the entropy and horizon problems. Ultimately, the review expresses the hope that future fundamental physics, the CMWC model, and related scalar physics will significantly contribute to our understanding of the universe. The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and employs two methods to calculate the t¯t cross-section. The differential t¯t distribution reveals an over-prediction of up to 20% by next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD compared to the two-loop truncated NNLLO prediction. Consequently, the integrated t¯t cross-section amounts to 48.6 pb, with a corresponding uncertainty of 3.8 pb resulting from systematic uncertainties and 6.0 pb arising from theoretical uncertainties, which aligns with theoretical predictions involving multiple-loop splittings and corrections as reported in the studies referenced above. Furthermore, data analysis yields constraints on the t¯t mass, specifically 340-580 GeV, and allows for constraints on NNLO QCD models by comparing with predicted t¯t masses of 543 GeV. The measured cross-section is also compared with trial gluon distribution functions modified at the level of parton showers. The modified gluon distribution functions result in a t¯t cross-section deviating by 1- to 5-σ from the SM value. The investigation into the influence of high-pT Poisson distributed minijets produced during t¯t events on the t¯t measurement reveals negligible effects. Lastly, the t¯t cross-section measured in 7 and 8 TeV collisions is employed to determine the value of the strange quark mass, which is found to be 93 MeV, with a corresponding uncertainty of 12% arising from theoretical uncertainties. Despite the significant impact urban dynamics hold on economic success, there is an alarming shortage of high-quality data available to study and measure these dynamics. In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy, known as probability-matching, as opposed to an ideal strategy, called maximization.  A specific mathematical model, established by Gilman and Edwards (2016), has a characteristic that causes a system of equations representing this model to have infinite solutions when a specific limit is reached, describing an optimal decision-maker's behavior.  This unusual property allows us to present a unique infinite ladder of probability-matching probabilities resulting from a particular system of equations with a specific coefficient value of 1.  Furthermore, we show that this ladder is consistent with the properties of a group under group operations, provided that the probability range remains within [0,1] and a specific mathematical operation is applied accordingly.  In addition, we present an alternate characterization of this ladder using commutative groups and identify existing instances of such group structures in mathematical literature.  Ultimately, our analysis provides a definitive understanding of how probability-matching probabilities are generated from an infinite ladder of group operations, with group identity serving as the starting point for minimization, as well as how they relate to specific strategic decision-making cases involving probability-matching.  Key to our proof is a previously published finding by Fung in 1998, showing that two related systems of equations have a unique solution for specific coefficient values greater than or equal to one.  Leveraging this result allows us to present our main contribution, consisting of a mathematical relationship between probability-matching probabilities and an infinite, group-operated ladder with identity as the starting point for minimization.  Importantly, our analysis corresponds to earlier findings by Gilman and Edwards (2016) concerning the characteristics of these probability-matching probabilities.  Consequently, our presentation of the group structure underlying the probability-matching probabilities of an optimal decision-maker, as described by the specific mathematical model, enhances our understanding of how these probabilities behave under certain strategic decision-making cases with specific coefficient values.  Finally, our findings validate a previously published finding by Fung in 1998 concerning the range of these probability-matching probabilities.  Importantly, our presentation of the group structure underlying the probability-matching probabilities of an optimal decision-maker, as described by the specific mathematical model, enhances our understanding of how these probabilities relate to specific strategic decision-making cases with specific coefficient values, as well as how they compare to other forms of strategic decision-making.  Lastly, our findings validate a previously published finding by Fung in 1998 concerning the range of these probability-matching probabilities.
