The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, while c-approximating the true distance. This research provides the first theoretical analysis of this problem for curves in d-dimensional space. It demonstrates that a data structure using balls of a certain size can be created for any given constant c > 1, allowing efficient and approximate nearest neighbor searches. This involves a trade-off between c and data structure size, proving an optimal balance for specific values of c. Curves complexity is not a factor that affects the efficiency of this problem. This problem's theoretical analysis also considers non-convex curves and establishes a lower bound on the data structure size for certain values of c. All results were theoretically proven and tested using synthetic data. These results show a lower bound on the data structure size for a specific case and the necessity of a balanced trade-off between c and data structure size. Using all the established results, an empirical study shows the performance impact of data structure size on execution time. It also shows how different curve types (non-convex and simple) affect the data structure size and search efficiency. Both types of curves were used to compute the Fréchet distance in the study. Combining the theoretical findings with practical experiments highlights the importance of different design choices for applications. Overall, this research provides an in-depth analysis of the theoretical efficiency of the c-approximate near neighbor problem for curves in high-dimensional space. It extends the efficiency analysis to real-world applications like map navigation by computing the similarity between road networks. A practical demonstration of the data structure's efficiency shows the impact of different curve types on road network navigation. It also shows the benefits of using approximate distance metrics like c-approximate near neighbor for specific use cases like top-1 exact match. Lastly, this research establishes a connection between the c-approximate near neighbor problem and solving linear field field equations precisely. It highlights the significance of this connection for future research in discrete algorithms. All the results were further validated by genetic algorithms and by computing the Frechet distance in the real world. An additional study shows the performance impact of different design choices for the c-approximate near neighbor problem on a data structure's size and execution time. It shows the effectiveness of approximate distance metrics like c-approximate near neighbor for specific applications. Finally, all the established results were further demonstrated by computing the Frechet distance in the real world and testing the efficiency of different curve types

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between effectiveness and reliability, as more reliable methods often provide less benefit, whereas the most powerful methods are less reliable. In this study, a new model-independent technique for measuring the performance gains from MEM is developed. The method makes use of repeated experiments with varying levels of complexity, calculating the expected outcomes with sampling-based estimates. Through analysis of actual quantum computer data, it's verified that the proposed metric accurately characterizes the effectiveness of MEM. A new benchmark is introduced to evaluate the reliability of MEM, with the top-tier methods being those with the highest tradeoff between effectiveness and reliability. The method's benchmark values are provided for multiple MEM scenarios, enabling the selection of the most suitable method for a given experiment. Additionally, the technique facilitates recommendations for optimal experimental designs, as shown through an examination of different strategies for reducing long-range coupling in the nuclear magnetic resonance quantum computer. The proposed method can potentially be adapted to other noisy quantum hardware. By identifying the tradeoff between effectiveness and reliability, it may be possible to improve the performance of MEM by optimizing these parameters. The method's development also inspires novel MEM methods that balance effectiveness and reliability. The proposed metrics and associated analysis provide a framework for a systematic evaluation of MEM, ultimately paving the way for strategic improvements. The metric-based assessment can lead to the discovery of MEM methods that are both effective and reliable, thereby fulfilling the primary objective of the technique. A Python package named QMEMMit for measuring the effectiveness of MEM methods with the proposed metric is available at the public GitHub repository address. The package includes functions to calculate the effectiveness metric, the reliability benchmark, and the optimal experimental design. A companion notebook detailing the steps to install the package and use it for analyzing the NMRQCD benchmark is included in the package. The authors' email addresses are listed in the author information section of the article. Furthermore, a data repository containing all the data analyzed in this research has been established at the specified address, with existing datasets IDED:99196. Existing datasets can be analyzed using the proposed metric by utilizing the provided package and following the instructions in the accompanying notebook. When analyzing new datasets, researches can simply run the commands listed in the notebook, with the necessary parameters defined. When humans operate robot arms, it's crucial they understand the robot is only informed about the commands it's explicitly instructed to use. Otherwise, unintended behaviors may arise. To rectify this, researchers proposed the Conventional Action Language (CAL), which ensures the robot comprehends its controller's intentions through embedded constraints. However, during actual tasks, instructors often deviate from established conventions to accomplish novel objectives. Consequently, robots must adapt their understanding mid-task. In our work, we introduce Multiple Belief Assignments (MBA) - a groundbreaking technique allowing a single robot to simultaneously understand multiple conventions from its same controller by assigning separate beliefs. Multiple convention awareness increases the robot's usefulness in tasks where multiple conventions coexist and when instructors dynamically change the controller conventions mid-task. Our experiments with up to four concurrent conventions have shown MBA-based robots successfully adapt to changes in conventions without interference from the tasks themselves. In a collaborative study involving human-robot interaction, it was observed that MBA-based robots receive better reception from human operators because they better grasp the controller's conventions. As a result, assistance from the robot increases when its understanding matches its instructor's intentions. Our analysis suggests an MBA-based robot can learn and understand up to four distinct conventions in about 15 to 18 seconds, a time frame equivalent to roughly five to seven robot arm movements. In contrast, a control switch when two conventions are understood would take about 35 to 43 seconds, roughly ten to twelve robot arm movements. The research has been made available online at: https://github.com/azamros/Multiple-Convention-Telrobot. The project includes an updated version of the CAL language, an MBA-based planning tool, and a user-friendly interface to view the research findings. The actual MBA-based planning tool and relevant dataset are planned for distribution in the future. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale in real-world environments is challenging due to their high demand on computational resources and poor resilience to dynamic changes. In order to tackle this problem, a new mapping system called Topological Hidden Markov Field (TopHMF) has been developed to efficiently create flexible and adaptable maps, especially suitable for large-scale environments. The TopHMF method consists of two main parts: a topological graph that represents an environment with connected locations and a spatially-organized occupancy grid map that represents local environmental features. The topHMF model observes sensor data while navigating, updating the topological graph and the OCC grid maps simultaneously using the message passing technique, thus achieving a mapping system that is both modular and computationally efficient. The message passing technique also enables topHMF to maintain a consistent and systematic mapping system even in the presence of uncertainty and dynamic changes. The method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through simulations and real-world tests that showcase its ability to create a systematic and flexible map using sensor data, thus demonstrating its superiority to other common mapping systems. The method's performance has also shown resilience to dynamic changes, minimal topological changes, and low demand on computational resources, making it a suitable mapping system for large-scale environments. The potential benefits of using the TopHMF method for 3D mapping are also analyzed. This paper presents a novel method to directly construct two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets by utilizing multivariable functions. To achieve this, an inter-group complementary code set is first developed using multivariable functions and subsequently utilized to produce the desired two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets. Utilizing multivariable functions enables the determination of two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of L1 x L2, where L1 can be set to a power of two (L1 = 2^m), and L2 can be set to a combination of powers of two or other prime numbers (L2 = p1^k1 * p2^k2... pm^km). Next, the two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of 2^5 x 16 can be constructed. Lastly, the two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of 2^7 x 16 can be built. In each instance, the generalized two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets consist of 128 sets of 2^5 x 16 code words. This number can be set to a power of two (2^8) based on the parameters chosen. An example of constructing two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of 2^5 x 16 showcases 128 sets of unique code words. A comparison between the proposed multivariable functions based two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets and traditional two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets reveals a significant reduction in size, with multivariable functions achieving 2.67 times more code sets of 2^5 x 16 compared to the traditional two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of 2^4 x 16. Furthermore, an analysis of the sidelobe leakage of multivariable functions can be achieved using a 2 x 16 two-dimensional zero-complementary array code set example. An ideal two-dimensional zero-complementary array code set is utilized as a reference for comparison. Utilizing multivariable functions results in a significant reduction in sidelobe leakage, showcasing a maximum sidelobe leakage of -22.18 dB, compared to the two-dimensional zero-complementary array code set's maximum sidelobe leakage of 0

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal objects. Most industrial and medical CT scanners rely on polyenergetic X-ray sources, which often lead to distorted image data due to variations in X-ray attenuation. In this study, a model-based CT image reconstruction algorithm tailored for use with polyenergetic X-rays is investigated. A simplified model representing the energy distribution of polyenergetic X-rays is initially outlined. Next, two algorithm implementations, tailored for use with either regular or dual-energy data, are described. Subsequently, several test scenarios with known outcome references are prepared. Finally, the performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated in comparison to a conventional CT reconstruction method and other reference data through metrics such as Spatial Resolution, Noise Level, and Artifact Presence. Notably, the results indicate that using dual-energy data leads to slightly improved Image Quality when compared to using regular-energy data. Moreover, the reconstructed images obtained with the proposed algorithm demonstrate superior spatial resolution, mild beam hardening artifacts, and moderate peak absorption values. In contrast, CT images reconstructed using the conventional algorithm exhibit decreased spatial resolution, severe beam hardening artifacts, elevated noise levels, and increased absorption values. In general, the reconstructed images obtained with the proposed algorithm and dual-energy data showed results intermediate between those obtained with the proposed algorithm and polyenergetic data and the conventional algorithm. Based on these findings, it is possible to enhance image quality by applying a filter with a cutoff frequency around 10-20 radian. In addition, the presence of significant beam hardening artifacts suggests potential benefits from using a correction algorithm. In contrast, the results obtained with the proposed algorithm and polyenergetic data showed intermediate results when compared to the other test scenarios, indicating the potential to further improve low spatial frequency details through a filter with a frequency below 10 radian. In order to verify these findings, a real test was conducted using data from a certified phantom. In this real test, the proposed algorithm demonstrated slight overestimation of materials with high atomic numbers when compared to reference data, whereas a generally low estimate error was observed for other materials. In contrast, CT numbers obtained using the conventional algorithm showed significant discrepancies with reference data for most materials. Notably, the reconstructed images obtained with the proposed algorithm demonstrated certified phantom details similar to those obtained with dual-energy data. In conclusion, the results from both test scenarios and a real-world experiment highlight the potential benefits of using the proposed algorithm for improved CT image quality when polyenergetic X-ray sources are involved

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a local approach leads to divergent field results in areas where the electron spillover from one metal overlaps with the other. By contrast, both the hydrodynamics model and a nonlocal approach derived from quantum hydrodynamics produce convergent field results. Furthermore, we find that the hydrodynamics model simplifies to a nonlocal approach when considering a relatively large distance between the metals, compared to the electron mean free path. We suggest that a nonlocal approach could be applicable to a wide range of metal structures due to spillover causing electron interactions across these structures. This could potentially enhance the resonant field strength, which may influence the rules governing spillover. We also identify a method to enhance surface plasmon coupling, which may lead to novel applications. Lastly, we compare our hydrodynamics model to a well-known nonlocal model by Silkin and Ezhov et al and demonstrate that the equivalent expression for the Silkin model's nonlocal conductivity matches our hydrodynamics model's nonlocal expression. Consequently, we can conclude that the hydrodynamics model is compatible with the Silkin model. Additionally, since the Silkin model is founded on quantum mechanics, this indicates that the hydrodynamics model is compatible with quantum mechanics. Therefore, the hydrodynamics model is a useful simplification of quantum mechanics for modeling light propagation between two metal structures. This study may also inspire further research into other scaling methods from quantum mechanics. Furthermore, the similarities between the hydrodynamics model and quantum hydrodynamics simulations of metals in ultrafast experiments highlight the potential for describing electron behavior using hydrodynamics, even at a quantum level. Ultimately, the concepts discussed may be developed into novel applications such as highly efficient surface plasmon-based couplers, switches, and sensors for detecting far-off photons. The mechanisms discussed could also potentially be applied in other metal structures beyond the simple slit model examined in this study. Generalizing these mechanisms could lead to the creation of superfluid-like phenomena in metal droplets, films, and other forms, which would have far-reaching implications for optical and photonic applications. The underlying theory has broad applications in optics and photonics due to the shared nature of hydrodynamics and quantum hydrodynamics simulations with ultrafast experiments and quantum mechanics. While some query refinement methods attempt to enhance effectiveness by simulating human input, a recent study suggests that human involvement typically leads to less precise results. To improve upon this, the researchers present ReMix, a hybrid system that combines the strengths of automated and user-driven query refinement by leveraging their respective advantages. As a result, ReMix achieves better retrieval outcomes compared to systems not utilizing user input, while also outperforming existing query refinement methods that rely on artificial intelligence. Furthermore, user testing indicates that the way ReMix presents alternatives aligns closely with how humans formulate queries. Overall, the approach demonstrates that human involvement in information retrieval tasks can be beneficial, and that intelligent systems should utilize human insight rather than attempting to simulate it. The researchers also present an evaluation method that views user input as a signal to learn an intelligent query refinement model, and highlight the differences between human and artificial intelligence in the ReMix framework. This allows the approach to bridge the gap between the two, while still delivering superior performance. The proposed model involves expressing data as a combination of distinct components, including a universal pattern and individual influences related to specific variables. The burgeoning quantity of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has ignited a surge in research aiming to utilize machine learning models as a tool for diagnosing and predicting patient health. By leveraging detailed, long-term insights into individual patient behavior, we aim to refine our understanding of disease progression and optimize therapeutic outcomes on a population scale. In recent years, various studies have employed graph-based frameworks to represent complex patient relationships and clinical pathways. However, most of these models have been developed in an unsupervised manner, limiting their potential for predictive analysis. In response, we have developed GraphBERT, a pioneering model that combines the strengths of BERT and graph convolutional networks to capture entity-specific correlations in EHR data. By incorporating attention mechanisms, we demonstrate the ability of GraphBERT to identify key entities and their interconnections, yielding superior predictive performance in a new state-of-the-art medical diagnosis system. Our system has achieved outstanding results, surpassing existing benchmarks in eight distinct medical scenarios, with remarkable accuracy rates between 86.7% and 95.9%. Notably, GraphBERT has played a pivotal role in this achievement, showcasing its versatility as a named entity recognition tool. Building upon this breakthrough, we have released our source code and dataset under an open-source license, aiming to facilitate future research and applications. The GraphBERT implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/ai4health3d/GraphBERT. Our dataset is publicly available through the McGill Access to Multimedia Educational Materials (M-LEM) platform at mcgill-lem.ai. Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and permittivity near the boundary. Significantly, our results show that taking solvent effects into account reduces the Donnan potential, contrary to the finite size of ions' influence previously found in other studies. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the permittivity of the solvent approaches its bulk value in this context, unlike scenarios with non-polarizable particles. Notably, our study reveals a high concentration of ions within the boundary, even without considering them as having a finite size. Ultimately, we find that the permittivity and ion counts exhibit a range of variations, influenced by both the electrostatic potential and water's sub-level behavior. These findings are relevant to a broad range of systems, including biological and soft matter systems, where system scale may not necessarily dictate particle size. Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information (RFI) documents. The fine-tuned BERT model achieved encouraging results on the PURE dataset, demonstrating superior performance on binary sentence classification with an impressive 0.16% advantage over fastText and a 3% advantage over ELMo. Moreover, BERT generated predictive models with high cross-validation scores of 0.90, outperforming existing models by 3-4% on the PURE dataset. To validate the model's applicability in more unrefined textual contexts, we tested it using the RFI dataset, yielding a predictive score of 0.65, accompanied by an analysis highlighting the significance of wording in the predictive model. Word importance evaluation, derived from the predictive model, showed interesting insights, pointing to specific phrases like "shall be provided" as indicative factors, useful for refining word selection during requirement writing. Lastly, we derived a binary classification model using the PURE dataset, achieving a 0.70 score; the model highlighted unique features, including location-related words, that significantly influence the prediction outcome. To facilitate future research, we will make the PURE dataset publicly available along with the annotated files and BERT models. Publicly accessible links will be shared upon acceptance of this work. The fine-tuned BERT model will also be integrated into an online tool supporting requirement engineers, helping identify relevant information in textual documents in the framework of REPRODUCT. The online tool's demo, including the integration of the predictive model, can be accessed at https://demoreprodt.com. To preserve transparency, our code will be shared on https://github.com/transparent-sdr/PURE/tree/master/code. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the manganese adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while the manganese dimer exhibited significant spin-orbit interactions, especially in the inter-atomic bound state. Additionally, the theoretical spectra for a non-magnetic atom were generated and compared with those of the manganese dimer to determine the impact of this atom's presence on the YSR states. Lastly, the theoretical spectra for a magnetic bi-atom with highly aligned spins were produced and the results compared with experimental data after accounting for spin-orbit interactions. After accounting for spin-orbit interactions, the theoretical spectra showed a better alignment with experimental results compared to unaligned spin axes. This specific example highlights the importance of spin-orbit interactions in certain magnetic bi-atom bound states. Consequently, spin-orbit interactions cannot be disregarded when analyzing YSR states, especially in situations involving strong spin-orbit coupling as seen in certain ferromagnetic materials. The developed theoretical framework is now ready for use in analyzing a wide range of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This research aims to provide valuable information regarding the magnetic, non-magnetic, or weakly ferromagnetic nature of these impurities, which in turn enables the identification of spin-orbit interactions and quantum phase shifts. Ultimately, precise analysis of YSR states and magnetic impurity states can be achieved through the understanding of spin-orbit interactions. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration in such situations, deep learning-based approaches have been developed, including the Pixel Registration Network (PRN).  Despite the good performance of PRN in registration, it does not provide accurate bounds on point cloud alignment errors in dynamic scenes, making it difficult to assess its level of reliability.  To address this shortcoming, a method combining PRN with an optimization technique has been proposed, incorporating a mean squared error loss with an inverse distance metric as a proxy for evaluating alignment errors.  Experimental results demonstrate that this new approach, dubbed PRN-INV, rivals the best current registration techniques in terms of registration accuracy and provides tight estimates of alignment errors in dynamic scenes, with potential applications in evaluating registration robustness and guiding learning algorithms.  Additionally, this new approach facilitates the evaluation of the impact of PRN's parameter count on registration performance and its potential trade-offs between accuracy and reliability.  Further discussion of the proposed method can be found in a related blog post at https://blog.pointcloudreg.io/2022/04/04/quantifying-registration-errors.html.  Related code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/PCReg.  Related video recordings of conference presentations can be found at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLdU0h7HzVp8s3XxvQkYxu0DQXqfYFwvF.  A related paper was presented at CVPR 2022, with a supplementary document containing additional information provided via arXiv.  A related video series detailing NDT, PRN, and PCReg can be found at https://www.youtube.com/pointcloudreg/playlist.  A related YouTube Live event discussing point cloud registration was held in November 2021, with related videos available at https://www.youtube.com/pointcloudreg.  A related research effort detailed in a PhD dissertation at University of Michigan, with related research papers listed at Defining Registration Errors.  A related research question was asked in a question paper at 3DVC 2020, with related information provided via a LinkedIn group called Point Cloud Registration.  A related research effort is being conducted with a related GitHub repository containing related research projects, including PCD registration.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning techniques have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure. In light of this challenge, a novel solution 
is proposed - using a powerful, AI-capable, programmable chip, the Peltier 
microarray controller, to develop a customized, parallel processing system for 
efficient image analysis. By adopting this experimental approach, a prototype 
board was designed and tested for evaluating and classifying images based on 
the speed and accuracy of its processing methods. In comparison to standard, 
non-reconfigurable computers, the results indicate a significant performance 
boost, with speedups of 80.57 times and accuracy improvements of 6% achieved 
when applying a specific image analysis algorithm to the LCENC dataset. This 
experimental outcome opens new avenues for the development of energy-efficient 
and adaptable processors capable of accelerated image analysis, thereby 
significantly reducing costs and promoting the widespread application of 
satellite imagery. The project's source code has been made publicly available on 
the GitHub platform. https://github.com/HiGrahame/AIC_AIPchip.article.liquid.

Subjecting amorphous iron oxide to intense X-ray pulses in non-resonant conditions causes significant changes in its XANES spectra, which greatly depend on the incoming fluence. These alterations can be attributed primarily to the increased ionization of the target material. However, discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental observations arise when attempting to explain the observed distortions in the spectra using ionization-induced disorder or transient magnetism. To address this gap, simulations incorporating all relevant physical processes and comparing experimentally measured and predicted spectra suggest that the observed changes may be mainly due to photoionization-induced changes in the orbital occupations and associated band shifts. Furthermore, it is observed that the transient state following photoionization exhibits prolonged persistence, which is significantly longer than previously anticipated. Notably, this persistence extends to sub-100 fs timescales, notably in iron but not oxygen; the underlying mechanisms behind these phenomena are explored. Consensus exists that total electron yield is an accurate measure for determining the state of the target following intense photon absorption. Moreover, electron-electron interactions in the target are found to have a minimal effect on the XANES spectra in this study. The observed extended persistence of the transient state could offer new opportunities for investigating electronic excitations and interacting electron sub-shells. Ultimately, this research sets the stage for leveraging XANES to directly probe electronic excitation dynamics using next-generation X-ray sources. Moreover, employing XANES to study ultrafast electronic excitation may become even more prevalent following the anticipated commissioning of the European XFEL in the near future. The findings from this research are anticipated to make significant contributions beyond the specific system studied here due to their general applicability to various systems. In particular, the observed extended persistence of the transient state is predicted to be relevant to a wide range of systems. Finally, it is demonstrated that the spectral features associated with 1s to 3d transitions persist until approximately 300 fs, which is significantly longer than previously anticipated. The underlying mechanisms behind these phenomena are explored in detail. Consensus exists that the extended persistence of the transient state offers novel opportunities for investigating electronic excitation and sub-lattice-dependent transitions using next-generation X-ray sources. The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN countermeasures were ineffective in our scenario, so we employed a new variant that uses multiple generators to avoid a mode collapsing issue common in radio signal classification. Simulation results indicate that this countermeasure can improve the DNN-based AMC's accuracy against attacks by 11% to 18% under different conditions, outperforming a baseline method by 6% in some scenarios. The approach also demonstrates general applicability to various DNN-based communication systems. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on the BER-robustness of the DNN classifier, showing improved resistance to attacks in scenarios with similar signal strengths. This method can be adapted to other machine learning-based communication systems. The paper conducts a comparative analysis of the computational cost and BER-robustness for three countermeasure methods like PCA, SEM, and our GAN-based approach, revealing a 20% lower computational cost compared to the GAN model. Furthermore, the DNN-based AMC with the proposed protection method still maintains a high BER of 0.083 when under attack, comparable to its robustness without attack. The method's efficacy is assessed under varying levels of interference and different types of attacks to simulate real-world wireless environments. The approach is evaluated under conditions with multiple attack types and varying levels of interference, showcasing its effectiveness in mitigating the effects of adversarial attacks on AMC systems. The simulation results can be applied to real-world scenarios with different levels of interference and attack strengths. The method's performance is evaluated under full-band interference and multiple attack types, demonstrating robustness to diverse adversarial attacks. The approach shows enhanced resilience to attacks compared to AMC systems without protection. The power of the proposed approach increases with the number of guard bits used. The method's performance is evaluated on real-world signals and shows robustness to varying attack strengths. The power of the proposed approach decreases with the presence of multiple attack types, revealing a trade-off between its effectiveness and computational cost. The method's performance is comparable to existing countermeasures under ideal signal conditions.

Recent studies have used deep learning techniques for MS lesion segmentation,
but they have yet to deliver satisfactory results in real-world scanning environments.
One major drawback of these methods is their reliance on extensive training datasets,
which are often difficult to come across.
We've made significant advancements in this area by training a novel deep learning
model using a large, publicly available dataset of 13,000 brain scans.

segmentation task into more manageable components, in order to deliver better
outcomes for a wider range of scanning environments.

In the context of continuous-time ergodic systems, determining the underlying parameter values $\theta$ from observed data is crucial yet challenging due to the lack of spatial or temporal sectionality. To address this issue, this research focuses on estimating $\theta$ based on continuous data streams and provides a theoretical framework for generalization. Our results demonstrate that the estimation error is influenced by both the sampling rate and the observation duration $T$. Building on this framework, regularized stochastic gradient descent is employed for parameter estimation. By combining the insights from the classical asymptotic analysis with the novel theoretical framework, our findings reveal that the estimation accuracy is largely independent of the specific algorithm used when the observation duration increases. However, the convergence rate at the initial stage is non-trivial and depends on the tuning of the regularization and step size. Utilizing the analysis from the classical literature, our research shows that the estimation risk exhibits a double-phased convergence behavior. The first phase of the risk curve exhibits an initial decrease with increasing sample size at a rate of $1/\sqrt{T}$. At the second phase, the risk plateaus at the $O(1/T)$ level. Our simulations verify the theoretical efficacy of the proposed approach. The presented framework is versatile and can be applied to a broader range of algorithms used for parameter estimation with continuous-time ergodic systems. Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Additionally, we develop a new dataset from a combined source of human annotated examples and machine generated text, which we believe offers a higher degree of accuracy. Our results indicate that all types of negation present significant challenges to various ranges of language models. Interestingly, models performed better on some negation types with controlled complexity than with complex forms. Our findings suggest that different types of negation require distinct approaches to overcome. Further investigation is needed to guide the development of more effective methods. In neural machine translation, the attention model contributes significantly to the model's ability to select relevant source words to predict target words. However, traditional decoder models that rely solely on the previous target word to calculate the attention weights are limited, as the importance of source words often changes across target words. This paper proposes a new attention model that allows the calculation of attention weights to be conditioned not only on the previous target word, but also on all previously generated target words. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance in modeling NMT and is named the "catalyst" model, which refers to the enhanced attention weights being calculated as the sum of contributions from source words and previous target words. The experimental results show that this model achieves a significant improvement in perforance, ranging from 0.6 to 2.1, on various data sets. The source code of the proposed model is available online at the URL https://github.com/yu-yiming/NMTNBLA. The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters are potential candidates. In this study, researchers used data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope to observe the non-ultrahigh-energy range of the emission spectrum of these galactic objects, specifically the Blaauw's Giant star cluster in W4 complex, a star-forming complex in the galaxy's bulge, and several galactic ridges. They collected 10-month data on the Blaauw's Giant star cluster in W4 complex and a nearby eclipse, as well as 4 and 17 month data on SF and Black Hole emissions. Analyzing these datasets using a double-exponential function, researchers found the following results: (1) The Blaauw's Giant star cluster in W4 emitted gamma-rays at an intensity of 8.8 x 10^-9 cm^-2 s^-1, within 100 MeV to 10 GeV, at a 95% confidence level; (2) The Blaauw's Giant star cluster in W4's emission spectrum followed a double-exponential function; (3) SF emitted gamma-rays at an intensity lower than the Blaauw's Giant star cluster in W4, at a 2 sigma confidence level; (4) Black Hole emissions agreed with prior research, at a 95% confidence level; (5) SF and Black Hole emissions' emission spectra followed double-exponential functions, at a 95% confidence level. Comparing these findings to prior research, researchers found the following: (6) SF and Black Hole emissions' emission spectra matched the diffuse gamma-ray background's emission spectrum, at a 95% confidence level. Researchers suggest that star-forming and starburst galaxies likely contribute to the diffuse gamma-ray background. If confirmed by prior research, researchers likely rules out galactic clusters as the diffuse gamma-ray background's source. Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints. To this end, it offers and analyzes a new iteration technique. When studying this algorithm, it was noticed that, for certain C\^a\'{c} type conditions, it allows for the generation of the Moreau proximal mapping's fixed points. Furthermore, it was also demonstrated that, under particular circumstances, it can serve as a primal algorithm for solving tri-variate minimization problems. To validate this, an example based on a particular finite polyhedral minimization problem was given. This algorithm's convergence was proven through establishing its ability to decrease the Moreau proximal mapping's distance in every iteration, as well as through its connection to the equilibrium problem's solutions under C\^a\'{c} conditions. To extend its applicability to equilibrium problems requiring C\^a\'{c} conditions, a new, hybrid algorithm that unifies the Buried Point algorithm and Neumann's algorithm was developed and proven convergent. To solve this problem, the proposed algorithm was modified into a algorithm for finding the minimum gap between $f$ and $f^*$. Through numerical tests conducted using random data, it was observed that, after some iterations, the equilibrium point was reached, and it was also noticed that, in the case of a specific instance of optimization problem (i.e., linear programming with a box constraint), the proposed algorithm reduced to a version of the Karmarkar algorithm. To further extend its applicability to equilibrium problems, the connection between the equilibrium problem and the least common fixed point of the Moreau proximal mappings of two proper functions was explored. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. By incorporating all relevant turbulent effects, we have found that the solutions of mean-field equations converge more effectively towards the results of global convective dynamo simulations compared to previous models based on the mean-field theory. The obtained solutions reveal that the alpha-effect driven oscillations are predominantly caused by helical buoyancy-driven convection patterns in the astrophysical context. Furthermore, we have identified and confirmed the presence of a delta-effect driven by toroidal field and a gamma-effect driven by both poloidal and toroidal fields. The delta-effect is primarily caused by the convection-driven lateral movement of magnetic fields, which is show to be the dominant effect in the bulk areas of the convective zone in stars like the Sun. The gamma-effect is a combination of several effects, including the vertical movement of magnetic fields, decay effects, diffusion, and the lateral movement of magnetic fields. Interestingly, we have found that the delta-effect is the primary source of helicity in the bulk areas of the convective zone in stars like the Sun. The obtained results provide significant insights into the underlying physical processes in global convective dynamo simulations and may lead to a better understanding of the underlying physics in global mean-field dynamo simulations in future studies. An investigation of the proposed method's order shows that its overall order is determined by the stage order of the predictor. We numerically test the method in both one and higher-dimensional spaces to evaluate its efficiency and numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness along with suggested guidelines for practical application. We conclude by providing some final remarks and suggestions for future research opportunities. Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem solution, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework. The analysis also extends to a stochastic horizon by applying a derivative approach, with an examination of the inherent risks. The combination of absolute and relative wealth maximization, with a flexible utility function, offers a more nuanced model of investor behavior, with potential applications in portfolio management and performance evaluation. The model's implications will be explored through numerical case studies, with an examination of the trade-offs between power law exponents in relation to market fluctuations, as well as scenarios in which the benefit of relative wealth maximization might outweigh absolute wealth maximization. Furthermore, the model will be evaluated using backtesting methods to assess its effectiveness in predicting portfolio returns. With the ability to estimate unique beta and gamma parameters tailored to individual benchmarks or market conditions, the model will be tested for its ability to predict parameter sensitivities and its performance relative to the Standard & Poor 500 index. The analysis will be extended to a multi-period setting, with an examination of the feasibility of multi-period relative wealth definition. The model's implications will be explored through multi-period numerical case studies, with an evaluation of the feasibility of direct multi-period relative wealth maximization in a single period. The results of our analysis will be compared to multi-period absolute wealth maximization, with a quantitative assessment of the trade-offs between these different scenarios. The knowledge gained from these case studies will enable the development of an investment strategy that effectively utilizes the combination of absolute and relative wealth maximization, with a tailored allocation of the exponents in power law utility functions, with potential overallocation observed in stochastic and multi-period settings, where the relative wealth maximization may offer greater benefits. The model's ability to generate realistic investment outcomes through backtesting will be demonstrated, with an evaluation of the sensitivity of the model's parameters to specific market conditions. We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle is resistant to collapse. The quasiparticle stability is reinforced by its high density of states and the energy cost of creating adjacent excitations, which greatly exceeds the excitation binding energy. Consequently, the mass of the quasiparticle remains unaffected by the presence of bosonic excitations. This stability robustness is an inherent characteristic of fermionic quasiparticles in various quantum systems, including high-temperature superconductors, where similar fermion-boson models have been employed. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen increasing attention due to its significant applications, although existing approaches have been limited by their lack of domain-specific adaptation capabilities, leading to suboptimal performance when dealing with novel, unseen videos. This has highlighted the need for a general, efficient framework that can effectively adapt to new videos across various domains. To address this challenge, a novel, token-shift based approach is proposed in TS2-Net, a flexible video-text adapter that utilizes relative position information through the employment of token-shift modules. This allows TS2-Net to easily support multiple tokenization strategies, including direct end-to-end fine-tuning from pre-trained models. Comprehensive experiments have demonstrated that, without requiring any hyperparameter tuning, TS2-Net has produced state-of-the-art results across various benchmark datasets, including BMVC's Text3D and TVS, as well as Kinetics-400 + VGG-CMP, yielding an impressive 12.6% absolute improvement in average recall at 32 frames. Furthermore, an insightful analysis of TS2-Net's gain in recall at various positions is also provided. The code and model of TS2-Net have been made publicly available. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a well-suited kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed these functions analytically or empirically chosen them from pre-existing options. Our research takes a distinct approach by leveraging a Genetic-Programming algorithm to dynamically evolve effective kernel functions. By allowing the parameters of these kernel functions to be adaptable and evolving kernel functions, we can easily apply Gaussian Processes to data with complex cyclic patterns, cyclic data requiring periodic kernels, and data with spatial structure requiring covariance functions based on geostatistics. By testing our algorithm with synthetic and real-world datasets, we have successfully derived kernel functions and observed substantial improvements in prediction accuracy, surpassing previously established benchmarks. Our research is available in an open-source form on GitHub, inclusive of the Code. Additionally, we have discussed additional aspects of our algorithm in a related paper. The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena, particularly the suppression of heat. A specific model involving a Bose gas with non-interacting particles in one dimension exhibits minimal thermalization in two dimensions through the application of a constant current, whereas it fully thermalizes in one dimension. 

In this study, we explore the boundary between these phenomena by isolating the spatial dimension's influence from other multibody effects through the use of a Gaussian boson model. When the temperature of this model increases, it undergoes a phase shift from a quasi-equilibrium steady state in one dimension to a non-thermal, quasi-equilibrium state in two dimensions.

In one dimension, the system remains cool because the energy is continuously increased in a manner that does not change the direction of an incoming flux. In this situation, even though the flux is constantly moving, the system does not reach a high temperature because the energy is not related to the flux's velocity. In two dimensions, the system does not remain cool because the flux's rotation causes the energy to increase in a manner that depends on the flux's direction, leading to a high temperature.

A key aspect of this study involves examining the relationship between the two-dimensional Gaussian boson model and the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type nonlinear diffusion equation. Notably, the model solves this equation exactly, leading to a first-order phase transition that occurs when a specific term in the equation changes signs. In this transition, the model exhibits a type of phase transition that is similar to the one observed in two dimensions. In one dimension, however, the model does not display this phase transition because the model behaves differently when the flux's velocity changes.

In summary, the study demonstrates that confinement to a single dimension prevents the suppression of heat and leads to a type of phase transition, revealing the interconnected nature of thermalization phenomena across spatial dimensions and multibody interactions. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often display shifting node relationships, neighbor transitions, and periodic patterns, making it essential to incorporate temporal dynamics into the embedding process. Consequently, researchers have developed various methods for dynamically embedding graphs that capture their evolving nature. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of these techniques, highlighting their strengths and limitations while also outlining open challenges and potential future directions in dynamic graph learning and embedding. Ultimately, we aim to encourage the development of more robust and transparent methods for dynamic graph representation learning. As this field is still in its early stages, there is considerable research potential for creating effective and scalable techniques to embed dynamic graphs accurately. The proposed overview is structured into three main categories: extension of static graph embedding methods, integral learning of shifting dynamics, and distributional learning of transient patterns. We discuss each category's core aspects, exemplified by existing methods, and discuss the issues of data scarcity, node isolation, subgraph sparsity, node churning, and periodic patterns. The distributional learning of transient patterns, in particular, requires further attention in order to capture the temporal nature of graphs that display periodical behavior, as observed in networks such as air transportation systems and football leagues. One way to quantify these properties is by calculating Betti numbers, which describe a space's connectedness structure. Research has shown that compressing data using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) preserves key topological features as measured by persistent homology. This study investigates whether PCA's ability to maintain topological properties holds true for datasets in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, considering a range of scaling parameters from the mean squared error to the Frobenius norm. It is demonstrated that using the Weyl operator for PCA, with a given parameter σ, results in a topological structure that resembles that of the original data set. This is characterized by calculations involving the cup product in an even Betti number context, or equivalently, through polynomial invariants in odd Betti number scenarios. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing gauge invariance as an argument, we then disprove the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene, revealing that the orbital magnetic moment cannot be considered a measurable quantity in this context.  Notably, our findings also dispprove previous studies claiming the occurrence of the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene.  Our work effectively dismisses the findings of recent experiments aiming to identify the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene.  Furthermore, orbital Hall effect arguments are also applied to a different system - monolayer MoS2.  Initially, predictions suggesting the occurrence of the orbital Hall effect in this system are produced using a specific type of band structure model.  Our research, however, demonstrates that these predictions are inaccurate and relies on gauge invariance to disprove them, ultimately concluding that the orbital Hall effect does not occur in monolayer MoS2.  Additional reasoning based on a more precise, accurate monolayer MoS2 band structure also dismisses any occurrence of the orbital Hall effect in this system.  Our research provides key insights into a more precise, accurate monolayer MoS2 band structure and can potentially apply these findings to other 2d semiconductors.  Our method of using gauge invariance to disprove previous studies of the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene and monolayer MoS2 is an essential tool, capable of being applied to other systems to confirm the occurrence or dismiss the findings of the orbital Hall effect.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected entities. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships. OntoPlot employs a dual-layer layout, where class hierarchies are displayed in a vertical stack and related class relationships are represented in a horizontal network. To enhance user comprehension, OntoPlot incorporates both hierarchical and network views. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in a user study comparing it to well-established visualisation tools. Our evaluation encompasses various tasks, including navigation, relationship verification, and new entity placement. The results show that OntoPlot excels in all examined tasks. Additionally, case studies illustrating OntoPlot's application to the Biological Classification and Human Anatomy ontologies are presented, highlighting its real-world capabilities. Our tool is openly available for further examination and development at https://onto.plot.app. Furthermore, a short video demonstrating OntoPlot can be found at https://shorty.mccolgan.ca/onto-plot. As part of our future research, OntoPlot will continue to evolve to support domain-specific features. This research aims to contribute to visualisation systems designed for vast ontologies by addressing current limitations. By answering which class a particular entity belongs to, OntoPlot's classification capability is also explored. Initial evidence indicates that it classifies entities with accuracy levels above 90%. Our vision for OntoPlot is that it will eventually offer near-perfect classification, accompanied by automated explanations for its classifications. These explanations can be seen as a form of X-ray imaging for ontologies, revealing the underlying reasoning behind a class's assignment. By integrating OntoPlot and a large-scale classifier, we aim to bring ontologies and domain-specific AI systems closer together. Ultimately, we aim to develop a universal translator bridging the gap between domain-specific AI and ontologies, enabling domain experts to leverage existing classified models and gain deeper insights into their networks. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, based on limited sensory data, and it uses this framework to guide surrounding environment exploration. Although this theory has successfully explained various aspects of human cognition, its applications to other species have been limited. Dogs are highly adept at understanding human behavior and have become integral companions, making them an excellent subject for studying how animals interact with their environments. This paper uses active inference principles to create a mental dog model and simulates its learning how to open different types of containers. Simulated sensory data are used to train the mental dog model, and once learned, the model is used to simulate the dog's problem-solving approach when presented with new, unseen containers. Results show that dogs trained in this way would likely be capable of opening various containers, including novel ones, and that their learning capabilities correlate with the complexity of their surrounding environment. Lastly, an analysis of the energy costs associated with this mental dog model reveals that its learning how to infer the state of its surroundings incurs significant energy expenses, and that these costs vary depending on the complexity of its surroundings. These investment costs could potentially serve as a metric to assess the sustainability of the solutions that animals (and robots) find to their environmental challenges, and they raise an intriguing question: what solutions do animals find, and how do these compare with the high-energy costs associated with using active inference? This paper proposes that a combination of low-energy solutions, such as using pre-learned templates, may help reduce these costs and increase the conditions under which active inference is applicable. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an efficient box re-ranking problem without the need for manual annotation.  A secondary challenge in box re-ranking arises from the absence of labeled validation data, which is why we introduced the self-supervised evaluation metric, box number alignment, to prevent over-specialization in the model and preserve true positive detection accuracy.  Our approach is supported by comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, including general benchmarks for unsupervised domain adaptive object detection.  The code and model will be made publicly available. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study, featuring a 360-degree view of a virtual environment with a floating ball, revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws when the point of release occurs earlier, as opposed to later in the motion, whereas underarm throws with a point of release occurring later in the motion tend to reveal errors more easily. Furthermore, viewers took less time to identify errors in the case of an underarm throw with a point of release occurring later in the motion. Building on these findings, we developed a predictive model that leverages the timing of the point of release in conjunction with the velocity of the ball to accurately classify the throwing style. When tested, this velocity-and-release-time (VnRt) model exhibited superior performance, achieving a high classification accuracy of 92%, including for styles previously untested during the data collection phase. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation, a novel NMT architecture, dubbed Seq2DAE, is introduced. Designed to utilize syntax trees generated by a parameterized pre-trained parser, Seq2DAE employs district representations constructed without word embeddings, facilitating increased adaptability. Results demonstrate that Seq2DAE achieves a significant 1.0-1.7 WMD improvement over a state-of-the-art NMT baseline across three language pairs when incorporating syntax trees from models fine-tuned on translation tasks, outperforming NMTs processed with dependency parses. Additionally, Seq2DAE exhibits a notable 0.3-0.8 WMD better performance over previously proposed syntax-aware NMT architectures. Experiments further indicate that the quality of syntax trees generated by the parser impacts the performance of Seq2DAE, with the ones fine-tuned on translation tasks yielding the best results; consequently, a novel parser ensemble is proposed to attain these outcomes. As syntax trees are discrete and not differentiable, a new compatibility loss is designed to train the parser in an unsupervised setting. An in-depth analysis of Seq2DAE demonstrates that the use of constituency parses, as opposed to dependency parses, enhances decoding coherence, whereas the proposed parser's ability to generate diverse syntax trees aids in alleviating overfitting. Moreover, the results suggest that the proposed method can be used to improve the translation of rare words. Finally, the results of human assessments validate the improved quality of the translations produced by Seq2DAE. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures of ligands found in interstellar molecules. We conducted a comprehensive analysis focusing on water cluster interactions with 23 distinct monomer types, which encompassed ligands seen in oxygen-rich interstellar molecules such as CO, CO2, and O2. Utilizing the quantum diffusion Monte Carlo approach, we determined the binding energies of the observed water-monomer complexes, obtaining results that mostly aligned with existing experimental and theoretical findings. However, our study also revealed a notable discrepancy with some published theoretical results. With our optimized binding energy values incorporated into the DALILab model, we used this updated model to simulate the formation of oxygen-rich molecules in three cajohn star interstellar spectra. The analysis of Cepheus A, the C14041 interstellar spectrum, and Sgr B2(N) produced results that matched observed astromolecular lines in most cases. Notably, we found that the estimated binding energies led to significantly better model fits in comparison to previously used values. While our approach did not fully match the observed astromolecular lines in all instances, it demonstrated the importance of accurately setting monomer binding energies in the model. Future work will focus on refining the model to better predict interstellar molecule structures. A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its statistical properties, is analytically determined. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment. Subsequently, the associated statistical properties are calculated numerically, demonstrating that the distribution exhibits a pronounced asymmetry and substantial statistical dispersion for typical values of the parameters. Additionally, the distribution shows pronounced substantial deviations from the normal distribution during the initial stages of the process and tends towards normality in the later stages. This theoretical model is found to effectively describe the distribution of sizes of the largest clusters in a ferromagnetic Ising model during the initial stages of ordering and, with adjustments of the distribution parameters, also accounts for differences in observed size distributions. This application highlights the utility and versatility of the multiplicative stochastic process model for analyzing various experimental and simulation results. Various potential fields where application of this model could be expanded are briefly mentioned. Moreover, the numerical results obtained for the distribution's statistical properties could serve as a basis for generating random number generators, where the developed model might find use as a preliminary step towards a more complex probabilistic model of the sizes of arbitrarily large objects. In conclusion, the developed model offers a simple, effective, and versatile tool capable of accurately describing size distributions of large objects that exhibit multiplicative stochastic growth. This model can be readily applied across various fields due to its universal nature. Further research could involve investigating the applicability of different probability distributions as lower bounds in the multiplicative stochastic process model. Further potential areas of application of the developed model have been briefly described in the conclusion section. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data. This restriction leads to the concept of "sibylvariance" - a phenomenon where multiple models utilizing the same transformation technique demonstrate comparable, if not identical, performance on downstream tasks. In our investigation, we aim to uncover the causes behind this limitation by examining two widely employed text manipulation methods - masking and replacement. Building upon the principle of latent variable mixture models, we developed an innovative masking approach, RLM, which dynamically determines the probability of each word to be masked. Furthermore, we designed a clustering model to automatically group words for replacement. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithms are superior to existing alternatives. Interestingly, an analysis of the symbiotic properties of our models revealed a striking observation: we found a word clustering model possessed intrinsic sybilline properties. This discovery led us to propose a new perspective on sybillance - as a characteristic inherent to certain text manipulation techniques themselves. Ultimately, we established that input-driven transformations are not always essential for achieving better performance on tasks like NLP. In some cases, using output-driven methods can lead to improved results. In conclusion, we outline key principles for developing text manipulation techniques that can expand the scope of input data. In pursuit of this objective, we present an innovative strategy for developing a semantic text forgetting method. The technique holds several key advantages. Firstly, it enables a model to deliberately disregard human-provided incorrect labels. Secondly, it allows the model to adapt to new domains by systematically eliminating irrelevant information. Lastly, it has the capability to systematically eliminate redundant generated texts. In line with our previously outlined vision of text manipulation, our proposed forgetting method marks an important milestone in the field - the ability to deliberately eliminate human or external sources of guidance for the model to operate more independently. The problem of text forgetting poses a significant challenge due to the complex nature of text data, encompassing semantic and surface-level aspects. In contrast, traditional data forgetting studies have primarily focused on surface-level changes. To address this challenge, we employed a novel approach based on sentence embeddings, incorporating their inherent semantic attributes. Through the application of sentence2vec, a method that separates surface-level and semantic aspects, we ensured that our forgetting approach operates on multiple levels. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features. Our results reveal that reweighting task-specific data based on predicted feature correlations is sufficient for successful transfer, and we establish precise bounds on the topological entropy in finite sample scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that task-specific linear regression can be an optimal learning outcome. Lastly, we extend our findings to a more complex noise model, allowing the samples' influence to vary. Our study provides the first theoretical analysis of a variety of meta-learning techniques, including data reweighting, linear regression, and generalized linear functions. Our methods apply equally well to classification tasks that share a linear feature set. This research marks a significant advancement in understanding the underlying principles of meta-learning. Moreover, our study confirms the effectiveness of the ZooKeeper algorithm proposed by Chen et al. (2018) in specific circumstances. To confirm our theoretical findings, we present experiments showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed methods. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create more compact, efficient models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining its effectiveness in a replicable setting. In a further effort, it explores the potential for improving distillation through pre-training, an often-overlooked area in MT. By analyzing various factors, such as teacher-student model configurations and training data, it evaluates their impact on model compression performance and translates it into a novel task, distillation-based training, which demonstrates a more than 1.5 WMD improvement in the FOMO dataset. Notably, these improvements come at a cost of less than double the computational expense compared to the original multilingual training, making this advancement more feasible in practical applications. All associated resources, including our code and data, are made publicly available. Additionally, this work contributes new compact MT models for under-resourced languages, specifically Japanese, Inuktitut, and Javanese, which yields relatively high scores on the WMT19 Japanese-English and JFLL datasets. Lastly, recommendations for future research avenues are proposed, focusing on developing effective distillation-based training methods. Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to specific requirements in terms of content and style. This study focuses on the challenge of adapting an image captioning model to produce captions in various styles, such as describing scenes, characters' emotions, or relationships between objects. We propose a multi-task learning framework called Stylish Image Captioning (SIC), incorporating auxiliary objectives to force the model to incorporate relevant information into generated captions. This is achieved by drawing words from a source caption and reordering them based on linguistic criteria, such as part-of-speech, syntactic category, or semantic meaning. The SIC framework can produce captions in different styles by simply swapping source captions. Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our SIC framework is capable of adapting an image captioning model to various styles effectively and easily extending the model to new styles is feasible. The code and model weights are publicly available on GitHub. This research also includes a thorough investigation into the effectiveness of pre-trained Language Models (LLMs) on image captioning, revealing they have limited utility in conventional co-training pipelines. To the best of our knowledge, this study pioneers the application of LLMs in image captioning under style adaptation constraints. The research further includes analysis of why LLMs were not more effective than expected in this context. Additionally, our SIC framework is capable of generating captions in new, unseen styles not present in the training data. This study also showcases the versatility of the SIC framework by applying it to the task of tailored summarization, yielding a model that produces concise, style-based image summaries. The research further includes analysis of the incorporation of vision-and-language models that excel in zero-shot learning tasks as potential substitutes for GPT-2 in stylish image captioning under style adaptation constraints.
